This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain<gloss>Works whose legal copyright term has ended or that were never subject to copyright, making them free for public use.</gloss></term>. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia present in the original volume will appear in this file <note>This refers to the handwritten notes often found in the margins of ancient manuscripts, which the scanners have taken care to preserve.</note> - a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

### Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their <term>custodians<gloss>Guardians or caretakers of a collection, rather than owners.</gloss></term>. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on <term>machine translation<gloss>The use of software to translate text or speech from one language to another.</gloss></term>, <term>optical character recognition<gloss>OCR: the electronic conversion of images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text.</gloss></term> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can't offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

### About Google Book Search

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. You can search through the full text of this book on the web at http://books.google.com/

<meta>This page continues the specific instructions for the ritual offerings. The previous page ended with the distribution of the grain offerings among the priests. # THE LAW OF THE LEVITES (LEVITICUS)

፲፩ It shall be holy for the holy ones from the sacrifices of the Lord. Every offering that you bring to the Lord shall not be made with **leaven**; for you shall not bring any leaven or any honey into an offering made by fire to the Lord for an offering. 

፲፪ However, for the **tithes** <note>original: "‘asĕrāt" — refers to the tenth part or firstfruits</note>, you may bring them to the Lord; but they shall not be offered upon the altar for a sweet aroma to the Lord. 

፲፫ And every offering of your sacrifice shall be made with **salt**; you shall not let the salt be missing from what you sacrifice to the Lord; in all your offerings you shall offer salt. 

፲፬ And if you bring a sacrifice of your firstfruits to the Lord, you shall bring parched, crushed, and ground grain of your firstfruits as a sacrifice. 

፲፭ And you shall pour oil upon it and 
፲፭ put frankincense upon it; it is a sacrifice. 

፲፮ And the **priest** <term>kahǝn</term> shall offer the memorial portion of that grain, together with its oil and all its frankincense; 
፲፯ it is a sacrifice to the Lord.

### CHAPTER 3

And if his offering is a **sacrifice of salvation** <term>peace offering</term> <note>original: "madḫānit" — meaning salvation, healing, or well-being; the Ge'ez term for the Hebrew Shelamim</note> to the Lord, if he brings it from the herd, whether it be male or female, he shall bring it without blemish before the Lord. 

፪ And he shall lay his hand upon the head of his offering and slaughter it at the door of the **Tabernacle of the Covenant** <note>original: "dabtarā za-marṭul" — the tent of the sanctuary</note>, and the **sons of Aaron** <term>deqiqa Aron</term>, the priests, shall pour the blood upon the altar. 

፫ And they shall bring from the sacrifice of salvation an offering to the Lord: the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is within the 

፬ belly, and the two kidneys and the fat that is upon them, which is on the flanks, and the smaller lobe of the liver which he shall remove with the kidneys.

<margin>5</margin> The rock hyrax <term>ṣē</term> <note>original: "ፄ"; often identified as the coney or rock badger</note>, because its hoof is not split; this is unclean to you. <margin>6</margin> And the hare <term>birgrəgliyos</term> <note>original: "ወቢርግርግሊዮስ"; a transliteration likely derived from the Greek word for a rabbit or rock-badger, though usually identifying the hare</note>, because it chews the cud but its hoof is not split; it is also unclean to you. <margin>7</margin> And the pig <term>waḥawya</term>, because it has a split hoof and its claws are divided, but it does not chew the cud; it is also <margin>8</margin> unclean to you. You shall not eat of their flesh and you shall not touch their carcasses <term>babannomu</term> <note>literally "their dead bodies"</note>, for they are unclean to you.

<margin>9</margin> And these are what you may eat of everything that is in the water: everything that has fins <term>kənf</term> <note>literally "wings"</note> and scales <term>qʷəśara</term> that is in the water, in the seas, and in the rivers—these you may eat. <margin>10</margin> But everything that does not have fins and scales in the water, in the seas, and in the rivers, among all that swarm in the waters and among every living soul that is in the water, it is detestable. <margin>11</margin> And they shall be detestable to you; you shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall abhor their carcasses. <margin>12</margin> Everything in the water that does not have fins and scales is unclean to you.

<margin>13</margin> And these are what you shall detest among the birds <term>a‘ʷāf</term>; they shall not be eaten, for they are detestable: the eagle <term>nəsr</term>, the bearded vulture <term>garēdā</term>, the osprey <term>alyāṭon</term>, <margin>14</margin> the kite <term>nīdā</term>, the falcon <term>galilāwyān</term>, the vulture <term>habay</term> and everything after its kind, <margin>15</margin> the raven <term>qʷəḥā</term> and everything after its kind, <margin>16</margin> the ostrich <term>sanaga</term> and everything after its kind, the owl <term>farḥā</term> and its kind, the seagull <term>ṣagudā</term> and its kind, the hawk <term>ṣagugā</term> and its kind, <margin>17</margin> the little owl <term>qaṭaraqʷəṭēn</term>, the cormorant <term>abun</term>, the ibis <term>arfāryānā</term>, the water hen <term>ayāg marāb</term>, <margin>18</margin> the pelican <term>qaqanon</term>, the carrion vulture <term>faryoyon</term>, the stork <term>barāyryon</term> and what is like it, the heron <term>aṗāṗā</term>, <margin>19</margin> the hoopoe <term>hənot</term>, and the bat.

<margin>20</margin> And all swarming birds that walk on four legs are detestable to you. <margin>21</margin> But these you may eat among the swarming birds that walk on four: those that have jointed legs <term>agayā</term> above their feet with which to hop upon the earth. <margin>22</margin> And these are what you may eat of them: the migratory locust <term>dagabīqā</term> and its kind, the solham locust <term>aṭāqān</term> and its kind, the hargol locust <term>afāyosākn</term> and its kind, and the grasshopper <term>anbaṭā</term> and its kind. <margin>23</margin> But all other winged things that have four feet are detestable to you. <margin>24</margin> And by these you shall become unclean: anyone who touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening. <margin>25</margin> And anyone who carries their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening.

**2** And the Lord spoke to him, saying: "Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: 'When you enter the land that I am giving to you, the land <insert>land</insert> that I am giving to you shall observe a Sabbath <note>original: "ታሰንብት" (tasänbət); a verb meaning to keep a day of rest</note> for the **3** Lord. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather its **4** fruit. But in the seventh year, it is a Sabbath of rest <note>original: "ሰንበተ ዕረፍት" (sänbätä ‘əräft); a period of total cessation from agricultural work</note> for the land; it shall be a Sabbath for the Lord. You shall not sow your field, and you shall not **5** prune your vineyard. And that which grows of its own accord in your field, you shall not harvest, and the clusters of the dedicated <note>original: "ዘቀደስ" (zä-qädäs); referring to vines that were left "untrimmed" or "consecrated" during the rest year</note> grapes you shall not pick during this year, because it is a **6** rest for the land. And the Sabbath of the land shall be food for you: for you, for your male servant, for your female servant, for your hired worker, **7** and for the stranger who dwells with you. And for your cattle and for the wild beasts of your land—all its produce shall be for food.

**8** And you shall count for yourselves seven Sabbaths of seven years, which is seven times seven years. And from this, you shall make for yourself fifty weeks <note>The Ge'ez "ሰናብተ" (sänabtä) here refers to the "Sabbaths" or "weeks of years" leading to the Jubilee</note> by which you shall announce with a trumpet **9** throughout all your land. Every forty-nine years, in the seventh month, on the tenth day of atonement <term>atonement<gloss>Ge'ez: "አስተስርዮ" (astäsər-yo); referring to Yom Kippur, the day of ritual cleansing and forgiveness</gloss></term>, you shall announce with a trumpet throughout all **10** your land. In proportion to the number of those years, he shall increase the price of the property; and if the years are few, he shall **17** decrease the purchase price, because it is the number of crop-years he is selling to you. And do not [wrong one another]..."

<meta>This page continues from the instructions given to Moses regarding the tribal leaders of Israel. The previous page concluded with the measurements for the Levite cities. ->### THE BOOK OF NUMBERS ###<-

<margin>13</margin> And the cities which you shall give, six shall be your cities of refuge <note>original: "ምስካይ" (meskay). These were specific cities where a person who killed someone accidentally could find safety from legal or personal retaliation.</note>. <margin>14</margin> Three cities you shall set apart across the **Jordan** <note>original: "ዮርዳኖስ" (Yordanos)</note>, and three cities you shall set apart in the land of **Canaan** <note>original: "ከናአን" (Kena'an)</note>; they shall be your cities of refuge. <margin>15</margin> For the children of **Israel** <note>original: "እስራኤል" (Israel)</note>, for the stranger <note>original: "ገያር" (geyar), referring to a resident alien</note>, and for the foreigner <note>original: "ፋላሲ" (falasi), referring to a traveler or exile</note> who is among you; these cities shall be a refuge for you, so that everyone who kills a person <note>original: "መንፈሰ" (menfesa), literally "a soul" or "a spirit"</note> unintentionally may flee there.

<margin>16</margin> But if he struck him with an iron tool <note>original: "ንዋየ፡ ሐዊን" (nwaye hawin)</note> and he died, he is a murderer <note>original: "ቀታሊ" (qetali)</note>; the murderer shall surely be put to death. <margin>17</margin> And if he threw a stone from his hand at him, or if it fell upon him and he died, he is a murderer; the murderer shall surely be put to death. <margin>18</margin> And if he struck him with a wooden tool and he died, or it fell upon him from his hand and he died, he is a murderer; the murderer shall surely be put to death. <margin>19</margin> The avenger of blood <note>original: "አበ፡ ደም" (aba dam), literally "father of blood." This refers to the relative of the deceased who had the legal right to seek justice.</note> shall himself kill the murderer.

<margin>20</margin> And if he pushed him out of hatred, or threw something at him while lying in wait so that he died; <margin>21</margin> [or] if he struck him in enmity with his hand so that he died, the one who struck him shall be put to death, for he is a murderer. The avenger of blood shall kill the murderer whenever he finds him.

<margin>22</margin> But if it was a sudden accident while he did not hate him, and he threw something at him without lying in wait; <margin>23</margin> or if it was a stone by which one could die, and it struck him unintentionally, and he was not his enemy and did not seek to do him harm; <margin>24</margin> then the assembly <note>original: "ትዕይንት" (te'yent), meaning the congregation or the camp community</note> shall judge between the killer and the avenger of blood according to this judgment <note>original: "ፍትሕ" (feth)</note>. <margin>25</margin> And the assembly shall deliver the killer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the assembly shall take him to the city of refuge where he fled; and he shall live there until the death of the High Priest <note>original: "ካህን፡ ዓቢይ" (kahan abiy)</note> who was anointed with the holy oil.

<margin>26</margin> But if the killer goes outside the borders of the city where he sought refuge; <margin>27</margin> and the avenger of blood finds him outside the borders of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the killer, he shall have no guilt. <margin>28</margin> For he should have stayed in his city of refuge until the death of the High Priest; but after the death of the High Priest, the killer may return to the land of his inheritance. <margin>29</margin> And this shall be a statute of judgment for you throughout your days in all your regions. <margin>30</margin> Anyone who kills a person, the murderer shall be killed upon the testimony of witnesses; but by the testimony of only one person, they shall not find the fault of the one who killed.

### Chapter 9
<margin>1</margin> Now Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal, went to **Shechem** <note>original: "Sĕqimā"</note> to his mother's brothers, and spoke with them and with the entire family of his mother's house. <margin>2</margin> He said to them, "Speak, I pray you, in the hearing of the people of Shechem: 'Which is better for you: that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, rule over you, or that one man rules over you?' Remember also that **I am your own flesh and bone**."

<margin>3</margin> And his mother's brothers spoke all these words on his behalf in the hearing of all the people of Shechem; and their hearts were inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother." <margin>4</margin> And they gave him **seventy pieces of silver** from the house of **Baal** <note>specifically from the temple of Baal-Berith</note>, with which Abimelech hired **reckless and headstrong men** <note>original: "ḥaqālyāna wa-madangḍāna"—describes men who were idle, frivolous, and easily terrified or prone to causing terror</note>, and they followed him.

<margin>5</margin> Then he went to his father's house at **Ophrah** <note>original: "Efrēm"—the OCR likely reflects a scribal variation or regional spelling</note> and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, upon a single stone. But **Jotham** <note>original: "Iy'atām"</note>, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, remained, because he hid himself.

<margin>6</margin> Then all the people of Shechem and all the house of **Millo** <note>original: "Malon"</note> gathered together, and they went and made Abimelech king by the **oak of the pillar** <note>original: "ʿeḍa balāno"—referring to a sacred tree</note> that was in Shechem.

<margin>7</margin> When they told Jotham, he went and stood on the top of **Mount Gerizim** <note>original: "Dabra Gārizēn"</note>, and lifted up his voice and cried out, saying to them: "Listen to me, you people of Shechem, so that God may listen to you!

<margin>8</margin> Once the trees went out to anoint a king over them. They said to the **olive tree**, 'Reign over us.' <margin>9</margin> But the olive tree said to them, 'Should I leave my fatness, by which God and men are honored, and go to hold sway over the trees?'

<margin>10</margin> Then the trees said to the **fig tree**, 'Come, you, and reign over us.' <margin>11</margin> But the fig tree said to them, 'Should I leave my sweetness and my good fruit [P] <note>the [P] in the OCR likely marks a page or paragraph break in the original manuscript</note> and go to hold sway over the trees?'

<margin>12</margin> Then the trees said to the **vine**, 'Come, you, and reign over us.'"

# THE BOOK OF RUTH

### CHAPTER 1

**1** And it happened in the days when the judges ruled, that a famine came upon the land. And a certain man from Bethlehem-Judah <note>original: "Bēta Lḥēm za-Yihudā," literally 'House of Bread of Judah'</note> went to dwell in the fields of Moab—he, and his wife, and his children. **2** The name of that man was Abimelech <note>original: "Abēmēlēk." In standard English Bibles, this is Elimelech; the Ge'ez transcription often uses the name Abimelech for this character</note>, and the name of his wife was Naomi, and the names of his two children were Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem-Judah. And they came into the fields of Moab and remained there. **3** And Abimelech, the husband of Naomi, died; and she was left with her two children. **4** And they took for themselves Moabite wives; the name of the first was Orpah and the name of the second was Ruth. And they lived there for about ten years. **5** And both of them died—Mahlon and Chilion—and the woman was left without her husband and her two children.

**6** Then she arose with both her daughters-in-law <note>original: "marāḥuṣāhā," referring to the wives of her sons</note> and returned from the fields of Moab, for she had heard that the Lord had visited His people to give them bread <note>original: "ekla," which can mean grain, food, or specifically wheat</note>. **7** And she went out from that place where she was living, and both her daughters-in-law were with her; and they went on the way to return to the land of Judah. **8** And Naomi said to both her daughters-in-law, "Go, return each to the house of your mother. May the Lord deal kindly with you as you have dealt with those who died and with me. **9** May the Lord grant that you find rest, each in the house of her husband." And she kissed them, and they [lifted up their voices and wept].

# 1. Concerning the manuscripts from which this edition of the Pentateuch was drawn.

The number of Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> codices <note>Handwritten manuscript books.</note> that I used in preparing this edition is not very large, and I was neither able nor willing to examine and compare every manuscript copy of the Pentateuch that exists in Europe. Regarding that famous Octateuch <note>original: "Octateucho"; the first eight books of the Old Testament, which in the Ethiopic tradition are often grouped together.</note> which Ethiopic monks kept in their hospice in Rome during the time of J. Ludolf <note>Job Ludolf (1624–1704), a German scholar considered the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe.</note> and which J. M. Wansleben <note>Johann Michael Wansleben (1635–1679), a traveler and linguist.</note> once described in that same place, I do not even know for certain where it might be hidden now. Certainly, I strongly doubt the assertion made by J. Ludolf in the *Commentary to his History of Ethiopia* (p. 299) that it was deposited in the Vatican Library, especially since Angelo Mai <note>An influential Italian cardinal and philologist known for recovering lost classical texts.</note> mentioned nothing of it in his *New Collection of Ancient Writers*, Vol. V, p. 94 ff.

Moreover, I would have been permitted to transcribe Wansleben's transcript—which later became the property of Louis Piques, a most famous Doctor of the Sorbonne, and finally moved to the French Imperial Library in Paris—as well as that Genesis from the Séguier Library <note>A significant collection of manuscripts formed by Chancellor Pierre Séguier.</note> (already known to J. Ludolf and now stored in the same place) during the time I stayed in Paris. However, when I learned that a certain copy derived from that Wansleben manuscript existed in Halle, Saxony, and that it was adorned with various readings from the Séguier Genesis, I chose to forgo the comparison of the Parisian books. Instead, I preferred to consult the Halle manuscript, which I hoped—not in vain—would be sent to me at Tübingen through the liberal permission of the Minister of the King of Prussia and the exceptional kindness of the head librarian at Halle.

Finally, I also deeply regret that I was unable to use for my own purposes those copies of the Bible which certain distinguished French travelers have brought back from Abyssinia <note>The historical name for Ethiopia.</note> in these last years, among which we have heard a Pentateuch is included. However, no opportunity has yet been given to me to add new expenses to those I spent on my work six or seven years ago, nor to travel to Paris again. For this reason, I was reluctantly forced to prepare this edition content with the four books to which I had open access. 

But although I frankly confess I would have examined more codices if I could have, I should not remain silent on this: it was not even my desire to compare all the books that exist, and I believe the gain I could have drawn from a comparison of many would not have been so great. I could certainly have accumulated a much larger abundance of variant readings <note>Differences in wording or spelling found between different manuscript copies of the same text.</note> collected from more books, but I do not know what the use of such a heap would be; indeed, I even disdained to transcribe all the readings from those four books into this Critical Apparatus <note>original: "Apparatu critico"; the organized system of notes at the bottom of a page that documents variations in the text.</note>. But what the most important...

--- Page 506 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's introduction to his critical edition of the Ethiopic Bible. Having previously discussed the scarcity of available manuscripts, he now defines his editorial goals and begins a detailed physical and textual description of the primary manuscript used for this work, referred to as Codex F.</meta>

The goal I set for myself in this edition was to present the genuine and ancient Ethiopic <note>original: "Aethiopis"</note> version, and to investigate and explain the corruptions and corrections it had undergone since ancient times. Although I was equipped with only a few resources, I believe I have achieved this so well that even if I had used many more books, I could hardly have succeeded much better. Indeed, the resources for our edition are such that one can extract from them not only the text of the ancient version—as it was considered best and most accurate during a certain era of the Abyssinian <note>original: "Abyssinicae"; an older term for Ethiopian.</note> church—but also another corrected recension <note>A specific version of a text that has been revised or edited.</note> of the same. This now seems to require a more detailed description.

Of the four books I possessed, that most excellent book far exceeds the others in age, authority, and quality; *it is now preserved in London in the Library of the Society established for the propagation of the Holy Bible in Britain and among foreign nations <note>The British and Foreign Bible Society.</note> and shall be designated by the sign F in this <term>Critical Apparatus</term> <note>The organized system of notations and footnotes that document variations in different manuscript versions of a text.</note>.* It is a vellum codex <note>A manuscript book made of parchment or animal skin.</note> in a large octavo format, comprising 286 leaves, where each page is divided into two columns. It is elegantly and diligently written in older capital letters and contains the Octateuch <note>The first eight books of the Old Testament: the five books of Moses plus Joshua, Judges, and Ruth.</note>, following a custom very common among the Ethiopians as it was among the Greeks, of transcribing and binding the books of Joshua, Judges, and Ruth together with the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> into a single volume. The seventh and eighth leaves are paper, written by a different hand and substituted for the ones originally held there; these offer a quite corrupted text (Genesis 4:15—6:11). No division of the text was made in this book, except that the <term>pericopes</term> <note>Set portions of scripture appointed to be read during church services.</note> to be read in church are noted in the margin; for the most part, the scribe began new lines only after completing individual sentences or larger sections of the text. However, what the scribe omitted, a certain European who examined the codex compensated for, writing the chapter and verse numbers for each book of the Octateuch in the margin using European numerals. Various illustrations, painted without any great skill by some unknown Ethiopian, are also found on the blank pages of the leaves ¹). Evidence of the diligence with which the scribes and owners of this volume worked to establish the genuine text of the ancient version is found in the fact that in various places—most notably in Genesis—the text has been corrected and restored to its original state as much as possible, either by erasing certain letters and words or by writing in better readings in the margins, between lines, or in place of erased words. It appears that the scribes and owners performed the duties of critics by comparing various manuscripts. But there are also other, more significant signs, which even those who—

<meta>This page continues the author's argument for the importance of Codex F. He focuses on the physical script and linguistic patterns that indicate the manuscript's extreme age, even before comparing it to the Greek Septuagint.</meta>

Even before comparing the text of this book with the Greek Septuagint <note>original: "graeco septuagintavirali"; the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, certain features can lead one to presume a favorable opinion of its authority. For although no date of transcription was recorded within it, the larger form of the letters and the somewhat monumental <note>original: "lapidarius"; literally "stone-cutter style," referring to a formal, square script found on inscriptions.</note> style of writing suggest great antiquity. Furthermore, various archaisms <note>Ancient forms of language that have fallen out of common use.</note> in the spelling of words and in the formation and pronunciation of certain nouns and verbs reveal and confirm this age. 

The lengthening of the **short A** vowel before stationary gutturals <note>Consonants pronounced in the throat, such as 'h' or 'ah'.</note> (of the sixth order <note>In the Ge'ez script, the "sixth order" refers to a consonant with a neutral or absent vowel.</note>) is very frequently—and in some words almost constantly—omitted (for example: **ምአበለ፡**, **ምሕሥአ፡**, **ሰአር፡**, **አት፡**, **ተሀባር፡**, and others). The prefix letters of the Imperfect tense, **ይ** (y), **ት** (t), and **ን** (n), are retained in the sixth order even before gutturals provided with a short A vowel (the first order) (for example: **ይሀበ፡**, **ይኑበአ፡**, **ይሐውረ፡**, and others). Before mobile consonants **የ** (y) or **ወ** (w), the vowels I or U (third or second orders) are preserved almost everywhere and are not changed into sixth-order vowels (namely **ርአየ፡**, **ይሀበዮ፡**, **ይሰቅየ፡**, **አበየዮ፡**, **አንስትዮ፡**, **ገበርኩዎ፡**, **ገበርክሙዎ፡**, **ሰሰቡዎ፡**, etc.); this spelling better represents the older pronunciation. In certain verbs where the middle letter is **ወ** (w), particularly the verb **ሖረ፡** (to go), the subjunctive and imperative moods are formed with the vowel O rather than U (**ይሖር፡**, **ይሖሩ፡**, **ሖር፡**, **ሖሩ፡**, etc.). 

One may also observe various other archaisms of writing and pronunciation throughout the text which you would seek in vain in more recent manuscripts. For example: **ተፋሥሕት፡** (rejoicing) in Genesis 31:27 and **ተወልደ፡** (was born) almost everywhere (though also **ተልደ፡** instead of **ትወልደ፡** in Genesis 15:2); **እግዚአ፡ብሔር፡** (Lord of the Land/God), written as two words, not joined as **እግዚአብሔር፡** like in all recent manuscripts; **አፋአ፡** (outside) rather than the modern **አፋእ፡**; and **ሀየተ፡** (instead of) almost everywhere instead of the more recent **ሀየንተ፡**. In certain prepositions that end in a short A sound, the longer and firmer E sound—which is usually resumed only when pronouns are attached—is sometimes preserved (for example: **ሀየቴ፡** in Gen. 47:19; **ሀየንቴዘ፡** in Gen. 44:33; **እስኬ፡** in Gen. 35:20; **እምኔ፡** in Lev. 20:5; although that E is often missing even before suffixes in prepositions, such as **ምአበለኒ፡** often appearing for **ምእበሌኒ፡**, and so on). The preposition **እምኔ፡** (from/out of) occurs almost constantly in its full form, whereas in more recent codices <note>Handwritten books.</note> the shorter **እም፡** is substituted for it almost everywhere. 

Various other examples of this kind, which appear throughout, may be read in the synopsis of variant readings we have described. It also seems worth noting here that in our book, quite a few obsolete words—or those less common in more recent speech—have been preserved, rather than being replaced by more common ones. Furthermore, primitive verbal structures and more elegant formations of speech are more faithfully preserved than in more recent manuscripts, many examples of which you may find among the <term>variants</term> <note>Differences in wording or spelling between different manuscript versions of the same text.</note>. It follows that the codex is quite ancient, and thus the authority of the version it contains is highly recommended. I cannot, in truth, define the antiquity of the codex more accurately, though I believe that anyone who wishes to assign it five or six centuries <note>Dillmann is likely dating the manuscript to the 13th or 14th century.</note> of age would not wander far from the truth. Because of its age, and even its origin and the journey of the manuscript, the version of the text it contains is highly recommended. From the subscriptions <note>Notes or signatures at the end of a manuscript.</note> added at the end, from folio 283 onwards, it appears that it was written in Axum <note>The ancient capital and religious center of Ethiopia.</note>, the metropolis of the kingdom and the church, and was sent from there by a certain Isaac, its owner, to Jerusalem as a gift for the Abyssinians <note>A historical name for Ethiopians.</note> living in the Ethiopian hospice in Jerusalem. I would like you to take good note of both these facts: for we have reason to believe that excellent archetypal codices were once not lacking at Axum; and by its transfer to Palestine, this book was well protected from that corruption of the sacred text which, as the fortunes of Ethiopia declined over the centuries, crept more and more into the Old and New Testaments. 

These conjectures are proven by the examination of the text itself which the codex provides; for it appears that the text of our book approaches the Greek <note>original: "Graecum"; referring to the Septuagint.</note> very closely. Although it is itself defiled by various glosses <note>Explanatory notes or alternative readings added by later scribes.</note> and is not without many gaps, it is nevertheless free from the useless "corrections" of scribes and from the verbose emendations of more recent scholars. It represents the form of the text that was considered the best in Ethiopia five or six centuries ago. Indeed, you will not find any Ethiopic codices much older than this one. 

Exactly when and by whom this book was brought from Jerusalem to Europe, I have not discovered. However, since the subject matter of the book was written in Latin on the first leaf, and the date September 20, 1696, was added in the same place, it follows that the volume was transported before this year. I wonder whether this codex—just like that most famous book, the *Synodus* <note>A collection of ecclesiastical canons and laws.</note>, which Wansleben <note>Johann Michael Wansleben (1635–1679), a German traveler and orientalist.</note> once described in Rome and which is known to have traveled from Jerusalem to Rome—was itself once brought to the Ethiopian hospice in Rome. Various inscriptions made on the blank leaves of the codex, which reveal the Roman Catholic religion of the author, as well as the intimate relationship of this book with Wansleben’s copy, have given me a certain suspicion: whether this might be the very same codex that was held in Rome during the time of Ludolf <note>Hiob Ludolf (1624–1704), the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe.</note> and Wansleben. Because this suspicion moved me, I acted quite vigorously to find out where the British had acquired the book and brought it to London, but although I inquired again and again, no one gave me the answers I wished to know.

Closely connected by an intimate relationship to this most excellent book just described is another which we used in composing the text, now *preserved in the Library of the Frederick University of Halle in Saxony, and designated by us with the symbol* H. It is a paper codex in quarto format, comprising 202 leaves, and it contains the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy).</note> "formerly described from the copy of Louis Piques in Paris, and now from the transcript of Dr. Johann Heinrich Michaelis, Halle 1732." Now, since the copy of Louis Piques was formerly transcribed by Wansleben from a Roman codex, it follows that the Halle book is the great-grandson of the Roman father. Ludolf also used a transcript of this same Piquesian Pentateuch in composing his Ethiopic lexicon; and in the margin of our Codex H, annotations to the Ludolfian text are sometimes written in red, as well as to the book...

## Signature 2 *

Various readings of Genesis, which Dr. Piques once collected from the Seguierian Manuscript <note>A manuscript from the collection of Pierre Séguier, a 17th-century French chancellor.</note> and sent to Job Ludolf <note>A 17th-century German scholar, widely considered the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe.</note>, are recorded here as annotations. In this particular codex, many slips of the pen and errors by both readers and scribes are found, which are unlikely to have existed in the original Roman source <note>original: "autographo Romano"</note>. It is frequently very clear that the scribe misread and transcribed the original source-copy incorrectly (for example, the symbols <note>original: "sigla"</note> used to mark specific passages to be read aloud in church were often mistakenly inserted directly into the flow of the text). Furthermore, since the creators of these transcripts were learned men who had studied the Ge'ez <term>Ge'ez: The ancient liturgical and literary language of Ethiopia, similar in status to Latin in the West.</term> language according to grammatical rules, they seem to have "corrected" certain words according to their own talent and judgment—sometimes rightly, but often wrongly.

However, once these errors and attempts at emendation are set aside—which one can easily detect by comparing this book with other manuscripts—the remaining text of this book is wonderfully consistent with the text of Codex **F**. It is so similar to that codex, even in its use of archaisms <note>Ancient words or linguistic forms that had fallen out of general use.</note> and other unique characteristics, that in many places I could not help but suspect that the Wansleben manuscript <note>Codex H, brought to Europe by the traveler Johann Michael Wansleben.</note> was derived directly from **F** without any other middle-copy. 

But since I cannot confirm this suspicion with evidence taken from the history of Codex **F**, and because various readings occur in Codex **H** that must have been drawn from other sources, I prefer to adopt the opinion that Codex **F** and the original source of Codex **H** are joined by a very close kinship. I propose that they both represent the same ancient and genuine lineage of the text. For this reason, I have not neglected to record the readings from Codex **H**.

Two other manuscripts that I was able to consult differ significantly from this pair: the codices of **James Bruce** and **Eduard Rüppell**. While the first two manuscripts rendered the ancient version more faithfully, the text in this second pair appears significantly changed and corrected in many places. Both are more recent in age and were brought from Abyssinia <note>A historical name for Ethiopia.</note> to Europe within the last ninety years. **James Bruce's Pentateuch** <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, which he himself commissioned to be written in Abyssinia, is transcribed on large quarto-sized parchment sheets and bound into two volumes. The first volume contains Genesis and Exodus, and the second contains the remaining books; it is now kept in the Bodleian Library at Oxford $^1$); we have designated it with the symbol **G**. Like many books that European travelers in our own times have had written at their own expense by unskillful and careless Abyssinian scribes, this Pentateuch was transcribed with little care and with undue haste. Many words, and even entire sequences of verses, were omitted through the pure negligence of the scribes, most often due to *homoeoteleuton* <term>homoeoteleuton: A common scribal error where the eye skips from one word to another with a similar ending, resulting in the loss of the text in between.</term>. 

Better and freer from such scribal errors is the *Rüppell Codex*, now kept in the Frankfurt Public Library, which was purchased by **Eduard Rüppell** in Abyssinia. It was formerly the property of the Abuna <note>The title of the head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.</note> **Walda-Samuel**.

...and was given by him as a gift to the church of Father Samuel; I estimate it is no more than two centuries old. It is composed of 181 parchment leaves in a very large quarto size and is written neatly and accurately. It contains: 1) the Book of Enoch, 2) Job, 3) the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> pages 81–298, 4) the Book of Joshua, 5) Judges, 6) Ruth; we have designated it with the symbol **C**. The division of the text, which is already standard in Greek Bibles, is used and noted throughout the entire Pentateuch.

Let us now discuss the text contained in books **C** and **G**. While Codex **C** was written with great care and its accurate handwriting can to some extent be compared with Codex **F**, the text it contains does not represent an ancient and original version, but rather a version that has been changed and corrected in various ways. To make this clearer, let us distinguish three types of changes. 

1) First, in many places where the ancient version differed from the Greek Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, produced in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE.</note> because of the Hebrew text, or due to errors or liberties taken by the Ethiopian translators, our codex contains restored readings that more closely match either the Hebrew or the Greek text. Likewise, many—almost all—of the gaps <note>original: "lacunae"</note> that gradually appeared in copies of the ancient version, whether through the carelessness of scribes or the damage of time, have been filled in. It follows that this codex contains an emended <term>Emended: A text that has been "cleaned up" or corrected by a later editor to improve accuracy.</term> version. Regarding the time when this correction of the ancient version was undertaken, nothing is certain so far. However, which version or text the emendator followed in correcting the old version cannot be discussed more fully or extensively here; yet, having compared its readings with the Hebrew text and other versions, I have no doubt that he relied on the authority of a certain Greek Hexaplaric <term>Hexaplaric: Referring to the "Hexapla," a massive six-column edition of the Old Testament compiled by the early Christian scholar Origen to compare different translations.</term> manuscript. Very often he rejects the reading of the Septuagint and agrees with the Hebrew; nevertheless, there are places where he expresses readings found in Greek manuscripts against the Hebrew. From this, one correctly concludes that a Greek text—corrected from Origen’s Hexapla or other Greek recensions <note>Specific versions of a text that have been systematically edited.</note> that agree more with the Hebrew—was available to him. 

If anyone believes his corrections rely on the authority of a Syriac or Arabic-Hexaplaric manuscript (due to the interactions between the Ethiopians and Syrian or Arabic Christians), various passages discourage me from this opinion and seem to prove that the readings were derived directly from the Greek text without any other intermediate version. Thus, equipped with a Greek Hexaplaric edition, the emendator reviewed the ancient text and corrected individual passages that seemed poorly translated or corrupt to him; he even completely revised and re-translated several whole chapters of Exodus, although he seems to have left untouched quite a few passages where the version differs from the Hebrew or is tainted by omissions and glosses <note>Explanatory notes or comments written in the margins or between lines.</note>. This is the first and primary type of emendations found in Codex **C**. 

2) There is another type, concerning whose author—whether it is the same person or someone else, one person or many—it will be difficult to establish anything for certain; I am speaking of emendations concerning style...

and are related to the nature of the speech. For the ancient translator, since he very often wished to imitate the Greek archetype more accurately in the very structure of the words, in the use of the tenses and moods of the verb, as well as the particles and other things of this kind, was unable to achieve this without some damage to both the Ethiopian style and the consistency of the speech; then, he rendered the Greek meaning sometimes more briefly than was proper and sometimes with more words than necessary; he translated one and the same word differently in different places; occasionally, a certain ambiguity of meaning clung to the Ethiopian version, about which it would be difficult for someone who had no Greek text at hand to debate; finally, very many words and names, as well as types of connecting speech, pronunciation, and writing, which had passed into the codices from the ancient translator's copy, had become either obsolete or less common and understood in the later era of the Ethiopian language. 

You might find many such and similar things changed in Codex **C**: archaisms <term>Archaisms: Old-fashioned words or expressions no longer in common usage.</term> of every kind corrected according to the spirit <note>original: "genium"</note> of the later language; through the shifting, addition, and omission of words, names, and particles, better care was taken for the clarity of sense and the elegance and continuity of the speech; a certain consistency in translating individual words across various passages was restored; some things were added voluntarily for the sake of clarification. 

Nor was the slightest effort of the emenders placed on ensuring that the entire speech and individual words were more strictly brought back to grammatical rules, which had become sacred in a later age. For there is no doubt that the Ge'ez language in its older age—when it had barely begun to be committed to letters and used in writing books—was cruder and, as it were, untamed, and quite inconsistent in observing certain grammatical laws which later writers observe more accurately; consider, if you please, that remarkable inconsistency in observing the gender of nouns and the number of nouns and verbs. Therefore, a wide field <note>original: "provincia"</note> was open to emenders in this matter. 

However, do not believe that all the changes to the text just mentioned are truly emendations; you might more rightly call many of them corruptions. 

3) The third type of change proceeded from a certain irreverence on the part of either readers or scribes, who, being less religious than was proper, changed whatever they pleased according to their own wit and judgment: they inverted the order of words, substituted synonyms for words without any reason, exchanged tenses and moods, forms of nouns and verbs, prepositions and particles, and supplied others, and did not hesitate to interpolate glosses <term>Glosses: Explanatory notes or comments inserted into a text, often to explain a difficult word or provide a theological interpretation.</term> and illustrations of meaning into the text itself. 

Corruptions of this kind—of which more are found throughout all the books of the Bible transcribed in Ethiopia <note>original: "Abyssinia"</note> in these last centuries than in older copies—also occur in no small number in Codex **C**, although we must acknowledge a certain purity <note>original: "castitatem"</note> for its age. All the types of changes we have listed are also found in the Bruce Codex **G** <note>referring to James Bruce, the Scottish explorer who brought several Ethiopic manuscripts to Europe in the 18th century.</note>, but mixed in a different proportion than in **C**. You might rightly say that the text of the book is a mixture of the ancient and the corrected version. A second type of correction was applied in Manuscript **G** no less frequently than in **C**, with the result that **CG** very often offer the same readings, which differ from the readings of manuscripts **F** and **H**. However, a third type of change and corruption is much more widely scattered in this book than in **C**; from this, it is clear that Bruce’s Pentateuch <note>original: "Brucii Pentateuchum"; referring to James Bruce, the Scottish explorer who brought several Ethiopian manuscripts to Europe in the 18th century. The Pentateuch consists of the first five books of the Bible.</note> was copied from a quite corrupt manuscript by careless scribes (as we noted above). From what we have said, everyone will understand that a great difference in the text exists between **FH** and **CG**. Nevertheless, since the text of manuscripts **CG** is not based on a new translation but only on a correction of the ancient translation, the most significant part of the version has remained untouched even in them. From this it follows that their use in establishing and confirming the ancient and genuine text should not be despised by an editor; indeed, there are various places where a better and more ancient reading can be taken from **C** or **G**, or both, than can be found in **FH**.

Equipped with these resources, I could not hesitate as to how I should compose the text. Since I intended to publish the ancient version, reason itself demanded that I follow the text of manuscripts **F** and **H** as religiously as possible, and that I keep all corrections or corruptions of a later age as far removed as possible. But since I intended not only to satisfy scholars and critics <term>Philologists: Experts in the study of language, especially in historical and literary contexts.</term>, but also to ensure that the Ethiopians <note>original: "Abyssini"</note> themselves could put my edition to their own use, I could not entirely refrain from all corrections, and other reasons also led me to make emendations. First, in both **CG** and in **FH**, certain additions have been pushed in here and there which neither flowed from the Greek source nor were made by the translator himself, but gradually crept in among the Ethiopians and were copied down in ancient times along with the rest of the text. I did not attempt to reject or omit these entirely, but saw to it that they were printed and—unless they were too short and trivial—enclosed within parentheses ( ). Furthermore, although manuscript **F** and the original source of book **H** are most excellent and contain the older text, even they have not remained pure from various corruptions. In the text of **F** and **H**, many gaps <term>Lacunae: Sections of text missing from a manuscript due to physical damage or scribal error.</term> are found, several of which were likely made by the translator himself either for the sake of brevity or because of defects in his own Greek manuscript; however, it is probable that many more—the vast majority—arose from the negligence of scribes, damage to the leaves, or the fading of letters. The corrector of the Ethiopian version filled many of the most serious of these (though not all) from a Hexaplaric manuscript <term>Hexaplaric: Referring to Origen’s *Hexapla*, an ancient six-columned Bible that compared various Greek and Hebrew versions.</term>; following him, I also filled many gaps which I thought would be inconvenient or harmful for the church’s use of this edition from book **C** or **G**, but I have enclosed the words supplied from there in brackets [ ]. More rarely, especially in the lists of proper names where I was deprived of all manuscripts, I restored the defects myself, and I have marked the words restored by me with the signs \* \* or [\* \*]. But I am so far from having restored everything that is missing that I have not even included those supplements which **C** provides,

<meta>This page continues the editor's explanation of his methodology in reconstructing the ancient Ethiopian Bible text. He previously established that while manuscripts F and H represent an older tradition, they are often flawed, necessitating the use of the more "corrected" manuscripts C and G to ensure readability and accuracy.</meta>

...I have accepted everything. Furthermore, the text of manuscripts **F** and **H** is deformed even by certain false or less-than-ideal readings: not only are the signs or numerical names and proper names very often corrupted and distorted in a miserable way, but other words and sentences have also degenerated due to the damage of time and the errors <note>original: "sphalmate"; a term derived from Greek meaning a slip or mistake, often used by scholars to describe a scribe’s blunder.</note> of scribes. I have found a significant number of poor readings which, while the consonants remained intact, seem to have arisen only through a distorted reading of the vowels. This should not surprise you if you consider—as I could support with other arguments—that in the older era of this language <note>Referring to Ge'ez, the classical liturgical language of Ethiopia.</note>, vowel signs were not written with enough consistency.

Therefore, wherever corrupt passages could be repaired by a slight change, or where the distortion was such that it resulted in a nearly false or contradictory meaning, I restored the better reading from codex **C** or **G** <note>Codex: An ancient manuscript in book form.</note>. However, I have enclosed these in brackets **[ ]** unless my change was very minor. Everything that I have amended in this way is either indicated in the text itself by specific signs or recorded in the summary of variant readings.

Finally, regarding the corrections found in **C** and **G** pertaining to grammar and style: although I never went so far as to substitute a different word for an obsolete one, I did not wish to suppress in the printed type those archaisms <note>Ancient or outdated forms of language.</note> of pronunciation and spelling which I described above as unique to books **F** and **H**. I chose this path partly because in the later era of the Ethiopians <note>The people of the Abyssinian Empire.</note>, these forms were abolished almost everywhere and are unfamiliar to modern Abyssinians reading the Bible, and partly so that my edition of the Bible would not appear inconsistent; for I do not possess manuscripts of the other books of Holy Scripture from the same age that contain similar archaisms. I also did not think it necessary to point out such spelling changes to the reader with special signs. Beyond the amendments just mentioned, I made no others.

Wherever I rejected a reading from **FH** and followed codices **C** and **G**, I have indicated this with brackets. The only exception is in the writing of proper names—where not only do individual manuscripts differ from each other, but even the pages and individual lines of the same manuscript differ strangely and show great corruption of the original sound. In those cases, I changed much and frequently restored names to match the sound of Greek pronunciation; however, it would have been tedious and of no value to indicate every change of this kind with signs.

By using such emendations, I have attempted to make my edition more useful and accessible to the Abyssinians themselves. Now, so that critics might not be unaware of the readings from codices **F** and **H** that I rejected or replaced, I have noted nearly all of them—provided they are not obvious scribal errors—among the variant readings for each book of the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>. Likewise, since I considered the corrections from the <term>Hexaplaric</term> codex <note>The Hexapla was a massive edition of the Old Testament compiled by the scholar Origen, which compared different translations; it heavily influenced later biblical corrections.</note> to be worthy of critical attention, I have noted all amendments of this kind among the variants from **C** and **G** if they were not accepted into the main text, so that scholars may collect them. Finally, other corrections from codices **C** and **G** and, in general, the most important variants of the four individual books...

...but in the annotations I have listed those which seemed to me to possess some value for the use of philologists <note>Scholars who study the history of language and literary texts.</note> and critics. ## 2. Annotations on the individual books of the Pentateuch <note>The Pentateuch consists of the first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note>.

### A) Annotations on Genesis.

#### 1. Regarding the condition of the text edited by us, and the nature of the version.

While we delegate the more subtle investigation into the age, source, and authors of the Ethiopic version of the Old Testament to the *Prolegomena* <note>original: "Prolegomena"; a formal scholarly introduction or preliminary treatise.</note> of our entire work, let us now take it as granted and sufficiently well-known that this translation of the Bible flowed from a certain recension <note>A specific version or revision of a text.</note> of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often abbreviated as LXX.</note> which was read in the Alexandrian church after the age of Athanasius <note>Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD), the Bishop of Alexandria and a major figure in early Christian history.</note>. Let us discuss at greater length what may be revealed through the investigation of individual books regarding the condition and character of the Ethiopic version, the skill and knowledge of the Ethiopic translators, and the Greek archetype <note>The original source text from which a copy or translation is made.</note> of the text.

If you are to judge the character of the Ethiopic version, you must be careful not to believe that the text contained in the older manuscripts **F** and **H** is identical to the primary translator's own version down to every single letter and word. A long series of centuries indeed stands between the time of the translator and the oldest manuscripts we possess, and it would be quite marvelous if his version had been passed down to later generations entirely intact and whole. For my part, although I cannot admire enough how in many places—where the material itself seemed to allow for a slight correction—the genuine reading has been preserved most faithfully, I would nonetheless not deny that many corruptions have crept into the primary text. Therefore, before asserting anything regarding the character of the version, I believed the condition of the text had to be investigated more accurately. The successful completion of this task is indeed hindered by the difficulty that, regarding many errors in the text...

Even among those passages which we shall list below as being poorly translated by the translator himself, I suspect several may have degenerated through corruption of the reading from better-translated versions: for many things in these matters are left in doubt, and not everything can be asserted with certainty. Now, from what we have described, I hope it will be sufficiently clear that the ancient version had been corrupted in many ways by the time our oldest manuscripts were written. This condition of our text had to be considered before we could judge anything regarding the character of the translation itself.

Now, setting aside such corruptions by which the text was gradually deformed without the translator's fault, let us see what judgment should be passed on the translator's art and work. And first, I believe that if I look at his version as a whole, the praise of a certain simplicity and clarity should not be denied to it. The sense of the sacred text, in my judgment, is aptly and skillfully expressed almost everywhere, and the meaning is almost everywhere perfectly clear even to one who does not have the Hebrew and Greek copies at hand. You might except certain passages which, either because of the obscurity of the Greek version itself or because of a less skillfully made interpretation, are burdened by a certain obscurity and indirectness of meaning; nevertheless, if you look at the work as a whole, you would justly grant him that praise; nor are there lacking places in which the translator surpassed the Greek itself and approached more closely than it did to the Hebrew sense. This character of the version was produced by a certain integrity of judgment, guided by which the translator disdained to imitate the words of the Greek anxiously and closely <note>the Latin 'presse' suggests a literal, cramped style</note> and proposed this especially to himself: to render the sense correctly and clearly. For although in many places he is found following his model *step by step* <note>original Greek: κατὰ πόδα</note> even in the very structure of the words, nevertheless far more numerous and frequent are those places where, having set aside the sound of the words, he studied only to express the sense faithfully. You have examples of individual words or sentences translated freely but well and aptly in the passages **6, 16. 7, 4, (23). 8, 10 (24, 16. 19, 8). 11, 6. 13, 2. 14, 10. 15, 17. 18, 5. 12. 19, 30. 24. 20, 8. 24, 32. 45. 26, 11. 27, 11. 27. 28 and 39. 30, 37. 38. 31, 35. 46. 47. 33, 19. 34, 31. 35, 2. 3. 36, 7. 37, 28. 35. 38, 25. 39, 2. 40, 5. 41, 7. 34—36. 42, 13. 22. 45, 19. 49, 12. 52**. I am led to believe that all these things were deliberately omitted by the translator himself by a certain appearance of plan and logic that is quite conspicuous throughout this whole series of omissions. If you except a few of the listed passages, you will rightly judge that in all the rest, those things were consistently discarded which were either understood of themselves and were clear and obvious from what was said before or after, or seemed somewhat superfluous because of a phrase or word of nearly the same meaning following or preceding. This same zeal for brevity shines through all these omissions equally, and it dissuades us from thinking that all these were lost by chance. Now, if all these omissions bear the mark of one and the same author, whom shall we more rightly consider the author than the translator himself? It should be added that other passages to be shown below, especially in Chapter 49, prove that this same method of translating—which is evident from these omissions—was characteristic of the translator, so that no doubt remains on the matter. Everything described so far indicates that the biblical translator [possessed] a specific style of version...

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Ethiopic (Ge'ez) translation of Genesis. While the previous page focused on omissions made by the translator to streamline the text, this page examines instances where the translator took too much liberty, leading to actual errors in meaning or a failure to capture the poetic nature of the original Greek text.</meta>

...show that he revered the power and sense of the words rather than the words themselves; these are examples of a certain freedom which, for my part, I would not wish to count as a fault in him.

But just as abuse is close to use, so our translator also seems to have overstepped the permissible liberty of an interpreter, provided that the errors we shall now list were introduced into the text by him and not by others. For various passages occur where even the sense of the words is not rendered accurately or faithfully. One may see this in: 8:25; 11:5; 11:31 (where he put **"the son of his brother"** <note>original Greek: υἱὸν τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ</note> instead of **"the son of his son"** <note>original Greek: υἱὸν τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ</note>); 15:9 (he translated **"to you"** <note>original Greek: σοι</note> instead of **"to me"** <note>original Greek: μοι</note>); 18:5; 19:8, 30 (**instead of "he sat"** <note>original Greek: pro ἐκάθητο</note>); 21:23; 22:11, 14; 24:32 (**"they gave"** <note>original Greek: ἔδωκαν</note> instead of **"he gave"** <note>original Greek: ἔδωκεν</note>); 24:33 (**"and they set before him"** <note>original Greek: καὶ παρέθηκαν αὐτῷ</note> instead of **"they set before them"** <note>original Greek: παρέθηκαν αὐτοῖς</note>, likewise **"and they said"** <note>original Greek: καὶ εἶπαν</note>, though this is on the authority of a manuscript); 24:62 (**"and he was dwelling"** <note>original Ge'ez: ወሀለወ፡ ነበረ፡ (wa-hallawa nabara)</note> instead of **"and he himself was dwelling"** <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς δὲ κατῴκει</note>) ¹). Further examples include 26:32; 30:32–35; 31:26, 29, 40; 32:11, 26; 33:11; 40:17; 41:34, 35, 43, 44, 47, 48; 42:5; 43:18; 45:6; 47:20; 49:2, 3, 6, 10, 11, 20; 50:17. ²) Of all these, however, the worst rendered are Chapter 30:30–43 and Chapter 49. But while several scribes seem to have contributed their part to corrupting the former passage, the Blessing of Jacob in Chapter 49 was further falsified and corrected by the translator himself. He was someone who did not always understand all the somewhat obscure Greek words, nor did he strive to translate what was spoken poetically into a poetic style; instead, he indulged too much in his own zeal for brevity and clarity. He corrupted many things either by shortening and mutilating them, or by substituting other words and meanings for those that were obscure. One can see many proofs of both these crimes in 49:2–24.

To those faults which arose from an abuse of the translator's liberty, other errors and defects in the version must be added. These arose because the Ethiopian translator read or understood individual words or sentences of the Greek text incorrectly or poorly. Not infrequently, he was led into error because the punctuation in his Greek manuscript was either non-existent or of poor quality. I have noted these particularly conspicuous examples: in 2:19, he poorly divided the words **"to see what he would call them"** <note>original Greek: ἰδεῖν τί καλέσει αὐτά</note>; in 3:6 (7), the words **"and it is beautiful to behold"** <note>original Greek: καὶ ὡραῖόν ἐστι τοῦ κατανοῆσαι</note> he expressed as **"and it was beautiful"** <note>original Ge'ez: ወሀየP፡ (wa-hayp)</note>; in 3:13 (14), he thought the word **"why"** <note>original Greek: τι</note> signified **"whether/if"** rather than **"why"**; in 4:4, the words **"and from their fat portions"** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν στεάτων αὐτῶν</note>, he translated as if they meant **"and from their fattest ones"** <note>original Ge'ez: ወእምነ፡ ሠቡሖኒሆሙ፡ (wa-em-na sabuhonihomu)</note>; in 4:5, the words **"and his countenance fell"** <note>original Greek: καὶ συνέπεσε τῷ προσώπῳ αὐτοῦ</note> were translated as **"and he fell on his face"** <note>original Ge'ez: ወወደቀ፡ በገጹ፡ (wa-wadaqa ba-gatsu)</note>, which hardly anyone would interpret as "his face fell [in sadness]," but rather as "he prostrated himself on his face" (my version—

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Ethiopic translation of Genesis. ...to note and describe them individually among the variant readings below. With these exceptions, therefore, the rest is clearly and well-translated; and although we cannot grant him the prize for exact fidelity, his work is nevertheless notable for that simplicity and clarity which we praised above. Now there remains a small number of passages in which we find the translator has departed from the Greek text in such a way that neither praise nor blame arises from it. For like other translators, our author could not help but allow the customs and manners of his own country to exert a certain influence when translating individual words and names. Since these instances are of some value for investigating and understanding the customs of this ancient people, we shall note some of them here.

In Chapters 37:28 and 45:22, he expressed the Greek "gold pieces" <note>original Greek: χρυσοῦς (chrysous), referring to staters</note> with the word **dinar** <note>original Ge'ez: ዲናር (dinar); Greek: δηνάሪον (denarion)</note>. Likewise, in Chapter 24:22, he translates the Greek "drachma" <note>original Greek: δραχμὴν (drachmēn)</note> with the word **weight** <note>original Ge'ez: ሕለቆ (haleqo); Greek: ὁλκὸς (holkos)</note>, and "ten gold pieces" <note>original Greek: δέካ χρυσῶν</note> with the words **ten weights** <note>original Ge'ez: ዐሥርቱ፡ሕለቆ</note>. From this, one might conjecture that these Roman-Greek terms had already been adopted into the citizenship of the Ethiopians by the translator's time. Indeed, I do not believe these terms were first claimed by them through the later translation of the New Testament, for long before that version was made, the Ethiopians had very frequent commerce with the Greeks, and certain Greek colonies were established in Abyssinia <note>Historical name for Ethiopia</note>. (The word for **ship** <note>original Ge'ez: ሐመር (hamar)</note> in 43:11 should perhaps be judged differently.)

Furthermore, note that for the word "silver" <note>original Greek: ἀργύριον (argyrion)</note>, meaning money, he everywhere uses the word **gold** <note>original Ge'ez: ወርቅ (warq)</note> in 42:25, 27, 28, 35; 43:12, 15; 44:1; 47:14, 15, and elsewhere. For "chariot" <note>original Greek: ἅρμα (harma)</note> in 41:43, he uses **horse** <note>original Ge'ez: ፈረስ (faras)</note>; for "milk" <note>original Greek: γάላ (gala)</note> in 18:8, he uses **honey** <note>original Ge'ez: ማር (mar)</note>¹); and for "the horses" <note>original Greek: τὴν ἵππον</note> in 14:16, he uses **mules** <note>original Ge'ez: አባቅል (abaqil)</note>. All of these seem to me to have been phrased this way according to the customs and habits of the Ethiopians. In 29:14, he explained "a month of days" as **thirty days**; and in 7:11, he indicated the Ethiopian **lunar reckoning**. Finally, the phrase "to put the hand under the thigh" in 24:2 and 9, he translates as **to place hand upon hand**; but in 47:29, for the same words, one reads **to place the hand upon the genital member**. I do not know whether this latter version is the original or was inserted later, nor whether it stems from a custom used among the Abyssinians or was taken from a certain interpretation of the Hebrew text.

Lastly, regarding what has already been said about the translator’s version, I consider it now sufficiently proven that there was only a single translator for this book—a point we have hitherto taken for granted. For with the exception of the passage in Chapters 4:15–6:11, about which we shall say more below, the other parts of the book display one and the same character of translation, and nothing warns us to suspect multiple authors. It is true, as we said above, that the same Greek words are often expressed differently in various places, but nothing follows from this except what we showed previously: that the translator by no means wished to translate accurately word-for-word, but reserved a certain freedom for himself and loved a variety of expression. This is most clearly shown by...

## 2. Overview of the readings which the Ethiopic translator had in his Greek manuscript that differ from the received Septuagint text.

From the very many places in our version that diverge from the Greek text, we have examined and described those that were either translated less accurately by the translator himself, or later corrupted and changed by scribes. To these two categories is added a third: those which, while relying on a faithful translation of the Greek manuscript, place before our eyes readings from the Greek archetype <note>The "archetype" refers to the specific ancient manuscript the translator was looking at.</note> that vary from the <term>textus receptus: the standard "received text" or commonly accepted version of the Septuagint</term>. Since these variants are of some value both for uncovering and establishing the text of the Septuagint version used by the Alexandrian church after the time of Athanasius <note>Athanasius was a 4th-century Bishop of Alexandria; this helps date the version of the Bible the Ethiopians received.</note>, and for defining the age of the Ethiopic translator, it will be worthwhile to review the most important of them here. We shall proceed by following the famous work of Holmes <note>Robert Holmes (1748–1805) published a massive collection of Greek Bible variants.</note> in citing the words of the received text, while we translate the Ethiopic readings back into Greek. They are as follows:

### 3. Variant readings, collected from our manuscripts, and notes on individual passages of the version.

In addition to what was said above on pages 10–12 regarding the plan of this catalog of variant readings, I would also like you to keep in mind that wherever words in the text are enclosed in square brackets [ ], they are taken solely from manuscript C and are missing in the others; no further note will be made about them here. If those same words are found in manuscript G or are sought from elsewhere, I will expressly indicate the source. Likewise, regarding words in the text enclosed in parentheses ( ), if nothing is mentioned in the following catalog, you should know they are found in all my manuscripts; if one or two do not show them, I will not fail to note it.

## Chapter 2.

Verse 2. **He made**] + **"what he commanded him to do"** <note>original Ge'ez: "ዘአዘዘ፡ ይግበር፡"</note> in manuscript H, taken from Verse 3. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 3. **for the day**] **"for the state of being"** in manuscripts F and G. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 5. **it sprouts**] + **"and before Adam was created,"** with the following word **"for"** deleted in manuscript C. **"before he was created"** and so forth.] **"And there was no man who worked the earth"** in manuscript C. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 6. **but**] **"he alone"** in manuscripts G and H, an incorrect reading. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 8. **the Lord**] + **"God"** in manuscript C. **Adam**] <insert>^</insert> in manuscript F, where it reads **"into the garden"**; likewise it is missing along with the word **"into"** in manuscript H. The other manuscripts provide **"Edom,"** <note>original Ge'ez: "ኤዶም፡"</note> the same as in chapter 4, verse 16; nor have I ever read the name "Eden" written otherwise than **"Edom"** in any Ethiopic books whatsoever. Nevertheless, this spelling, as one which arose from a bad reading of vowels, had to be amended, lest the region of paradise be confused with the borders of the Edomites. <note>The translator explains that Ethiopic scribes often confused "Eden" with "Edom" due to similar sounds, and he has corrected it to avoid geographic confusion with the land of Edom.</note> &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 9. **and a tree**] **"and the tree of"** in manuscript F. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 10. **before him**] **"Adam"** in manuscript G, emended. It seems probable that the word **"before him"** <note>original Ge'ez: "ቅድሞ"</note> was corrupted from the word **"Adam"** or **"Edom"** and a pronoun was attached to it by later scribes. An editor corrected the word, but since that reading is not entirely out of place, the correction was not accepted by the scribe of manuscript C. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 11. **Ewilat** <note>The biblical Havilah</note>] **"Awlat"** in manuscript F. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 12. **which is that**] **"which is those"** in manuscript F, I am not sure if this is better. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 13. **Gihon**] **"Gewon"** in manuscript F. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 14. **Tigris**] **"Tigris"** in manuscripts C and G. It should be noted that the name **"Phark"** <note>original Ge'ez: "ፋርክ፡"</note> is used for <term>Ἀσσυρίας</term> <note>Assyria</note>; it is translated differently elsewhere (25:18). **Euphrates**] **"Aphrates"** in manuscripts F and G, a spelling which occurs here and there in the manuscripts; but the other spelling is more common. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 17. [**but/and**] in manuscripts C and G. **which makes one understand**] **"which shows and makes one understand"** in manuscripts C and G. In manuscript C, the words **"you shall eat"** and **"you shall die"** are emended from the plural form. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 18. **who helps him**] **"who causes him to be helped"** in manuscript F. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 19. The words enclosed in parentheses ( ) are missing in manuscript C. **and he brought them**] **"and he brought"** in manuscript F, **"and he brought me"** in manuscript H. **and what**] <insert>^</insert> "and" in manuscript G. **and all that he named them**] **"and all (for G): that which he named them"** in manuscripts C and G. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 22. **woman**] **"a woman"** [as an object] in manuscripts C and G. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 23. **this is**] **"this"** [feminine] in manuscripts C and G. **and she shall be my woman**] **"she shall be called woman"** in manuscript G. &nbsp;&nbsp; Verse 24. In place of the subjunctive mood, manuscript C provides the indicative.

## Chapter 3.

Verse 5. ### Chapter 4.

**Verse 1.** **Cain** is written sometimes as **Qayen**, sometimes as **Qayen**, and sometimes as **Qayel**. **because of]** **"who is from"** in Manuscript G; Manuscript H has C. **Verse 2. she gave birth to him]** **"and she gave birth to him"** in Manuscripts C and G, incorrectly. **Verse 3. and after this]** missing from H in Manuscript C. **Verse 4. he made (and)]** missing in Manuscripts C and G. **he brought]** + **"a sacrifice (to the Lord, in G)"** in Manuscripts C and G. **"and his offering also"** is missing in Manuscripts C and G. **Verse 5. on his face]** **"his face"** in Manuscripts C and G. **Verse 7. his deed]** + **"for the evil one,"** wrongly inserted in Manuscripts C and G. **Verse 8. **Verse 15.** The entire passage from Chapter 4, verse 15 all the way to Chapter 6, verse 11 is thoroughly corrupt, not only in Manuscript F but also in Manuscript H, which is closely related to it. We have already mentioned above that two leaves of Manuscript F, which contain this passage, are made of paper and were written by a different hand and inserted into the volume. The reason for this can be explained as follows: the original writing on those leaves having been worn away, the Ethiopian community in Jerusalem <note>A historic community of Ethiopian monks and pilgrims in the Holy City.</note>, having no other copy of the Ethiopic Genesis at hand, filled the gaps from some other version. Which version this was is difficult to say; but since the text substituted there is marred by many explanatory notes, we believe it was a paraphrase rather than a direct translation—undoubtedly an Arabic one. Now, since one of the books we used in composing our edition does not show the ancient version but rather this "corrected" version, it has resulted in the genuine text of this passage being established with less certainty in our edition. For although we were convinced that in this passage Manuscripts C and G come closer to the genuine text than F and H, nevertheless, since we had proposed to follow Manuscripts F and H as our primary guides, we have received many readings from them, and even...

...I remember reading. For it is related there that Lamech, advanced in age and blind, while guarding his flocks together with his young nephew who was also a shepherd, killed Cain as he approached—suspecting him to be a bandit—with an arrow and a stone sent from a sling. Then, when they came closer to the slain man, the youth, having recognized Cain, shouted: "Alas, you have killed Cain!" Hearing this, Lamech was moved by repentance and terror; he beat his breast in lamentation and struck the head of the youth so hard that he fell down as if dead. From this, you may understand why he says, "I have killed a man **in my old age**" <note>original Ge'ez: "በርሥወነየ፡" (barshweneya)</note>—that is, in my senility (unless it rather means: by oversight, or rashly)—and a young man **by the clapping of my hands** <note>original Ge'ez: "በጠፈሐትየ፡" (batafahatyeya)</note>—that is, by striking my hands together in grief." — The words included in brackets are taken from manuscripts C and G.
