### Chapter 5.

The interpretation of the first two verses is foreign to the character and simplicity of the ancient version. Manuscript C has a better version: **"The book of the creation of the offspring of the mother of the living (mankind); and on the day when God made Adam, in the likeness of God He made him; male and female He made them, and He blessed them and called her name Adam on the day He made them."** <note>original Ge'ez: "ዘመጽሐፈ፡ ዘፍጥረት፡ እጓለ፡ እመሕያው፡ ወበዕለት፡ አመ፡ ገብረ፡ እግዚአብሔር፡ ለአዳም፡ በአምሳለ፡ እግዚአብሔር፡ ገብሮ፡ ተባዕተ፡ ወአንስተ፡ ወባረኮሙ፡ ወሰመያ፡ ስሞ፡ አዳም፡ በዕለት፡ እንተ፡ ገብሮሙ፡"</note> Manuscript G has almost the same, except it shows from the beginning: **"This is the book of when the offspring of the mother of the living (mankind) was created, and when He made them..."** and so forth.

***Verse 3.*** **to him]** omitted in C and G. **a son]** omitted in C and G.

***Verse 4.*** **And Adam lived]** replaced by **And the days of Adam that he lived were** <note>original Ge'ez: "ወኮኑ፡ መዋዕሊሁ፡ ለአዳም፡ ዘሕይወ፡"</note> in C and G.

### Chapter 7

## Chapter 10

In the writing of proper names, as is often the case elsewhere, there is also in this chapter an immense variety among the manuscripts; nowhere has a greater corruption of letters occurred than in these proper names. Even in Manuscripts C and G, many names are more deformed than they are corrected. For this reason, we have emended the text ourselves wherever the reason for the corruption was obvious, following the original Greek source, although we have followed Manuscripts F and H more closely than C and G.

### Verse 19.
Hiob Ludolf <note>a 17th-century German scholar regarded as the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe</note> seems to have been mistaken when he attributed an error to the Ethiopian translator. Ludolf argued that the translator, who usually translates the Greek word for **borders** <note>original Greek: "τὰ ὅρια" (ta horia)</note> with the word **mountains** <note>original Ge'ez: "አድባር:" (adbar)</note>, was confused; however, the same word was also used by those who translated from Arabic into Ethiopic to mean "borders." Indeed, in many lands, natural mountains serve as the borders of regions. There is a great variety of readings in the proper names, which it would be tedious to enumerate. [**Tergar:** <note>A proper name</note>] manuscripts: **Tirga**, **Terga**, **Tirge**; otherwise in Verse 9. *Verse 2.* **and they hid them** <note>original: "ወሀብአዎሙ"</note> [additional **wa** (and)] in manuscripts C and G. [**a**] manuscripts: **a** and **s**, otherwise in Verse 8. *Verse 3.* **they gathered together** <note>original: "ተጋብኡ"</note> in Manuscript C. [**the sea**] **the land/region** in manuscripts F and H, because the vowels were read incorrectly <note>In the Ge'ez script, small changes to a character indicate different vowels; scribes often confused 'sea' (bahra) and 'land' (behera) due to their visual similarity.</note>. *Verse 4.* **they served** <note>original: "ተዋኒዩ"</note> in manuscripts F and H. The words included in parentheses have crept in from verses 5 and 17. *Verse 5.* **and to the Kerenyos:** It is doubtful whether the prefix **to/for** <note>original: "ለ"</note> was placed by the translator himself (interpreting the Greek: "and those of Karyain"), or whether it was corrupted from the prefix **in/at** <note>original: "በ"</note>. *Verse 6.* **Seyar:** **Seyer** in manuscripts F and H. *Verse 7.* **and having gathered** [**and they gathered**] in Manuscript C, incorrectly. All manuscripts have **which**. [**wara**] **wa** in F and G, **wa** in C, **war** in H. *Verse 8.* **and he was commanded**] **and he commanded** in F and G. *Verse 9.* [**r**] was inserted by us. [**Selasyon:**] Manuscript: **Salasyon** and **Salalayon** and **Selasyan**. **they are** in C. *Verse 12.* **and their goods/possessions:** **and to her goods** in C; likewise **and he** **dwells** **in** instead of **and their dwellings**. But the translator, since he used a plural pronoun everywhere in verses 12 and 13, seems to have understood Abraham along with his people; likewise in verse 16. *Verse 13.* **from those who** **fled**] **those who** **escaped** in C. **toward**] **with** in C. *Verse 14.* **there** + **Abram** in C. [**his son**] inserted by us from Manuscript C; the translator, along with many Greek sources, read **brother** <note>original Greek: "ἀδελφὸς"</note>; likewise in verse 16. **and they were**] **and they were** in C and G. *Verse 15.* [**ko**] **ke** in F and H, **a** in G. *Verse 16.* Note, if you please, that here instead of "their horse(s)" <note>original Greek: "τὴν ἵππον (αὐτῶν)"</note>, the phrase "their mules" is expressed, even though in verses 11 and 21 he translates it as "horses"; for the Ethiopians use both horses and mules in wars (referencing Hiob Ludolf's *History of Ethiopia* I, 10, 7–12) <note>Hiob Ludolf was a 17th-century scholar considered the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe.</note>. **and their goods**] — **mu** (their) in C and H. **and the people** + **he brought back** in C. *Verse 17.* **of his kingdom** in C. *Verse 18.* **and they joined** in C and G; **and the king** in C. *Verse 21.* **and his horses**] **and the property** in C. *Verse 23.* **he does not take**] **he did not take** in C and G. **I cause to prosper/enrich**] **I caused to prosper** in F, **we have enriched** in C and G. *Verse 24.* [**we have begun**] was restored by us in place of the word **they believe**, which the manuscripts provide.

### Chapter 15.

*Verse 1.* **in a vision** in G. *Verse 2.* **Iyawabber** seems to have arisen from the name **Eliezer** <note>original Greek: "Ἐሊéዝερ"</note>, with the letter *b* <note>beta</note> being read instead of *z* <note>zeta</note> (see 4:20). *Verse 4.* **another** was read by the translator as *allos* <note>another</note> instead of *all' hos* <note>but he who</note>. It seems the translator or interpolator indicated by this version that the birds descending were of the species **Zamaya** <note>original: "ዘመያ፡"</note>—a type of slaughtered bird—which by no means agrees with the Hebrew and Greek; therefore in manuscripts C and G, **they were not** <note>original: "አልብቱ፡"</note> was deleted, and in manuscript C, **houses/dwellings** <note>original: "አብያት፡"</note> was substituted for **Zamaya**.] + **and they closed/shut them** <note>original: "ወዓጠሙ፡"</note> in manuscript C.

*Verse 13.* Manuscripts C and G: **and he said to him** <note>original: "ወይበሎ፡"</note> instead of **and he said to them** <note>original: "ወይበላሁ፡"</note> (Greek: *and it was said*). **They shall be** and **let them be** are found in manuscripts C and G.

*Verse 17.* **It shall pass** <note>original: "ይሀረብ፡"</note>] **it passes** in manuscripts C and G, which is less correct. **We passed** <note>original: "ንለፈ፡"</note>] **and we passed** in manuscripts C and G, incorrectly. **Which he promised** <note>original: "ዘአሰፈዎ፡"</note>] manuscript C prefixed **his covenant** <note>original: "ኪዳኑ፡"</note>.

*Verses 19–21.* I have frequently corrected the writing of Codex F based on the other manuscripts. Likewise in manuscripts F and H, as well as in G, from **and the Perizzites** <note>original: "ወዘፈረዘወከ፡"</note> until the end, **to/for** <note>original: "ለ"</note> was placed instead of **which/who** <note>original: "ዘ"</note>; because this seemed intolerable, I have corrected it.

### **CHAPTER 16.**

*Verse 2.* **In the land of Canaan** <note>original: "በምድረ፡ ከነአን፡"</note>] omitted in manuscript C. **God** <note>original: "አምላክ፡"</note>] omitted in manuscript C.

*Verse 7.* [**Ku**]**bu** in the manuscripts.

*Verse 10.* Manuscripts C and G: **he shall not be numbered** <note>original: "ኢይትኈለቍ፡"</note>, since the word **until** <note>original: "እስከ፡"</note> usually governs the indicative mood.

*Verse 13.* **He who spared me** <note>original: "ዘመሐረኒ፡"</note> in manuscript G (see 19:16, 20:6, 22:12, 16); in its place manuscript C has: **You who spared me** <note>original: "ዘመሐርከኒ፡"</note>.

*Verse 14.* [**Ba**] manuscripts: **Ga**.

*Verse 16.* [**80**] <note>The Ethiopic numeral ፹</note> manuscripts: **70** <note>The Ethiopic numeral ፸</note>; I corrected it myself.

### **Chapter 18.** 

Verse 1. **to Abraham** <note>original: "ለአብርሃም፡"</note> in manuscript G. **throne/dwelling** <note>original: "መንበረ፡"</note>] **throne** <note>original: "መንበር፡"</note> in F, **seat** <note>original: "መበር፡"</note> in H, as if it were a common noun rather than a specific title. Verse 6. **three measures** <note>original: "መሠለሰ፡"</note>] **measures** <note>original: "መስፈርተ፡"</note> in manuscript C. **cakes** <note>original: "ዪፋንተ፡"</note>] this is how it appears in manuscripts F and C both here and in Chapter 19:3, and elsewhere; although manuscripts G and H show the same form in Genesis 19:3 and Exodus 12:39, they provide the form **cakes** <note>original: "ዪፋንታ፡"</note> in this specific passage. 

Verse 8. **and he taught/showed** <note>original: "ወመሀረ፡"</note>] all manuscripts provide this; the Greek text says <term>καὶ γάλα</term> <note>original: "and milk"</note>. Verse 9. In manuscript C, **and he said to him** <note>original: "ወይቤሎ፡"</note> is read twice instead of **and they said to him** and **and he said to them**. Verse 10. **I will come to you** <note>original: "እመጽእ፡ ንቤከ፡"</note> in manuscript G. **child/son** <note>original: "ወሉድ፡"</note>] see 17:16 and 18:14; manuscript C substituted **son** <note>original: "ወልደ፡"</note>; the same emendation appears in Verse 14 in manuscripts C and G. 

Verse 14. **to you** <note>original: "ንቤከ፡"</note>] + **together/in unity** <note>original: "በኅብረት፡"</note> in F, H, and C, which I do not know how it agrees with the Greek <term>εἰς ὥራስ</term> <note>original: "at the appointed time"</note>, and for that reason, I have omitted it. Verse 15. **no** <note>original: "አልቦ፡"</note>] **but** <note>original: "አላ፡"</note> in manuscript C. Verse 16. **and he looked/beheld** <note>original: "ወአንጸረ፡"</note>] **and he went** <note>original: "ወሖረ፡"</note> in manuscript C. **he sends them** <note>original: "ይፈንዎሙ፡"</note>] see the notes recorded at 12:20. Verse 17. At the beginning of the verse in manuscript C, these interpolated words are read: **And Abraham turned and stood before the Lord.** 

Verse 18. **because of him** <note>original: "በእንቲአሁ፡"</note>] **in him** <note>original: "ቦቱ፡"</note> in manuscript C, see 12:3. Verse 19. **I know** <note>original: "አአምር፡"</note>] **He knows** <note>original: "የአምር፡"</note> in manuscripts F and G. **He commands them** <note>original: "የአዝዞሙ፡"</note>] **He commands them** <note>original: "የአዝዞሙ፡"</note> in manuscripts F and H, an archaic subjunctive form, while manuscript C uses the standard **He commands them**. But I preferred that first reading, which contains good sense, over the reading **He commands them**, both because of the authority of the Hebrew and Greek, and because I suspected the latter was corrupted from our version. **almsgiving/righteousness** <note>original: "መጽዋተ፡"</note>] regarding this version of the word <term>δικαιοσύνης</term> <note>original: "righteousness"</note>, see Ludolf's Lexicon <note>referring to Hiob Ludolf, the 17th-century founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe</note> under this entry. **for Abraham** <note>original: "ለአብርሃም፡"</note> (second instance)] in manuscript G; it is placed after **which he said to him** <note>original: "ዘይቤሎ፡"</note> in manuscript C. 

Verse 21. Manuscripts F and H add **also** <note>original: "ኒ፡"</note> after **their crying out**. Verse 24. **region/land** <note>original: "ብሔረ፡"</note>] **city** <note>original: "ሀገረ፡"</note> in manuscript G, see Verse 26. Verse 25. **for all** <note>original: "ለኵሉ፡"</note> in manuscripts F and H. Verse 30. Manuscript G: he spared you** <note>original: "መሐከሙ፡"</note>, see also 16:13. **Verse 17. Until** <note>original: "እስከ፡"</note>] **if** <note>original: "እመ፡"</note> in manuscripts C and G. **With her** <note>original: "ምስለቲ፡"</note>] **then** <note>original: "ዋገሰ፡"</note> in manuscript G. **And I shall die** <note>original: "ወእመውት፡"</note>] **And I shall not die** <note>original: "ወእይመውት፡"</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 24. There** <note>original: "ወትየ፡"</note>] **there** <note>original: "ወትየ፡"</note> in manuscripts C and G. **Verse 28. He sees and behold** <note>original: "ይረኢ፡ ወነሁ፡"</note>] **he saw, behold** <note>original: "ርእየ፡ ናሁ፡"</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 29. He destroyed us** <note>original: "ዳመሰሰኑነ፡"</note> 1st instance] + **God** <note>original: "እግዚአብሔር፡"</note> in manuscripts C and G. **Verse 30. Cave** <note>original: "መት፡"</note>] **cave** <note>original: "ጻብር፡"</note> **fled** <note>original: "ጒያ፡"</note>] **and he dwelt in a cave** <note>original: "ወኀደረ፡ ውስተ፡ ጻብር፡"</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 31. You grow up** <note>original: "ትልህቁ፡"</note> and **you are small** <note>original: "ትንእሱ፡"</note>, these are transposed in manuscripts F and H, but restored to their proper place in C and G. **They are born** <note>original: "ይትዋለዱ፡"</note>] **they are born** <note>original: "ይትወለዱ፡"</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 32. To him** <note>original: "ኀቤሁ፡"</note>] **with him** <note>original: "ምስሌሁ፡"</note> in manuscripts C and G. **Verse 33. And she entered** <note>original: "ወቦአት፡"</note>] **she entered** <note>original: "ቦአት፡"</note> in manuscripts C and G, because they have **and** <note>original: "ወ"</note> before **in that** <note>original: "በይእቲ፡"</note>, just like manuscripts F and H. **In that night** <note>original: "በይእቲ፡ ሌሊት፡"</note> 2nd instance] missing in C and G, agreeing with the Greek manuscripts. **Verse 35. And the younger [daughters]** <note>original: "ወሰበብት፡"</note>] **and the younger** <note>original: "ወሰበብት፡"</note> in manuscripts F and H. **Verse 37. Manuscript H: for the Moabites** <note>original: "ለሞአብያኒ፡"</note>, manuscripts C and G: **for the Moabites** <note>original: "ለሞአባውያኒ፡"</note> which is the more common form. **Verse 38. Manuscript F: you are small to me** <note>original: "ትትንሿኒ፡"</note> correctly (25:23). **And she called him** <note>original: "ወሰመያቶ፡"</note>] + **his name** <note>original: "ስሞ፡"</note> in manuscripts C and G. — Manuscript C: **for the Ammonites** <note>original: "ለአሞናውያን፡"</note>, which is the form otherwise common.

## CHAPTER 20.

**Verse 1. [Nations]** <note>original: "አሕዛብ፡"</note> All manuscripts provide **he moved/journeyed** <note>original: "መከሁ፡"</note>, likewise in 24:62; even in manuscript C this reading was not corrected, which is all the more strange because the translator correctly rendered the Greek word for "South" in Chapters 13:14 and 28:14. **Gerar-ki** <note>original: "ገረርኪ፡"</note>] **Gerar** <note>original: "ገረራ፡"</note> in manuscript C (see Verse 2).

**Verse 3. Manuscripts C and G** insert **while being** <note>original: "በሀልዎ፡"</note>, G after **they sleep** <note>original: "ይነውሙ፡"</note>, C after **and he said to him** <note>original: "ወይቤሎ፡"</note>. But in **Verse 6. In their dream** <note>original: "በሕልመሙ፡"</note>] missing in C and G. **To/for me** <note>original: "ሊታ፡"</note>] missing in manuscript C. **Verse 7.** In place of the words included in brackets, manuscripts F and H have nothing except **then** <note>original: "እንከ፡"</note>, and in G even this is not read. **Verse 10. Having seen you** <note>original: "ርኢየከ፡"</note>] **Having seen you** <note>original: "ርኢየከ፡"</note> in manuscript C, which is the more common form. **Verse 12. Until** <note>original: "እስከመ፡"</note>] **and towards the widow** <note>original: "ወኅበበ፡ አልማን፡"</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 14. They fell, and the daughters** <note>original: "ወደቁ፡ ወአዋልደ፡"</note>] **and the servants, and the maidservants** <note>original: "ወአገብርቲ፡ ወአህባተ፡"</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 15.** Manuscript C supplied from the end of the verse: **wherever you wish, we will do** <note>original: "ኀበ፡ ፈቃደከ፡ ንገብር፡"</note> (as written). **Verse 16. And in all — he spoke to her** <note>original: "ወበኵሉ፡ — ተናገራ፡"</note>] “and in all justice he spoke with her”; manuscripts C and G: **he was justified** <note>original: "ጸድቀ፡"</note> = “and in all things he spoke justice to her,” but it seems probable that, due to poorly read vowels, **he spoke to her** <note>original: "ተናገራ፡"</note> arose from **he spoke** <note>original: "ተናገረ፡"</note> and **was justified** <note>original: "ጸድቀ፡"</note> arose from **was right/justified** <note>original: "ጸደቀ፡"</note>.

### Chapter 21.

*Verse 2.* Manuscripts C and G: **at Beersheba:** <note>original: "በርስባቲሃ:"</note> following an emendation made according to Verse 7. — In this same verse, after [the word] **and she gave birth:** <note>original: "ወወለደት:"</note> manuscripts F and H added **Sarah:** <note>original: "ሣራ:"</note> again. *Verse 4.* see 17:12, 14. *Verse 7.* **And she said:** <note>original: "ወትቤ:"</note> is missing in manuscript G, but manuscript C reads **she said:** <note>original: "ትቤ:"</note>. **to [P]** <note>original: "ለፕ"</note>] missing in manuscript C. *Verse 9.* **playing/mocking:** <note>original: "ይትዋኒያ:"</note> ] manuscript C and G read **playing:** <note>original: "ይትዋኒያ:"</note>. Also in 26:8. *Verse 12.* **he shall be counted:** <note>original: "ይትኃለቍ:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **he shall be named:** <note>original: "ይሰመያ:"</note>. *Verse 14.* **and Sabsoyen:** <note>original: "ወሳብሶየን:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **and Sebsoyen:** <note>original: "ወሰብሶየን:"</note>, missing in manuscript G. *Verse 16.* **she looks:** <note>original: "ትነጽር:"</note> ] manuscript F reads **she looks:** <note>original: "ትኔጽር:"</note>, which now seems better to me. **Do not fear:** <note>original: "ኢትፋርሂ:"</note> ] manuscript G reads **Do not be troubled:** <note>original: "ኢትትበሀሊ:"</note>, manuscript C reads **Do not grieve:** <note>original: "ኢትሣዘኒ:"</note>. *Verse 18.* **And I strengthened him:** <note>original: "ወአጽነዕሁ:"</note> ] manuscript C and G read **Hold him fast:** <note>original: "ወአጽንዒዮ:"</note> (see 16:6; but also 24:17, 23, 43, 45, 47; 35:17; 38:16.) *Verse 21.* **And after this:** <note>original: "ወእምዝ:"</note> ] adds **he dwelt:** <note>original: "ኀደረ:"</note> in manuscript C; manuscript G reads **And it happened in those days he stayed in the field:** <note>original: "ወኮነ: በውእቱ: መዋዕል: ነበረ: ሕቅለ:"</note> etc. *Verse 22.* **and his vision/appearance:** <note>original: "ወራዕያሁ:"</note> ] manuscript H reads **and his vision:** <note>original: "ወሬዕዩሁ:"</note>, but elsewhere like the others; regarding this word, consult Ludolf’s Lexicon, pages 68 and 139 <note>Hiob Ludolf was a 17th-century scholar who produced the first major Ge'ez-Latin dictionary for Europeans</note>. **and Phicol:** <note>original: "ወፋስል:"</note> ] manuscript F and H read **and Phisla:** <note>original: "ወፋስላ:"</note>; but below in Verse 32 and 26:26 it is **Phicol:** <note>original: "ፋስል:"</note>. *Verse 23.* Manuscripts C and G: **Do not deal falsely with me:** <note>original: "ኢተሀመሀኒ:"</note>, manuscript H: **Do not swear falsely to me:** <note>original: "ኢትሤመሀኒ:"</note>. **You have been:** <note>original: "ሀለውከ:"</note> ] manuscripts F, G, and H read **I have been:** <note>original: "ሀለውኩ:"</note>. *Verse 28.* **seven:** <note>original: "ሰብዐ:"</note> ] manuscripts F, G, and H read **seventy:** <note>original: "ሰብዓ:"</note>, manuscript C reads **7** <note>original: "፯"</note> (as written); likewise in Verse 29; and manuscript G also uses the numeral **7** <note>original: "፯"</note> in Verse 30. *Verse 30.* **these (feminine):** <note>original: "እላንተ:"</note> ] manuscripts F, G, and H read **these (masculine):** <note>original: "እላንቱ:"</note>. *Verse 31.* **the Well of the Oath:** <note>original: "ሀዘቅተ: መሐላ:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **Beersheba:** <note>original: "በርስባሄ:"</note> (26:33). **they swore:** <note>original: "ተወሐሉ:"</note> ] manuscripts C and H read **they swore:** <note>original: "ተወሐሉ:"</note>, likewise in Verse 27 for manuscript G (see 26:28). *Verse 33.* **and he sowed a field:** <note>original: "ወዘርአ: ገራህተ:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **and he planted trees:** <note>original: "ወተከለ: ዕፀወ:"</note>.

### Chapter 22.

*Verse 1.* **Abraham:** <note>original: "አብርሃም:"</note> after **and he said to him:** <note>original: "ወይቤሎ:"</note> is placed only once in manuscripts C and G. *Verse 2.* **[for Isaac]** <note>original: "ንዘየያህያ:"</note> ] unclear in manuscript C. **whom you loved:** <note>original: "ዘአህለለከ:"</note> ] manuscript G reads **whom you loved:** <note>original: "ዘአህለለከ:"</note>. *Verse 3.* **early in the morning:** <note>original: "በጊዜሃ:"</note> ] missing in manuscript C. *Verse 5.* **to the young men:** <note>original: "ለደቅ:"</note> ] manuscripts C and G read **to his young men:** <note>original: "ለደቁ:"</note>. **stay you:** <note>original: "ንበክሙ:"</note> ] manuscripts G and H prefix the word **here:** <note>original: "ዝየ:"</note> to this, while manuscript C places it after. *Verse 7.* Manuscripts C and G: **for the sacrifice:** <note>original: "ለመሥዋዕት:"</note>. *Verse 8.* Manuscripts C and G: **for the sacrifice of:** <note>original: "ለመሥዋዕተ:"</note>. *Verse 9.* see 12:7. *Verse 11.* **God:** <note>original: "አምላክ:"</note> ] missing in manuscripts C and G. *Verse 12.* Manuscript C: **and I worship:** <note>original: "ወአምልክ:"</note> (16:13). *Verse 13.* **And he took:** <note>original: "ወነሥአ:"</note> ] manuscript G adds **the ram:** <note>original: "ለበግዕ:"</note>. *Verse 14.* **appearance/vision (first occurrence):** <note>original: "ርእያ:"</note>] manuscript C reads **vision:** <note>original: "ራእየ:"</note>. *Verse 16.* Manuscript C: **And I swore:** <note>original: "ወአምህኩ:"</note>. *Verse 21.* **[in] the...** <note>original: "[በ] መ"</note> in F, C, and H. **to Syria:** <note>original: "ለሱርያ:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **to Aram:** <note>original: "ለአራም:"</note>. *Verse 22.* **[8]** <note>original: "[ቱ]"</note> in H, F, G, and H. *Verse 23.* **these:** <note>original: "እሉ:"</note> ] manuscript C adds **these are 8:** <note>original: "እሙንቱ: ፰"</note>. *Verse 24.* **Kahath:** <note>original: "ቃህት:"</note> or **Kahat:** <note>original: "ቃሃት:"</note> in all manuscripts. [**Gaham:** <note>original: "ገሐም:"</note> ] manuscripts F and H read **Bek:** <note>original: "ቤክ:"</note>, manuscript C reads **Beko:** <note>original: "ቤኮ:"</note>, manuscript G reads **Sek:** <note>original: "ሰክ:"</note>.

### Chapter 23.

*Verse 6.* **we heard:** <note>original: "ሰማዕነ:"</note> and **listen to us:** <note>original: "ስማዕነ:"</note> appear in the manuscripts, except for manuscript C. *Verse 8.* **your thought/mind:** <note>original: "ሐለክሙ:"</note> in manuscripts F and H, **your will/desire:** <note>original: "ፈቃድክሙ:"</note> in manuscript C. **Ephron:** <note>original: "አፈርን:"</note> ] manuscript C and G read **Aphron:** <note>original: "አፋርን:"</note>, also manuscript C in Verses 10, 13, 14, 16, 17, and 25:9. *Verse 9.* **he gave me:** <note>original: "ወሀበኒ:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **let him give me:** <note>original: "የሀበኒ:"</note>. **give it to me:** <note>original: "ሀበኒያ:"</note> ] missing in manuscript C. *Verse 11.* **approach me:** <note>original: "ቅረበኒ:"</note> ] manuscript F reads **bring near to me:** <note>original: "ቅርበኒ:"</note>, but see 27:21. Manuscript C reads: **the field and its cave:** <note>original: "ገራህተሃ: ወበአቶሃ:"</note>. *Verse 15.* **I heard:** <note>original: "ሰማዕኩ:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **listen to me:** <note>original: "ስማዐኒ:"</note>. *Verse 16.* **and he sent/dispatched:** <note>original: "ወፈነወ:"</note> ] manuscript C reads **and he weighed out:** <note>original: "ወደለወ:"</note> <note>This refers to Abraham weighing out the silver for the land purchase</note>. Manuscripts G and H: **he turned away/changed:** <note>original: "ተመየነ:"</note>.

### Chapter 24.

**Verse 2.** **[to his son:]** **to his servant:** <note>original: "ለገብሩ:"</note> in Manuscript C; also in **Verse 5**, **his servant:** <note>original: "ገብሩ:"</note> in Manuscript C. **Verse 6.** **[to his son:]** <note>original: "ለወልዱ:"</note> is missing in Manuscript C. **[your head:]** <note>original: "ርእሰከ:"</note> is missing in Manuscript C. **Verse 7.** **[my fathers:]** **my father:** <note>original: "አቡየ:"</note> in Manuscripts C and G. **Verse 9.** **[son:]** **servant:** <note>original: "ገብር:"</note> in Manuscript C; also in **Verse 10**. **Verse 10.** **[among the rivers:]** **at the rivers of Aram:** <note>original: "ንበ: አፋላግ: አራም:"</note> in Manuscript C. **Verse 11.** **[and he made...]** **and he made them rest:** <note>original: "ወአሕረፋ:"</note> in Manuscript C. **Verse 13.** **[upon:]** **towards:** <note>original: "ኀበ:"</note> in Manuscripts C and G. **Verse 14.** Manuscripts F and H read: **he has shown kindness to you:** <note>original: "አስተያለወከ:"</note>; also in **Verses 31, 44, 27, and 14** in Manuscripts F, G, and H. **Verse 15.** **[son:]** **daughter:** <note>original: "ወለተ:"</note> in F, G, and H (just so). **[she responded:]** **she responded:** <note>original: "ዋሥታ:"</note> in F, G, and C. **Verse 17.** **give me a little:** <note>original: "ዐይ:"</note> in Manuscript H. **Verse 18.** **[on the hand:]** **from the hand:** <note>original: "እምደበ:"</note> in Manuscripts C and G; the translator incorrectly rendered the Greek term <term>tòn brachíona</term> <note>meaning "the arm"</note> with the word **shoulders:** <note>original: "መትንፍት:"</note>. **Verse 21.** **[as:]** **as:** <note>original: "ከመ:"</note> in Manuscripts F and H. Manuscripts C and G read: **I went:** <note>original: "ሆርኩ:"</note>. **Verse 22.** **satisfied:** <note>original: "ረወየ:"</note> is found in all manuscripts. **Verse 25.** **[and enough for me:]** **and straw:** <note>original: "ወሣህር:"</note> in Manuscript C. **Verse 29.** **[to Rebekah:]** **Rebekah:** <note>original: "ርብቃ:"</note> in Manuscripts F and H. **[her brother:]** **brother:** <note>original: "እኈ:"</note> in Manuscript F. **Verse 30.** **[when:]** **and when:** <note>original: "ወሶበ:"</note> in Manuscript C, but the translator <note>D refers to the scholar Dillmann</note> seems to have omitted it deliberately. **Verse 31.** **[there:]** **there:** <note>original: "ኂየ:"</note> in Manuscript F. Manuscripts F, H, and G read: **he showed me kindness:** <note>original: "አስተያለወኒ:"</note> (see Verse 14). **Verse 32.** **[to him (first instance):]** **to them:** <note>original: "ሎሙ:"</note> in Manuscripts C and G. **[and enough for me:]** **and straw:** <note>original: "ወሣህረ:"</note> in Manuscript C. **Verse 36.** **[in her old age:]** **in her old age:** <note>original: "በርስከሃ:"</note> in Manuscript C, **in his old age:** <note>original: "በርስከሃሁ:"</note> in Manuscript G. **Verse 37.** **[among them:]** **with them:** <note>original: "ምስሌሆሙ:"</note> in Manuscript C. **Verse 40.** **[he:]** **and he:** <note>original: "ወውእቱ:"</note> in Manuscripts F and H. (**[and if not:]**) <note>original: "ወእመአኮ:"</note> is missing in Manuscript C. **Verse 42.** **[you:]** **is it you?** <note>original: "አንተኑ:"</note> in Manuscripts F and G; see Verse 49. **Verse 43.** **[give drink:]** **give drink:** <note>original: "አስተይይ:"</note> in Manuscripts F and H; **Verse 21.** In manuscripts F and H, **Galaad** <note>original: "ገላኤድ"</note> is written; better see 37:25. **Verse 23. Eight days]** <note>original: "ሰሙን"</note>: I do not know whether the span of a week is customarily defined by "eight days" among the Ethiopians; perhaps the note on 17:12 pertains to this. **Verse 25.** [The name is omitted in] manuscript C; the others read very poorly: **Jacob to Laban** <note>original: "ያዕቆብ፡ ለላባ"</note>.

**Verse 26. thirst]** <note>original: "ጸምዐተ"</note>: **in battle** <note>original: "ጸባተ"</note> in manuscripts C and G. FH: **that you might take me away** <note>original: "ዘትትነሠአኒ"</note>; but compare <term>Ludolf's Grammar</term> <note>A foundational 17th-century work on the Ge'ez language by Hiob Ludolf</note> pages 18 and 19. **Verse 29. evil]** <note>original: "እኩይ"</note>: written as **evil** <note>original: "እኩይ"</note> in manuscript C. ->CHAPTER 32.<-

**Verse 2. he encamped]** <note>original: "ኀደረ"</note>: **he encamped** in G, **he encamped with me** <note>original: "ኀደረኒ"</note> in C. **Verse 4. apostles or messengers]** <note>original: "ሐዋርያ"</note>: **messengers** <note>original: "ሐዋርያተ"</note> in C and G; see Verse 7. **Verse 5. Laban]** <note>original: "ላባ"</note>: Wherever a message is carried from someone to another, the letter **a** <note>original: "አ"</note> is attached to the words being delivered, either to all of them or to certain specific ones in the manuscripts; the codices differ in how often or how rarely they place it.

**Verse 8. and he divided]** <note>original: "ወነፈቀ"</note>: **and he divided it** <note>original: "ወነፈቆ"</note> in F (see 33:1). **and the cattle]** <note>original: "ወአልሀምተ"</note> + **and the servants** <note>original: "ወለአገልገልት"</note> in C; but in the translator's Greek manuscript, as in many others, this word seems to have been missing. **camp]** <note>original: "ትዕይንተ"</note>: **tribes or camps** <note>original: "ትህየነ"</note> in C and G. **Verse 10. the Lord Himself]** <note>original: "ውእቱ፡ እግዚአብሔር"</note> missing in C. **Verse 11. he did good]** <note>original: "ያሠነ"</note>: **he does good** <note>original: "ያሠኒ"</note> in G and H. **which you have done upon me [for your servant]]** <note>original: "ዘገበርከ፡ ላዕሌየ [ለገብርከ]"</note>: In place of these words, F provides: **which I have done** <note>original: "ዘገበርኩ"</note>; G and H have: **which you have done upon me, I have done** <note>original: "ዘገበርከ፡ ላዕሌየ፡ ገበርኩ"</note>; I do not doubt that this latter reading arose from a false reading of the vowels, and the former from an emendation of the latter; C has: **which you have done for your servant, I have found** <note>original: "ዘገበርከ፡ ለገብርከ፡ ረከብኩ"</note>. **Verse 13. [your seed or offspring]]** <note>original: "ዘርእከ"</note> in manuscript C; others have **this** <note>original: "ዘንቱ"</note>. **Verse 15.** [The number **20** <note>original: "፳"</note>] the manuscripts have **20** <note>original: "፳"</note> and **sixty** <note>original: "ስሳ"</note> (the symbols for **20** <note>original: "፳"</note> and **6** <note>original: "፮"</note> are often confused). **Verse 16.** [The number **30** <note>original: "፴"</note>] the manuscripts have **50** <note>original: "፶"</note> and **fifty** <note>original: "ኀምሳ"</note>.

**Verse 10.** All the text included in brackets from Verse 10 through Verse 24 has been taken from Manuscript C; we have only slightly corrected the spelling of certain proper names. In Manuscripts F, G, and H, all those words in brackets are missing up to Verse 14. Furthermore, from Verse 15 to Verse 24, the text in those same manuscripts is found only in a very corrupt and mutilated state; they read as follows: 

**Verse 15.** **the chiefs of Saban, the chief and Nazar, the chief and Kenaz, the chief and Akor, the chief.** **Verse 16.** **and Gothon the chief, and Saphan the chief, and Korah the chief, and Alaq the chief; these are the chiefs who are in the land of Edom; these are the children of Hadas.** **Verse 17.** **and the children of Reuel, son of Esau: Libek, and Zer, and Samo; these are the chiefs for Rnuyo in the land of Edom; and these are the children of Basemath, wife of Esau.** **Verse 18.** **Yohar and Yonur and Korah, the chiefs of Zaldabo.** **Verse 19.** **and these are the children of Esau.** **Verse 24.** **and these are the children of Sibbeon: Aa and Anana; this is the Hafan** (as written). 

Otherwise, these same manuscripts vary greatly in the spelling of these names. Furthermore, **Verses 25–30** are missing in F, G, and H, and were taken by us from Manuscript C; we have corrected some parts ourselves. Likewise, the portions of **Verses 31–33** in brackets were obtained from Manuscript C. Finally, for **Verses 34–39**, and from the latter part of **Verse 40** through the first part of **Verse 43**, we have supplied the text ourselves, as we were left without any manuscript sources. It is easy to understand how so many and such significant gaps occurred in this chapter; proper names are highly susceptible to corruption when books are transcribed. Additionally, the Ethiopian scribes likely had little interest in the genealogies of the Edomites, and therefore preferred to entirely omit names that were badly corrupted or scarcely understood.

### **Chapter 42.**
*Verse 1.* **grain** <note>original: "እክለ"</note>] **grain** <note>original: "እክል"</note> in CG; likewise in *Verse 2.* *Verse 3.* **in the land** <note>original: "በብሔረ"</note>] **from the land** <note>original: "እምብሔረ"</note> in CG. *Verse 18.* **for now** <note>original: "ለኑሰ"</note>] ^ omitted in C. *Verse 19.* **peaceful** <note>original: "ሠኒአ"</note>] **peaceful** <note>original: "ሠንአ"</note>; likewise in *Verse 34* in CG, and *Verses 31 and 33* in C. **stay** <note>original: "ንበሩ"</note>] <note>original: "remanete, scilicet unus vestrûm"</note> "remain, namely one of you"; C reads **stay** <note>original: "ንበር"</note> <note>singular</note>. *Verse 20.* CG: **be entrusted** <note>original: "እትዋከሙ"</note>, see 24:29. [**Gab** <note>original: "ገብ"</note>] the manuscripts provide **Gaba** <note>original: "ገባ"</note>, which I have emended. *Verse 21.* **and you say to one another** <note>original: "ወትባህሉ"</note>] see 37:19. **each** <note>original: "በበ"</note>] **in/with** <note>original: "በ"</note> in CG; likewise in *Verse 28.* *Verse 23.* **interpreter** <note>original: "ትርጐምን"</note>] **interpreter** <note>original: "መተርጐም"</note> in C. *Verse 25.* I do not know whether **they come** <note>original: "ይመጽኡ"</note>, which the manuscripts provide, arose from a corruption of **they fill** <note>original: "ይመልኡ"</note>. **each** <note>original: "ለለ"</note>] **to those who** <note>original: "ለእለ"</note> in FH, compare 25:16; 47:12; 49:28. **their provisions** <note>original: "አኀትሌሆሙ"</note> <note>the second instance</note>] **their provisions** <note>original: "አኀላሲሆሙ"</note> in C, likewise in 43:22 and twice in 44:1. *Verse 27.* **sack** <note>original: "ዕቝረ"</note>] **sack** <note>original: "ዕዋረ"</note> in C, likewise in *Verse 35* in CG. *Verse 30.* [**Ba**] **ila** <note>original: "ባዕለ"</note> <note>meaning 'lord' or 'ruler'</note>] **Upon** <note>original: "ላዕለ"</note> in FH, **He said** <note>original: "በሀለ"</note> in CG; but having compared verses 33 and 43:3, you may see that **Upon** <note>original: "ላዕለ"</note> is corrupted from **Lord** <note>original: "ባዕለ"</note>. *Verse 31.* **our peace** <note>original: "ስንአነ"</note>] **our peace** <note>original: "ስንአንን"</note> in G, likewise in *Verse 33*; see also *Verse 19.* *Verse 33.* **Lord** <note>original: "ባዕለ"</note>] **He said** <note>original: "በሀለ"</note> in CG, likewise in 43:3. *Verse 35.* **all** <note>original: "ኵሎ"</note>] **all of them** <note>original: "ኵሎሙ"</note> in C. *Verse 36.* **you deprive me** <note>original: "ትትሠአሩኒ"</note>] **you deprive me** <note>original: "ተነሠአሩኒ"</note> in G, **you take me** <note>original: "ትነሥአኑ"</note> in C. *Verse 37.* G: **entrust him to me** <note>original: "አውፈያኒዮ"</note> with the **and** <note>original: "ወ"</note> deleted.

### **Chapter 43.**

[**terebinth resin** <note>original: "ጠርቤን"</note>] **tebereno** <note>original: "ጠቤረኖ"</note> in FH. **and blessings** <note>original: "ወብርኅሳ"</note>] **and blessings** <note>original: "ወብርካህ"</note> in CG, but the <term>construct state</term> <note>A grammatical form where words are linked to show possession or relationship</note>, where several nouns are listed, eventually gives way to the <term>absolute state</term>. *Verse 14.* **may he give you** <note>original: "ይሁብክሙ"</note>] **may he give you** <note>original: "የሀብክሙ"</note> in CG, likewise later **and may he return** <note>original: "ወያግብአ"</note> in C. *Verse 15.* **from him** <note>original: "እምነሁ"</note>] **they** <note>original: "እሙንቱ"</note> in CG. *Verse 18.* **this** <note>original: "ዘከቱ"</note>] **this** <note>original: "ዘንቱ"</note> in CGH. [**ny** <note>original: "ኝ"</note>] **ni** <note>original: "ኒ"</note> in FHG. *Verse 19.* [**the one over** <note>original: "ዘላዕለ"</note>] in C; the others read **and they entered** <note>original: "ወቦኡ"</note>. *Verse 22.* C: **he destroyed me** <note>original: "አኅጎለኒ"</note> (see 42:25), likewise twice in 44:1. *Verse 23.* [**Fa** <note>original: "ፋ"</note>] **Fu** <note>original: "ፉ"</note> in FH.

### Chapter 44

*Verse 3.* **When]** **And when** <note>original: "ወሶበ"</note> in CG. *Verse 6.* **Good]** **Good things** <note>original: "ሠናያተ"</note> <note>plural form</note> in CG. *Verse 9.* **Which you found]** which <note>original: "ዘ"</note> is omitted in GH. **To God]** **To our Lord** <note>original: "ለእግዚእነ"</note> in G emended. *Verse 10.* **Let them be]** **You shall be** <note>original: "ትኩኑ"</note> in F. **Let them be to us]** **Let them be for us** <note>grammatical variation</note> in C. *Verse 11.* **[Fa]** **Fe** <note>original: "ፋ ፈ"</note> in FH, but the subjunctive mood is better. *Verse 12.* **And he found]** **And they found** <note>original: "ወረከቡ"</note> in GH. *Verse 14.* In place of the words included in brackets, FGH have nothing except **and Joseph [there]** <note>original: "ወዮሴፍሰ [ህየ]"</note> which is omitted in FGH. *Verse 16.* **In payment]** CG prefix **and** <note>original: "ወ"</note>. *Verse 17.* **Word]** + **but** <note>original: "አላ"</note> in C. *Verse 20.* **Old man]** see the note for 39, 14. ### Chapter 45

*Verse 2.* **And he cried out]** + **with a loud voice** <note>original: "በዐቢይ፡ ቃለ"</note> in C. *Verse 3.* **My father]** **My father** in C. *Verse 4.* **The country]** C prefixes **toward,** <note>original: "ኀበ"</note> which is superfluous. *Verse 5.* appears to be corrupt from the beginning. *Verse 6.* **Which remains]** + **and they do not sow** <note>original: "ወኢይዘርዑ"</note> in C. *Verse 7.* **And it remained]** **And it will remain** in C. *Verse 8.* Those things included in brackets are taken from CG. *Verse 11.* **Which destroyed you]** **Your destruction** <note>original: "ጥፈትከ"</note> in CG. *Verse 12.* **Separately]** **Separately** in CG. *Verse 13.* **All 2°]** CG prefix **and**. *Verse 16.* **Their word]** **Their voice** <note>original: "ቃሎሙ"</note> in G. **And they say]** **And they said to him** in C. *Verse 17.* **Fill up]** **They filled up** <note>original: "መልኡ"</note> in CG (as written). *Verse 19.* **To your father]** **To their father** <note>original: "ለአቡሆሙ"</note> in CG; but the second person pronoun is good <note>meaning: correct</note>, because Jacob is also the father of Joseph. *Verse 20.* **Your goods]** see what was noted at 31, 18. *Verse 22.* **He gave]** **He gave to him** <note>original: "ወሀቦ"</note> in CG. **[13]** **Other hundred** <note>original: "ካልእት፡ ምእተ"</note> in FH, undoubtedly arising from a bad reading of the sign for **3**. *Verse 23.* **And he who carries]** the prefix **and** is omitted in C. *Verse 24.* CG: **That you might be troubled.** *Verse 26.* **And while he was there]** + **the house of Pharaoh** <note>original: "ቤተ፡ ፈርዖን"</note> in G; + **the district** <note>original: "ደወለ"</note> in C. *Verse 27.* **(And)** in FH, omitted in CG. **He lived]** **He lived** <note>spelling variant</note> in CG.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly comparison of biblical manuscripts for the Book of Genesis, moving from the genealogy of the sons of Israel in chapter 46 into the narrative of their settlement in Egypt in chapter 47. It notes where specific names were omitted in some versions and how later scribes or editors attempted to reconcile these lists with other biblical books like Exodus and Numbers.</meta>

**The Arrival:** <note>original Ge'ez: "ምጽአወ" (mṣ’awä)</note> From Verse 9 onwards, in all the manuscripts, the names of the children belonging to each of the individual sons of Israel have been omitted, and only their total sums are recorded. For this reason, we have supplied the names ourselves from Exodus 6, Numbers 26, and other passages. The manuscripts count *four* sons of **Ruben** <note>Reuben</note> in *Verse 9*. In *Verse 10*, they count the sons of **Simeon**: manuscripts F, H, and G count *five*, while C counts *six*. In *Verse 11*, they count *three* sons of **Levi**. In *Verse 12*, they count *five* sons of **Judah**, then it follows: **And they [were] in the land of Canaan; and these are the two sons of Perez**; <note>original: "ወእቱ፡ በምድረ፡ ከናአን፡ ወእሉ፡ እሙንቱ፡ ደቂቀ፡ ፋሬስ፡ ከለአቱ፡"</note> in *Verse 13*, they count *four* sons of **Isaschar** <note>Issachar</note>; in *Verse 14*, *three* sons of **Zabulon** <note>Zebulun</note>; in *Verse 16*, *seven* sons of **Gad**; in *Verse 17*, *five* sons of **Aser** <note>Asher</note>; then **the two sons of Beriah** <note>original: "ደቂቀ፡ ባላ፡ (C: ባርያ፡) ከለአቱ፡"</note> in *Verse 18*. The phrase **And these are they** <note>original: "ወእሉ፡ እሙንቱ፡"</note> is only read in manuscript C. *Verse 20.* In place of the words [**and there were born... to Gilead**], the manuscripts read nothing but **two**; <note>original: "ከለአቱ፡"</note> and in place of the words [**Becher... Ezan**], nothing but **three**. <note>original: "ሠለስቱ፡"</note> *Verse 21.* For the words included in brackets, the manuscripts have nothing except **sons of** <note>added by manuscript G</note> **seven.** <note>original: "ቦኑኬቦ፡ ስያኮኑቱ፡" — the latter is a corruption involving the number seven</note> *Verse 22.* [**seventeen**] is written as **16** in C (following the Hebrew). *Verse 24.* For the words in brackets, the text reads **four**. <note>original: "አርባዕቱ፡"</note> *Verse 26.* [**and sixty**] is read in manuscripts F and H as **and seventy**, <note>original: "ወሰባህቱ፡"</note> where the symbol for 7 (Z) was misread. *Verse 27.* [**seventy**] — the manuscripts have a corrupted form for **seven**, again misreading the symbol Z; C was emended to "seventy" following the Hebrew. Likewise, the word **and five** is omitted in manuscript C. *Verse 28.* **Into the land]** **Before him]** <note>original: "ቅዳሜሁ፡"</note> in manuscript C. Likewise, instead of **into 2°]** **as far as Rameses]** **Ramse** in C. **Qateras** <note>original: "ቃቴርአስ"</note> is a corruption of the Greek *kath’ Herōōn* <note>meaning "City of Heroes"</note>. *Verse 31.* **land]** **in the land** in C. *Verse 32.* **cattle]** + **and men, and he placed** in C. **And all]** be careful not to think this is positioned in the accusative case.

->**CHAPTER 47.**<-

*Verse 2.* **they were]** **he was** <note>a slight grammatical change in the verb "to be"</note> in CG. *Verse 4.* **his pasture]** **pasture** <note>plural or collective form</note> in CG. *Verse 6.* **you shall dwell]** + **the land** in C. *Verse 7.* **and he blessed him]** **and he greeted him** <note>or "acknowledged him"</note> in C. *Verse 9.* **living [years]]** **brief [years]** <note>original: "ኅያጠ"</note> in G, **living + years** in C. *Verse 11.* [**Rameses**] **Rasem** in FH, **Goshen** in G. *Verse 12.* [**for**] added in FCH. **for each]** **for those who** in FH (see the note on 25:16). *Verse 13.* **fainted]** <note>referring to the land failing or being exhausted</note> a variation in CG. *Verse 14.* **into it]** manuscript C adds the preposition **into**, which is redundant here. *Verse 15.* **lest we die]** **do not die** in FH. *Verse 17.* **their food]** a spelling variation in F, and the same with a prefix in C. *Verse 18.* **and we will not fail]** **and let us not fail** in CG. **what remained]** a slight spelling variation in CG. *Verse 21.* **for a servant — their borders]** missing in G. **their borders 2°]** + **of Canaan** in C. *Verse 22.* **and he divided them]** **and he freed them** <note>original: "ወፈትሖሙ"</note> incorrectly in G; for indeed, **fetete** <note>ወፈተተ</note> seems to mean "to bestow or grant," similar to the word **fata** <note>ፋታ</note> meaning "a gift." *Verse 23.* Manuscript C reads: **and your land.** *Verse 24.* **and you shall give back]** **and you gathered** in HC, as if it were the eighth conjugation of Ludolf <note>Hiob Ludolf, a 17th-century scholar of Ethiopian languages</note>; you should also consult his lexicon. Manuscript F uses the imperfect form of the verb **to bring back.**

Regarding our reading, see Verse 26. (**Section**) <note>original: ክፍለ፡ (kəflä)</note> ^ C. Verse 28. [**Seven**] <note>original: ሰባዕቱ፡ (säba'tu)</note> **Eight** <note>original: ሰማኝቱ፡ (sämanyətu)</note> in manuscripts F, G, and H; compare with 17:12. See the note for Verse 29. [**Joseph**] <note>original: ዮሴፍ (Yosēf)</note> ^ F and H. **My body** <note>original: ሥጋየ፡ (śəgayä)</note> ] **My hand** <note>original: እዴየ፡ (ədēyä)</note> in manuscript C; see Chapter 24, verses 2 and 9. Verse 31. **Upon the head of his staff** <note>original: ውስተ፡ከተባ፡በትረ፡ (wəstä kätäba bäträ)</note> ] **Upon the head of his bed** <note>original: ላዕለ፡ርእሰ፡ዓራቱ፡ (la‘lä rə’sä ‘aratu)</note> in manuscript C.

### CHAPTER 48.
Verse 1. **They said to him** <note>original: ይበልዎ፡ (yəbälwo)</note> ] + **as follows** <note>original: አንደሁ፡ (ändähu)</note> in manuscript C, which someone undoubtedly inserted <term>interpolation: text added by a later scribe</term> because of the suffix "him" that follows. Verse 3. **In Luz** <note>original: በሉዛ፡ (bäluza)</note> ] see Chapter 35, verse 6. Verse 4. Manuscript C reads: **And I will multiply you** <note>original: ወአስተባዛኅከ፡ (wä-astäbazahkä)</note>, just as the other manuscripts do in other places. Verse 6. **By name** <note>original: በስም፡ (bäsəm)</note> ] **By the names** <note>original: በአስማተ፡ (ba-asmatä)</note> in manuscripts C and G. **And they shall be called** <note>original: ወይሰመዩ፡ (wäyəsämäyu)</note> ] ^ **And** <note>the prefix 'wa'</note> is missing in C and G. Verse 7. **Canaan** <note>original: ከናአን፡ (käna’an)</note> ] + **on the way** <note>original: በፋኖት፡ (bäfanot)</note> in manuscript C. **Ephrathah (1st instance)** <note>original: ኤፍራታ፡ (Ēfrata)</note> ] **At-Ephrathah** <note>original: አጸፍራታ፡ (’äṣäfrata)</note> in F, G, and C. **Ephrathah (2nd instance)** ] **Af-rathah** <note>original: አፋራታ፡ (’afarata)</note> in F and G; see also 35:16 and 19. **Lehem** <note>original: ሌሔም፡ (Lēḥēm)</note> ] **Lihem** <note>original: ልሔም፡ (Ləḥēm)</note> in H and G; also H in 35:19. Verse 12. **And he bowed** <note>original: ወሰገደ፡ (wäsägädä)</note> ] **And they bowed** <note>original: ወሰገዱ፡ (wäsägädu)</note> in manuscript H. Verse 14. **And he placed** <note>original: ወወደየ፡ (wäwädäyä)</note> ] **And he placed it** <note>original: ወወደዮ፡ (wäwädäyo)</note> in H; **placed** without the "and" in G; **and he set** <note>original: ወአንበረ፡ (wä’anbärä)</note> in C. **Placed** <note>original: ወደየ፡ (wädäyä)</note> ] **Placed** in G; **Set** in C. Also in the following verses, manuscript C usually substitutes the word **set** for the word **placed**. Verse 16. **Upon them** <note>original: በላዕሌሆሙ፡ (bäla‘lēhomu)</note> ] **His name** <note>original: ስሙ፡ (səmu)</note> in manuscript C. Verse 20. [**In you**] <note>original: ብክሙ፡ (bəkəmu)</note> ] **As** <note>original: በከመ፡ (bäkämä)</note> in F and H, due to the vowels being read incorrectly. [**Saying**] <note>original: በሉ፡ (bälu)</note> ] **He said to him** <note>original: በሎ፡ (bälo)</note> in F, G, and H, again due to vowels being read incorrectly. **May he bless** <note>original: ይባርክ፡ (yəbark)</note> ] **That he may bless** <note>original: ይባርከ፡ (yəbarkä)</note> in manuscript C, which is more consistent with the Hebrew and Greek texts. Verse 22. **And behold** <note>original: ወነሁ፡ (wänähu)</note> ] **And I** <note>original: ወአነ፡ (wä’anä)</note> in C and G. **Your portion** <note>original: ምሀርካ፡ (məhärka)</note> ] This is a strange translation of the word *Shechem* <note>original Greek: Σίκιμα</note>; the same reading is found in Psalm 60:8, and Hiob Ludolf, in the notes to his edition of the Psalms (p. 374) and in his dictionary, suspected that the translator misread the word as "spoils" <note>original Greek: σκύλα (skyla)</note>.

### CHAPTER 49.
Verse 1. [**You**] <note>original: አንተ፡ (’antä)</note> ] ^ missing in F and H. Verse 2. This verse is corrupted, for they substituted perfect verbs <term>completed actions</term> for the commands <term>imperatives</term> at the beginning of the verse, and then they inserted **and he said to them** <note>original: ወይቤሎሙ፡ (wäyəbēlo-mu)</note>. **And they came** <note>original: ወመጽኡ፡ (wämäṣ’u)</note> ] ^ missing in G. **Hear him** <note>original: ስምዕዎ፡ (səm‘əwo)</note> ] written twice in manuscripts C and G. Verse 4. **You have boiled over** <note>original: ሞረረ፡ (morärä)</note> ] **Mo-ra** <note>original: ሞረ፡ (morä)</note> in C and G. I suspect this reading, which is entirely foreign to the Greek text, has degenerated from **Bitterness** <note>original: ሞርር (morr)</note>; the translator omitted "having acted insolently" <note>original Greek: ἐξυብρίσας</note> and translated "do not boil over" <note>original Greek: μὴ ἐክζέσῃስ</note>. Manuscript C reads: **He climbed** <note>original: ሀ[ረ]ገ፡ (hä[rä]gä)</note> ] the manuscripts have **Harg** <note>original: ሀርገ፡</note>, but since I believe *Harg* was corrupted from *Harega* (climbed), I have restored the second person form. **Your bed** <note>original: ምስካብከ፡ (məskabkä)</note> ] + **that is the couch** <note>original: ይእቲ፡ አዐላ፡ (yə’ti ’ä‘äla)</note> in C and G. Verse 6. **And let it not descend** <note>original: ወኢይረድ፡ (wä’iyəräd)</note> ] **And he did not see** <note>original: ወኢአረያ፡ (wä’i’aräya)</note> in F, G, and H. Verse 7. **They made their anger hard** <note>original: አገገዱ፡ ቅጥዓሆሙ፡ (’ägägädu qəṭ‘ahomu)</note> ] **They were perverse in their wrath** <note>original: አተወያጡ፡ እመዐቶሙ፡ (’atäwäyaṭu ’əmä‘ätomu)</note> in manuscript C. Verse 8. **They praised you** <note>original: ሰብሑከ፡ (säbḥukä)</note> ] **May they praise you** <note>original: ይስብሑከ፡ (yəsbəḥukä)</note> in manuscript C. **Let them bow** <note>original: ይስገዱ፡ (yəsgädu)</note> ] **Let them bow** <note>grammatical variation</note> in C and G. Verse 9. **From your shoot** <note>original: እመሕዘትከ፡ (’əmäḥzätkä)</note> in F, **From your branch** <note>original: እመሕዝትከ፡</note> in G. **Climb!** <note>original: ዕረገ፡ (’ərəgä)</note> ] **He climbed** <note>original: ዐርገ፡ (‘ärgä)</note> in C and G; see 35:3. However, I suspect this command was also changed from the completed action "he climbed" due to a poor reading of the vowels. Verse 10. **The scepter** <note>original: መልእክቲ፡ (mäl’əkti)</note> ] **The message** <note>original: መልእክት፡ (mäl’əkt)</note> in H, G, and C; nevertheless, I hold our reading to be better, as it is more consistent with the Greek word for "ruler" <note>original Greek: ἄρχων (archon)</note>. Verse 13. **They asked** <note>original: ሠአሉ፡ (śä’älu)</note> ] **He was unable** <note>original: ሥአኖ፡ (śə’ano)</note> in C and G; concerning this word, you should consult Ludolf’s dictionary. **He shall sound and he shall spread** <note>original: ይነቍር፡ et ይስፋሕ፡</note>]

<meta>This page transitions from the specific textual corrections of Genesis 49 and 50 to a broader philological analysis of the Book of Exodus. <page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>58</page-num>
<header>B) **Annotations on Exodus.**</header>

### 1. Concerning the nature of the version and the condition of the text edited by us.

**Anyone who, having examined the Ethiopic version of Genesis, proceeds to Exodus, will find in the first third of the chapters hardly anything from which he might rightly conjecture that he has crossed into the domain of another translator. The same type of interpretation, almost the same vocabulary, and the same style shine through everywhere, nor do individual words occur except very rarely which seem foreign to that translator's method (for example, the translation of the word <note>original Greek: τετράፖδες (tetrapodes)</note> **four-footed animals** in 9:9, although another more common translation is read in the same place in verse 10). ^1) But from the middle of chapter 14, the traces of some other translator become more frequent; in chapters 20–23 there is such a great difference in the version from Genesis and the first chapters of Exodus that even less keen eyes cannot help but notice it, and if anyone compares chapters 25–30 with chapters 35–40, he will no longer doubt that this version of Exodus was made by two translators. One may see that Job Ludolf <note>a 17th-century German scholar who was the pioneer of Ethiopian studies in Europe</note> was already convinced of this in his *History of Ethiopia*, book 3, chapter 4, section 6. Therefore, as we are about to discuss the version of this book, let us begin by explaining the nature of this double version.**

Having compared the individual parts of Exodus again and again, both with each other and with the rest of the Pentateuch, I personally maintain that Exodus chapters 1–14:28 and 31:8–40:38 were translated by the same person to whom we owe our text of Genesis, but that chapters 14:29–31:7 were translated by another translator from a later period. For although I myself will prove below that the domain of each translator cannot be circumscribed by absolutely certain boundaries, it nevertheless appears from this that the greatest part of those things which are to be derived from the second translator are contained in the section I mentioned, because many of its chapters differ entirely from the remaining chapters of this book in both vocabulary and diction. What especially led me to that definition of limits was that the phrase <note>original Greek: υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ (huioi Israēl)</note> **sons of Israel** from 14:29 up to 31:7 is constantly translated with the phrase <term>ወሉድ፡ እስራኤል፡ (wälud əsra'el)</term> <note>literally "children of Israel," using a specific word for children</note>, whereas in the rest of the book, as in Genesis and the other books, it is translated with the word <term>ደቂቅ፡ እስራኤል፡ (däqiqa əsra'el)</term> <note>the more standard term for "children of Israel" in Ethiopic scripture</note> (compare also 28:1 and 4), which is a notable trace of this second translator. Led, therefore, by this evidence, if we separate that section from the rest of the book and investigate it more carefully, we will find many marks by which the work of the second translator is distinguished from the work of the first. We encounter a large abundance of words which the second translator was accustomed to translate differently than the first. He translates <note>original Greek: Θεὸν (Theon)</note> **God** and even twice <note>original Greek: Κύሪον (Kyrion)</note> **Lord** as <term>ፈጣሪ፡ (fätari)</term> <note>meaning "Creator"; see the places noted at 15:15, although the word <term>እግዚአብሔር፡ (əgzi'abəher)</term> "Lord" is also sometimes used in this section</note>; he either omitted the word <note>original Greek: συναγωγὴν (synagōgēn)</note> **assembly/synagogue** or translated it very poorly with the phrase <term>ንባበ፡ ትእይንት፡ (nəbabä tə'əyənt)</term> <note>literally "the speech of the camp"</note>; he translates <note>original Greek: ἁግιάζειን (hagiazein)</note> **to sanctify** as <term>ባረከ፡ (baräkä)</term> <note>to bless</note> and <term>አጽደቀ፡ (asädäqä)</term> <note>to justify/rectify</note> in 19:14, 22, 23; 28:37; 20:8, 11 and with nouns from the same roots...

---

1) It is also strange that from chapters 1–9:19 the word <note>original Greek: Κύሪος (Kyrios)</note> **Lord** is constantly rendered by the word <term>እግዚእ፡ (əgzi’)</term> <note>Master/Lord</note>, whereas from chapter 9:20 it is mostly rendered by the word <term>እግዚአብሔር፡ (əgzi'abəher)</term> <note>the standard Ethiopic word for God/Lord</note>, which is not yet sufficiently clear how it should be explained.

[The translator] also renders **holy** <note>original Greek: ἅγιον (hagion)</note> [in this way] in 10:23 and 19:6; he translates **glory** <note>original Greek: δόξαν (doxan)</note> either as **power** <note>original Ge'ez: ኃይል (hayl)</note> in 16:7, or as **chariot** <note>original Ge'ez: ሠረገላ (seregala)</note> and **his chariot** in 16:10, 24:16–17, and 28:2, or as **praise** <note>original Ge'ez: ስእብርት (se’ebret)</note> in 28:36, or as **honor** <note>original Ge'ez: ክብረ (kebra)</note> in 29:43. He renders **elders** <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτέρους (presbyterous)</note> as **chiefs/elders** <note>original Ge'ez: መላህቅት (malahəqt)</note> in 17:5 and 24:1 (though the version common to the other translator occurs in 18:12, 19:7, 24:9, and 24:14). He translates **priest** <note>original Greek: ἱερέα (hierea)</note>—referring to both pagans and Israelites—as **sacrificer** <note>original Ge'ez: ሠዋዒ (sawa’i)</note> in 18:1, 19:22, and 19:24 (the former translator calls the pagan priest **lord/husband** <note>original Ge'ez: ባል (bal)</note> and the Israelite priest **priest** <note>original Ge'ez: ካህን (kahin)</note>). He renders **face** <note>original Greek: πρόσωπον (prosōpon)</note> as **face/appearance** <note>original Ge'ez: ገጽ (gats)</note> in 16:14 and 28:33; **year** <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτὸν (eniauton)</note> as **year** <note>original Ge'ez: ዓመተ (’amata)</note> in 16:35, 21:2, 23:10–11, and 30:14 (though **year** <note>original Ge'ez: ዓመት (’amat)</note> is read in 23:16); **beast of burden** <note>original Greek: ὑποζύγιον (hypozygion)</note> as **donkey** <note>original Ge'ez: በእረቂ (ba’ereqi)</note> in 20:17 and 22:9 (though **donkey** <note>original Ge'ez: አህያ (ahya)</note> is read in 20:10, 22:8, 22:29, 23:4–5, and 23:12); **north** <note>original Greek: βοῤῥᾶν (borrhan)</note> as **north** <note>original Ge'ez: መስሜን (masmen)</note> in 26:18, 26:35, and 27:11; **south** <note>original Greek: νότον (noton)</note> as **west/south** <note>original Ge'ez: ዓረብ (’arab)</note> in 26:20 and 26:35; **the rear** <note>original Greek: τὸν ὀπίσθιον (ton opisthion)</note> as **the back/behind** <note>original Ge'ez: አኃሬ (ahare)</note> in 26:27; **the son** <note>original Greek: τὸν υἱὸν (ton huion)</note> as **the child/son** <note>original Ge'ez: ርቤ (rebe)</note> in 21:4 and 21:31; **firstfruits** <note>original Greek: ἀπαρχὰς (aparchas)</note> as **firstborn/firstfruits** <note>original Ge'ez: በኵራት (bakwrat)</note> in 22:28 (better in 25:2–3). He renders **breadth** and **width** <note>original Greek: πλάτος (platos) and εὖρος (euros)</note> as **breadth** <note>original Ge'ez: ፅፋሕ (tsəfah)</note>; **side** <note>original Greek: κλίτος (klitos)</note> as **side** <note>original Ge'ez: ምስልስጥ (məselsət)</note>; **seed** <note>original Greek: σπέρማ (sperma)</note> as **seed** <note>original Ge'ez: ዘር (zar)</note> in 28:39; **the sanctuary** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἅγιον (to hagion)</note> as **sanctuary** <note>original Ge'ez: መቅደስ (maqdas)</note>; **fruit/offering** <note>original Greek: κάርπωμα (karpōma)</note> as **fruits** <note>original Ge'ez: ፍረያት (freyat)</note> in 29:25, 38, 41 and **fruit of the sacrifice** <note>original Ge'ez: ፍሬ፡ መሠዋዕት (fre masawa’t)</note> in 30:9; **salvation/peace offering** <note>original Greek: σωτήሪον (sōtērion)</note> as **salvation/ransom** <note>original Ge'ez: ፋርቃን (farqan)</note> in 29:28; **generations** <note>original Greek: γενεὰς (geneas)</note> as **generation/age** <note>original Ge'ez: ዶር (dor)</note> in 30:8 and 30:10; **tablets** <note>original Latin: tabulas</note> as **tablets/boards** <note>original Ge'ez: ሰሌዳት (salidat)</note> in 27:8 and 24:12 (the former translator uses **tablets** <note>original Ge'ez: ፅላት (tsəlat)</note>); **dung** <note>original Greek: κόπρον (kopron)</note> as **excrement** <note>original Ge'ez: ፅሩዕ (tsəru’)</note> in 29:14; and he renders **visitation/census** <note>original Greek: ἐπίσκεψιν (episkepsin)</note> in 30:13 following with the word **visitation** <note>original Ge'ez: ተሐውጾ (tahawtso)</note>.

Furthermore, you may see how he translated **good** (20:11), **bread** (16:29), **to prevail** (17:11), **by the edge of the sword** (17:13, 22:23), **basket** (29:3, 23, 32), **to set apart/separate** (19:12), **slavery** (20:2), **sojourner** (20:10, better in 23:9, 12), **it may go well** (20:12), **doorpost and gate** (21:6, 27:16, in contrast to 12:7, 12), **to make atonement** (30:10), **and above** (30:14), **the sixth day** (16:5, 22:29), **the seventh day** (16:29, 30—differently in 16:26, 27, 20:10, 11, 24:16), and how he wrote the name **Joshua** <note>original Greek: Ἰησοῦν (Iēsoun)</note> (see the passages cited below at 17:9). Instead of **what?** <note>original Ge'ez: ምንት (ment)</note> he used **what?** <note>original Ge'ez: ሚ (mi)</note> in 17:4, and he delighted in the words **to send** <note>original Ge'ez: ፋኖ (fano)</note> and **to approach/be near** <note>original Ge'ez: ጠቃ (taqa)</note>. All these terms we have enumerated are usually translated differently by Translator I.

To these is added, in the description of the sacred tent <note>the Tabernacle</note>, a huge abundance of technical terms translated differently by Translator II than by Translator I, which we shall review below. Furthermore, there is also a great difference between the style of each. The speech of the first is fluent and flows smoothly; the style of the second is cruder and more awkward, and how much his speech lacks in ease and facility can best be seen from chapters 21–23. Not without a great loss of clarity, he very often omitted the use of the particles **and** <note>original Ge'ez: ወ (wa)</note> and **but/and** <note>original Ge'ez: ሰ (sa)</note>, the conjunctions **that/as** <note>original Ge'ez: ከመ (kama)</note>, **if** <note>original Ge'ez: እመ (’emma)</note>, and **whether** <note>original Ge'ez: እመሂ (’emmahi)</note>, and the relative pronoun **which/who** <note>original Ge'ez: ዘ (za)</note>. At times, he departed from the Greek words more freely than was proper, expressing with many circuits of words what ought to have been said briefly; at other times, having followed the Greek words with strange anxiety, he introduced obscurity of meaning through excessive brevity. 

Just as his style betrays a lesser skill in speaking and writing, so very many errors of interpretation show that he was inferior in the knowledge of Greek letters. The passages 15:27, 16:3, 17:12, 19:16, 20:24–26, 21:8, 21:35, 22:16, 23:16–18, 24:11, 28:34, and 29:27 are most miserably translated. In 15:13, he read **remnant** <note>original Greek: κατάλειμμα (kataleimma)</note> instead of **lodging/abode** <note>original Greek: κατάλυማ (katalyma)</note>; in 16:23 **you shall make** <note>original Greek: ποιείτε (poieite)</note> instead of **you shall bake** <note>original Greek: πέስσητε (pessēte)</note>; in 19:10 **let them widen** <note>original Greek: πλατύνωσαν (platynōsan)</note> instead of **let them wash** <note>original Greek: πλυνάτωσαν (plynatōsan)</note>; in 19:13 **he shall see** <note>original Greek: ὄψεται (opsetai)</note> instead of **he shall touch** <note>original Greek: ἄψεται (apsetai)</note>; in 29:23 **of all** <note>original Greek: πάντων (pantōn)</note> instead of **unleavened** <note>original Greek: ἀζύμων (azymōn)</note>; in 29:27 **as** <note>original Greek: ὡς (hōs)</note> instead of **who** <note>original Greek: ὃς (hos)</note>. He wrongly or not at all understood and translated **they spoke saying** (15:1), **to comfort/exhort** (15:13), **dances** (15:20), **Red [Sea]** (15:22), and **torches/fire-elements** <note>original Greek: πυρενέባሎን (pyrenebalon)</note> (15:27).

These unique features are so numerous that I am inclined to wonder whether we should conclude that this translator’s homeland was a different province of Abyssinia <note>Ethiopia</note> than that of the previous translator. From all these signs we have described, it is clear enough that the work of some other translator is contained in that section of Exodus. This is further confirmed by comparing passages such as 18:4 with 2:22, 28:17–20 with 36:17–20, Exodus 20 with Deuteronomy 5, and Exodus 21:23–25 with Leviticus 24:19–20 and Deuteronomy 19:21.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the Ethiopic (Ge'ez) translation of Exodus. The author is arguing that certain sections of the book were lost early on and replaced by a second, less skilled translator, whose work is interspersed with the original translation.</meta>

...was it lost? Indeed, since I cannot conceive why the main author would have left that specific part of Exodus to be translated by someone else, I respond that this "new version" was substituted in place of a lost primary one. This is further proven by the fact that not all parts of that section show the fingerprints of the later author; rather, many remnants of the primary version seem to have remained within it. The translation of chapters 18:6—19:11 and many verses in chapters 23, 24, 29, and 30 is of better quality and more closely matches the style of the principal translator. Furthermore, throughout this entire section, certain individual words are translated inconsistently—sometimes following the style of the first translator, sometimes the second—as proved by the examples mentioned above. Anyone who undertakes a review of the book will find many more examples; we will note some others below. 

Furthermore, just as not everything in this section reflects the "Second Translator," certain things occur in the rest of Exodus that I would attribute to the Second rather than the First. The phrase **Children of Israel** <note>original Ge'ez: ወሉድ፡እስረ“ (Welud Esre['el])</note> is also found in 34:20; the term **festivals** <note>original Ge'ez: ይር (yir), likely an abbreviation for 'years' or 'appointed times'</note> appears in 31:16; and **revelry** <note>original Ge'ez: ፋርቃን፡ (farqan)</note> appears in 32:6. A poor interpretation of a command in 23:18 also occurs in 34:25. Even before 14:29—specifically in 14:1–28—there are so many and such glaring translation errors <gloss>1)</gloss> that we must suspect the Second Translator supplemented certain parts there in his own way. In chapter 15 itself, verses 1 and 21 are translated so differently that it is necessary to recognize the hands of two different translators even within this one chapter. 

Since the boundaries between the two translators are not clearly divided by fixed limits, but rather their works are mixed together, I do not hesitate to resolve the question as follows: I propose that many passages of the primary version—especially those contained between chapters 14 and 31—were either corrupted or lost early on, but were later restored and supplemented by another translator using a new version made from a Greek manuscript. Just as he preserved and approved many parts not yet lost in that section, he also seems to have restored certain things in his own way in the rest of the book, and perhaps even in other books of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>. It follows, therefore, that even before the new "recension" <note>A revised edition of a text</note> of the version which we described on page 8, a correction of the text had already been established for at least some passages.

This concludes the discussion of the "Second Version." Regarding the nature of the "Principal Version," I have nothing new to add to what was said on page 16 and following; it only remains for me to confirm the opinion I gave above with arguments and examples drawn from the translation of Exodus. I have noted the following passages which the translator understood and rendered poorly: in 1:7, he gave the word *common/abundant* <note>original Greek: χυδαῖοι (khudaioi)</note> a sense of "vileness" or "meanness" and translated it as **wretched/scanty** <note>original Ge'ez: ሕቈረን፡ (heqworen)</note>; in 10:13, he mistakenly joined the word *all* <note>original Greek: ὅλη (holē)</note> with *earth* <note>original Greek: γῆ (gē)</note>; in 12:42, he translated *watch/vigil* <note>original Greek: προφυላክὴ (prophylakē)</note> poorly; and in 12:29, the phrase *of the one in the pit/dungeon* <note>original Greek: τῆς ἐν τῷ λάκκῳ (tēs en tō lakkō)</note>...

---

<gloss>1) In chapter 14, verses 1 and 9, the translator thought the word for "farmsteads/encampments" <note>original Greek: ἐπαύλεως (epauleōs)</note> was a proper name; in verse 5, he read "he said" <note>original Greek: εἶπεν</note> instead of "they said" <note>original Greek: εἶπαν</note>. In verse 7 (as in 15:4), he misunderstood the term for "officers/captains" <note>original Greek: τριστάτας (tristatas)</note>; in verse 11, he seems to have incorrectly translated "graves" <note>original Greek: μνήματα (mnēmata)</note>; in 13 and 16, he translated "time" <note>original Greek: χρόνον</note> and "divide/break" <note>original Greek: ῥῆξον</note> poorly; in 27, he incorrectly rendered "toward daybreak" <note>original Greek: πρὸς ἡμέραν</note>. Furthermore, verse 10 "they encamped" <note>original Greek: ἐστራቶπέδευσαν</note>, verse 15 [corrupt text], and verse 25 "axles" <note>original Greek: ἄξονες</note> are poorly translated. Verse 27 is poorly translated in its entirety.</gloss>

He provides linguistic evidence of translation errors and inconsistencies to support this theory of a "restored" text.</summary>

With the word **deep waters** <note>original Ge'ez: ቀላያት (qallāyāt)</note> he rendered it, as if the Greek **pit or cistern** <note>original Greek: λάκκος (lakkos)</note> here signified a well; in 33:3, he read **of you** <note>original Greek: σοῦ (sou)</note> instead of **you** <note>original Greek: σέ (se)</note>; regarding 34:25, see page 61; he did not understand 34:26 well (it is translated better in Deuteronomy 14:21); in 13:4 **the month of young shoots** <note>original Greek: μὴν τῶν νέων (mēn tōn neōn)</note> and 34:22 **the feast of the gathering** <note>original Greek: ἑορὴ συναγωγῆς (heortē synagōgēs)</note> were translated using names that seem to be derived from Ethiopian festivals; I do not know if they were coined by this translator himself.

Finally, it should be noted and criticized that this translator was not consistent in translating individual technical terms found in the description of the Tabernacle; rather, he sometimes translated the same words differently in different places. But although such errors are present in this version, the praise we awarded the translator of Genesis also applies to the translation of Exodus. Anyone will grant this praise even more willingly the more diligently they compare his translation with the work of the later translator. It is truly a great pity that a large part of this superior version has been lost: a great loss has thus been inflicted upon the sacred text.

...indeed were translated by the same interpreter in the same way. Finally, this also pertains here: that in the Septuagint text itself, both descriptions, having been made by different authors, agree with each other very little; no one fails to see that because of this variety in the Greek archetype, the variety of names in the Ethiopic version was also increased. As a result, a great confusion of technical terms invaded the Ethiopic text.

To **hyacinth** <note>original Greek: ὑακίνθῳ (hyakinthō)</note>, version II responds with **yahaknt** <note>original Ge'ez: የሀክንት፡; also in 35:6, 36:12, 15</note>, while version I uses **daresnā** <note>original Ge'ez: ደረስና፡</note>;

From these things which we have already said concerning the art and work of the interpreters, it is naturally clear that to that reviser of a later age, who undertook the new recension of the text described on page 8, a sufficiently large cause and material for correcting was offered in this book. Those things which had been translated less well, especially by the **Second Interpreter** <note>original Latin: interpreተ IIᵉ, likely "the Second Translator"</note> throughout chapters 20–23, demanded correction, although in those very places we notice that he satisfied his duty as an emendator less than elsewhere; for there he regarded the style and form rather than the matter and the sense of the sacred text. He performed the task of an emendator better in the description of the Tabernacle; for as much as he was able, he corrected and supplemented the Ethiopic text offered to him according to his Greek exemplar, and he looked well both to the clarity of the sense and to the agreement of parallel passages. However, in chapters 35–40, where the Greek Septuagint text [diverges] from the words and order of the book...

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the Ethiopic translation of Exodus. Having previously discussed specific vocabulary discrepancies between different translators (Translator I and II), the author now shifts to discussing the broader textual history, the influence of Origen’s Hexapla, and the specific manuscript evidence from Codex C and Codex G.</meta>

page 64

It is well known that the Hebrew text deviates significantly [from the Ethiopic]; an editor, using a manuscript of the **Hexapla** <note>A famous six-columned edition of the Old Testament compiled by the scholar Origen in the 3rd century to compare different versions of the Bible.</note> that he had at his disposal, established what was almost an entirely new version. This text, thus corrected and emended, is copied with sufficient faithfulness in **Codex C**; **Codex G**, however, represents the ancient version more accurately than it did in the book of Genesis, and contains only a few slight corrections. While we had intended to note the most important readings of this new revision in our critical notes, we found we could not avoid printing certain chapters of the book from the revision in **Codex C** in their entirety. As for the readings pertaining to stylistic improvements and grammatical rules, so many are found in **Codex C** throughout that section of Exodus that we could in no way list all of them, or even the greater part of them.

Now that we have said enough regarding the authors of our version, it remains for us to add some details about the condition of the text we have published. It is clear from the notes we made on Genesis that the sacred text has been corrupted and defiled in many ways by readers and scribes. In Exodus as well, we have noted many errors of this kind, which we believe should be attributed to the readers and scribes rather than the original translators; perhaps even some of those passages we listed above as being poorly or ignorantly translated by the interpreters should be blamed on these later hands. The following phrases were omitted in our text:

*   3:15 **God of Abraham... Jacob** <note>original Greek: Θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ—Ἰακώβ</note>
*   5:20 **to meet them** <note>original Greek: εἰς συνάντησιν αὐτοῖς</note>
*   8:18 **God** <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεός</note>
*   11:8 **whom you lead** <note>original Greek: οὗ σὺ ἀφηγῇ</note>
*   12:9 **and with the inner parts** <note>original Greek: καὶ τοῖς ἐνδοσθίοις</note>
*   13:21 **to show them the way** <note>original Greek: δεῖξαι αὐτοῖς τὴν ὁδόν</note>
*   14:20 **and the night passed** <note>original Greek: καὶ διῆλθεν ἡ νύξ</note>
*   14:28 **behind them** <note>original Greek: ὀπίσω αὐτῶν</note>
*   14:29 **in the midst of the** <note>original Greek: ἐν μέσῳ τῆς</note>
*   15:13 **by your righteousness** <note>original Greek: τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ σου</note>
*   15:23 **and they came** <note>original Greek: ἦλθον δέ</note>
*   15:24 **unto Moses** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ Μωυσῆ</note>
*   18:21 **god-fearing** <note>original Greek: θεοσεβεῖς</note>
*   19:20 **and he called... of the mountain** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐκάλεσε—τοῦ ὄρους</note>, due to **homoeoteleuton** <note>original Latin: ob homoeot.; a common scribal error where the eye skips from one word to another with a similar ending, resulting in missing text.</note>
*   20:10 **the servant... your ox** <note>original Greek: ὁ παῖς—ὁ βοῦς σου</note>
*   20:20 **take courage** <note>original Greek: θαρσεῖτε</note>
*   21:34 **silver... of them** <note>original Greek: ἀργύριον—αὐτῶν</note>
*   22:8 **and of a garment** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἱματίου</note>
*   22:13 **or should it become a captive** <note>original Greek: ἡ αἰχμάλωτον γένηται</note>
*   30:34 **onycha** <note>original Greek: ὄνυχα; a fragrant shell used in incense.</note>
*   32:13 **the land which you spoke of** <note>original Greek: τὴν γῆν, ἣν εἶπας</note>
*   34:28 **of the covenant** <note>original Greek: τῆς διαθήκης</note>
*   35:11 **and its carrying poles** <note>original Greek: καὶ τοὺς ἀναφορεῖς αὐτῆς</note>
*   36:3 **all** <note>original Greek: πάντα</note> (the first instance); 

Furthermore, gaps that existed in the passages 2:15, 4:3, 12:22, 15:17, 16:1, 16:8, 18:3, 18:4, 19:24, 20:24, 21:17, 22:14, 22:25, 22:26, 23:12, 25:23, 25:30, 25:34, 26:1, 26:9, 26:15, 26:19, 26:35, 27:11, 27:19, 28:12, 28:18, 29:2, 29:21, 30:8, 30:37, 32:2, 34:27, 38:20, 38:23, 39:9, and 40:26 have been supplied from **Codex C** or **G**, or by our own efforts. We have enclosed certain **spurious additions** <note>Additions not found in the original source but added later by scribes.</note> within parentheses in passages 7:26, 10:8, 10:10, 12:49, 13:4, 14:21, 21:5, 21:18, 21:31, 28:5, 33:10, and 35:5; see also 6:6, 7:28, 14:6, 14:18, 14:32, and 30:14. You will find passages that are more or less corrupt in 10:6, 12:42, 13:4, 14:11 (?), 15:16, 16:23, 18:19, 18:20, 18:26, 21:13, 22:17, 25:38–40, 26:4, 26:14, 26:27, 26:29, 28:12, 29:5, and 32:21; additionally, the text of the entire section from chapters 21–29 is less well preserved in **Codex FHG**. Finally, just as in Genesis, there occur a few places in Exodus where individual words seem to have been changed according to the authority of a certain **Arabic version**, for example, 5:14, 12:8, and others.

Whoever carries out a comparison will see that by these readings a text is represented that is indeed similar to the text of the most famous Codex Alexandrinus, but nevertheless differs from it in many various ways. They agree almost more frequently with the readings of Codex Ambrosianus (VII) and Codex Coislinianus (X) and others of this type compared in Holmes’s work than with that one.

[ነር] <note>scribal marker</note> "Ra" <note>original: ረ</note> in manuscripts F and H. *Verse 15.* ("Phinehas" <note>original: ፈኒከ፡</note>) "Phania" <note>original: ፈኒአ፡</note> in manuscripts F and H, "Phanika" <note>original: ፋኒከ፡</note> in manuscript G, "Phanias" <note>original: ፋኒአስ፡</note> in manuscript C; since these readings prove that this word was not understood in Ethiopic, I myself substituted "Canaanite" <note>original: ከነናዊት፡</note>. *Verse 16.* "Kohath" <note>original: ቃሃት፡</note>] also written as "Qahat" <note>original: ቀሃት፡</note>. *Verse 17.* Manuscripts F and H: "Gershom, father" <note>original: ገርሶም፡ አቡ፡</note>] "their fathers" <note>original: አበዊሆሙ፡</note> in manuscripts C and G. *Verse 18.* [አ] "Ka" <note>original: ከ</note> in manuscript F, "Ko" <note>original: ኮ</note> in manuscript G, just as if it were "Issachar." *Verse 19.* "Mahali" <note>original: መሎሊ፡</note>] "Mahali" <note>original: መሐሊ፡</note> in manuscript C. *Verse 22.* [የላ] "Yan" <note>original: ያን፡</note> in the manuscripts. — Manuscript C also has "and Kotara" <note>original: ወኮተራ፡</note>. *Verse 23.* Manuscripts C and G: "for Nahshon" <note>original: ለነአሶን፡</note>; also "and he shall know" <note>original: ወይታምር፡</note>, likewise in 28:1. *Verse 25.* Manuscripts C and G usually show "Phinehas" <note>original: ፈኒሐስ፡</note>. "This is the Ko[rathite]" <note>original: ዝውእቱ፡ ቆ፡</note>] "And these are the heads" <note>original: ወእሉ፡ ቀዳምያተ፡</note> in manuscript C. *Verse 26.* [ው] "Wa" <note>original: ወ</note> in manuscripts F and H. *Verse 27.* "He brought them out" <note>original: ያወፅአሙ፡</note> in manuscript H. *Verse 29.* Manuscript C precedes "Speak" <note>original: ተናገር፡</note> with "And" <note>original: ወ</note>.
