### Chapter 7

**Verse 2.** "He spoke to him" <note>original: ነገሮ፡</note>] "He spoke to him" <note>original: ነገሮ፡</note> in manuscripts C and G. **Verse 5.** [-behe <note>original: -በሔ</note>] "the sea" <note>original: ባሕ</note> in manuscripts F and H, where the vowels were read incorrectly; see Genesis 14:3. **Verse 7.** "And it was" <note>original: ወኮነ፡</note>] "And it was for him" <note>original: ወኮኖ፡</note> in manuscripts C and G. **Verse 9.** "They are" <note>original: ሀሉ፡ ነ፡</note>] "They were" <note>original: ሀለዉ፡</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 12.** "Their staffs" <note>original: አብት“፡</note>] "Their staffs" <note>original: አብትረሆሙ፡</note> in manuscripts C and G. "And it was" <note>original: ወኮነ፡</note>] "And they were" <note>original: ወኮኑ፡</note> in manuscript C, "And it was for him" <note>original: ወኮኖ፡</note> in manuscript G. **Verse 15.** "For me" <note>original: ልዪ፡</note>] "For me a memorial" <note>original: ልየ፡ ተዝካረ፡</note> in manuscript C. "Guardian" <note>term: Gebez (ገበዝ); a title for a church warden or custodian</term>] I did not wish to correct this word, since it appears in three manuscripts and is also recognized in Ludolf's lexicon; however, I have no doubt that it has degenerated from the word for "side" <note>original: ገቦ፡</note> in manuscript H; manuscript G actually has "side" <note>original: ገቦ፡</note> without the H. I noted in the *Catalogue of Ethiopic Manuscripts of the Bodleian Library* (Oxford, 1848, page 72) that the word "guardian" <note>original: ገበዝ፡</note> signifies something else. Manuscript C reads: "And for that female" <note>original: ወለእንተ ክቲ፡</note>. **Verse 16.** "His people" <note>original: ሕዝቦ፡</note>] "The people" <note>original: ሕዝበ፡</note> in manuscripts G and H, "My people" <note>original: ሕዝብየ፡</note> in manuscript C. Manuscript C reads: "He shall sacrifice to me" <note>original: ይሤወይኒ፡</note>. Manuscripts C and G read: "You did not hear this" <note>original: ኢሰማዕከ፡ ዛቲ፡</note>] + "day" <note>original: ዕለት፡</note>. **Verse 17.** "I" <note>original: እነ፡ 2°</note>] manuscript C prefixes "Behold" <note>original: ናሁ፡</note>. [Te <note>original: ጥ፡</note>] "To" <note>original: ጦ፡</note> in manuscripts F and H. **Verse 19.** "Their rivers" <note>original: አፋላጊሆሙ፡</note> in manuscript C. "And they became blood" <note>original: ወኮኑ፡ ደሞ፡</note>] omitted in manuscripts C and G. Manuscript C: "Stones" <note>original: አዕባነ፡</note>. **Verse 21.** "And they died" <note>original: ወሞቱ፡</note> in manuscript C. "Blood" <note>original: ደሞ፡</note>] "Blood" <note>original: ደየ፡</note> in manuscripts C and G, but the Greek text has *to haima* <note>original: τὸ αἷμα; "the blood"</note>. **Verse 22.** Manuscripts C and G: "The magicians" <note>original: ሐራክያኒ፡</note>. **Verse 23.** "And he entered" <note>original: ወአተ“፡</note>] "And he turned back" <note>original: ወአተወይጠ፡</note> in manuscript C. "And in this" <note>original: ወበዘንቱ፡</note>] "And" omitted in manuscript C. **Verse 25.** "Seven days" <note>original: ሰበሀ፡ ዕለት፡</note>] compare Genesis 47:2; "Seven days" <note>original: ሰቡዕ፡ መዋዕለ፡</note> in manuscripts C and G. **Verse 27.** "It sent" <note>original: ፈነወት፡</note>] "It sent" <note>original: ፈነወተ፡</note> in manuscript G, "He sent them" <note>original: ፈነወቶሙ፡</note> in manuscript C. Manuscript C: "Frogs" <note>original: ቈርናንዛት፡</note>, likewise in Verse 28, 29, and Chapter 8:1–9. Manuscript G: "Frogs" <note>original: ቍርዛንዛት፡</note>, likewise in Verse 28, 29, and Chapter 8:1–9. **Verse 28.** "Your house" <note>original: ቤተከ፡</note>] "Your houses" <note>original: አብያቲከ፡</note> in manuscript C. **Verse 29.** "Your people" <note>original: ሕዝብከ፡</note> and "Your servants" <note>original: ሀበይትከ፡</note> are transposed in manuscript C.

## Chapter 13.

*Verse* 2. Manuscript C: **"Sanctify five" <note>original: ቀዳሴ፡ ሐመሰ</note>] "In his grief" <note>original: በሕዝኑ</note>** in manuscript C; because the former word is obscene, the corrector substituted this; likewise in *Verses* 12, 13, and 15. **"Even until" <note>original: እስከኒ</note>] "Until" <note>original: እስከ</note>** in manuscript G, **"And until" <note>original: ወእስከ</note>** in manuscript C. *Verse* 4. All manuscripts have **"Hallelujah Nisan" <note>original: ሃሌሉያ፡ ኒሳን</note>**; but the first word seemed sufficient to me; for since the feast of unleavened bread is named **"at the feast of Hallelujah" <note>original: በበዓለ፡ ሃሌሉያ</note>** in Deuteronomy 16:16, it follows that **"the month of Hallelujah" <note>original: ወርኃ፡ ሃሌሉያ</note>** is the month of the feast of unleavened bread. Therefore, I have bracketed the word **"Nisan" <note>original: ኒሳን</note>**, as it was inserted for the sake of illustration. A different version of the Greek phrase *tōn neōn* <note>meaning "of the new [fruits/ears of grain]"</note> occurs in 23:15 and another in 34:18. *Verse* 5. **"And if" <note>original: ወእመ</note>] "And when" <note>original: ወአመ</note>** in manuscript C. **[is/exists]** see 3:18. *Verse* 7. Instead of **"into" <note>original: ውስጥ</note>** manuscript C substitutes **"into" <note>original: ውስጥ</note>** <note>referring to a minor spelling variation</note>, which is a useless correction. **[ ]** in manuscripts C and G; manuscripts F and H [read] **"of a female ass" <note>original: አድገት</note>**, so that it signifies the womb "of a female ass." *Verse* 15. **"He killed" <note>original: ቀተለ</note>] + "the Lord" <note>original: እግዚአብሔር</note>** in manuscript C. *Verse* 16. **[Re]** in manuscripts C and G, **Er** in manuscripts F and H. **CHAPTER 15.** *Verse* 1. **"Children" <note>original: ውሉደ</note>] "Children" <note>original: ደቂቀ</note>** <note>A subtle change in the Ge'ez word for "children" or "descendants."</note> in C; the same correction appears in 14:29 and in several other places from Chapter 15 through Chapter 31; see what we said above on page 58. **"Of the Cherubim" <note>original: ዘኵራቤ</note>]** placed after **"Israel" <note>original: እስራኤል</note>** in H; it is read twice, in both locations, in F. 

Regarding the Song of Moses which now follows, since it is found attached to the Psalms themselves in almost all Ethiopic manuscript Psalters (along with the other songs and prayers of the prophets), Hiob Ludolf <note>a famous 17th-century German orientalist often called the founder of Ethiopian studies</note> also ensured it was printed in his edition of the Psalter (Frankfurt, 1701, page 320). Its text most closely agrees with that shown in C, taken from the corrector's revision. — After **"He has triumphed" <note>original: ስብሐ</note>** in C, another version of the Greek words *ᾌσωμεν—δεδόξασται* ("Let us sing—he is glorified"), which Ludolf provides, is written as: **"Let us praise the Lord, the praised one who is glorified" <note>original: ንሰብሖ፡ ለእግዚአብሔር፡ ስቡሐ፡ ዘተሰብሐ</note>**. Finally, another version of the Greek words *ἐνδόξως γὰር δεδόξασται* ("for he is gloriously glorified") is read below in Verse 21. G: **"And the one who delivers us" <note>original: ወመስተጽአነ</note>**.

[**"His name" <note>original: ሰሙ</note>**] in C, **"Siwa"** <note>an obscure reading, possibly a corruption</note> in F and H. C and G: **"The God of my father" <note>original: አምላክ፡ አቡየ</note>**. *Verse* 4. In C, **"The chosen" <note>original: ኀሬያን</note>** and the following name are placed in the nominative case; nevertheless, **"and they were drowned" <note>original: ወተሠጥሙ</note>** is read. *Verse* 13. **"Those who" <note>original: እለ</note>] "To those who" <note>original: ለእለ</note>** in C and G. *Verse* 16. **"Power" <note>original: ኀይል</note>** etc.] I suspect these words may be corrupted from **"By the power—firm" <note>original: በኀይለ፡—ጽኑዕ</note>**. Instead of **"He passes over" <note>original: የኀልፍ</note>**, C and G read **"He passes over" <note>original: የኀልፍ</note>** twice. **Verse 10. ኢየሀዌ፡ <note>original: iyahawe</note>] ኢየሀወዌ፡ <note>original: iyahawawe</note>** in manuscript **C** from a correction. Ludolf <note>Hiob Ludolf, 1624–1704, a foundational scholar of Ethiopic studies</note> indeed did not record that word from our text in his lexicon, but having compared the passage in Exodus 23:29, I certainly do not doubt that the word **ሀዌ፡** <note>original: hawe</note> or **ሀወዌ፡** <note>original: hawawa</note> should be established, in which the sense of "to orphan and deprive" is inherent. **Verse 13. ለአምርከ፡ <note>original: la’amreka, "to your knowledge"</note>] ለአምርኮ፡ <note>original: la’amreko</note>** in **FCG**, **ለአምርኩ፡ <note>original: la’amreku</note>** in **H**; I have restored that reading from which I thought the others were corrupted. **Verse 15. ይትከሤ፡ <note>original: yitkasē, "he shall be punished"</note>] ይሙት፡ <note>original: yimut, "he shall die"</note>** in **C**, likewise in **Verses 16 and 17.** **Verse 16. በውስተ፡ <note>original: bawesta, "within"</note>] እም፡ <note>original: em, "from"</note>** in **CG**. **Verse 17** is taken from manuscript **G**, but is missing in the others; however, so that the verse may be made conformable to the others, I substituted **ይትከሤት፡ <note>original: yitkasēt</note>** for **ይሙት፡ <note>original: yimut</note>**. **Verse 18. **Verse 1. and he said to him** <note>original: ወይቤሎ፡</note> [the first instance]] **and he spoke to him** <note>original: ወነበቦ፡</note> in C. **Verse 2. **[in the things] which are in it** <note>original: ba-lattā; Ge'ez: በ፡ለታ፡</note>] which, although it is actually unnecessary <note>Latin: quod cum re vera superfluum sit</note>, is omitted <note>indicated by the symbol ^</note> in Manuscript G. **Verse 15. [ ]** omitted in Manuscript G. **in the rings** <note>original: ba-ṣabāʼ; Ge'ez: በጸባእ፡</note>] Manuscript C; **of the fingers** <note>original: za-ʼaṣābəʻ; Ge'ez: ዘአጻብዕ፡</note>] Manuscripts F and H; likewise F and H in Verses 26 and 27. I do not know <note>Latin: nescio</note> whether the translator read the Greek phrase "in the fingers" <note>Greek: ἐν τοῖς δακτύλοις</note>, or whether the word **rings** <note>original: ḥəlaqāta; Ge'ez: ሕለቃተ፡</note>, which should have been placed before the word **fingers** <note>original: ʼaṣābəʻ; Ge'ez: አጻብዕ፡</note>, was omitted by the scribes; see 27:4. **in [that] which I commanded you** <note>original: ba-za-ʼazazkukəmu; Ge'ez: በዘአዘዝኩክሙ፡</note>] The translator had the reading "of the covenant" <note>Greek: τῆς διαθήκης</note> (instead of "of the ark" <note>Greek: τῆς κιβωτοῦ</note>) in his Greek copy; in Manuscript C, this has been corrected to **which is on the Ark** <note>original: za-dabe tābot; Ge'ez: ዘደቤ፡ ታቦት፡</note>.

**Verse 17. Manuscript G:** **it was given** <note>original: tawəhba; Ge'ez: ተውኅበ፡</note>. Manuscripts C and G are accustomed to substitute **half** <note>original: manfaq; Ge'ez: መንፈቅ፡</note> for **division/half** <note>original: nəfāq; Ge'ez: ንፋቅ፡</note>.
**Verse 18. beaten work** <note>original: fāḥqo; Ge'ez: ፋሕቆ፡</note>] **he polished it** <note>original: fāḥaqo; Ge'ez: ፋሐቆ፡</note> in Manuscript G. **[they became]** <note>original: honu; Ge'ez: ሆኑ፡</note>] **hu** <note>Ge'ez: ሁ፡</note> in Manuscripts F, G, and H. **[at its two ends]** <note>original: bābātihā; Ge'ez: ባባቲሃ፡</note>] **bābātihā** <note>Ge'ez: ባባቲሃ፡</note> in Manuscripts F, G, and H, both of which are nonsensical <note>Latin: absonum</note>. In Manuscript C, a simpler version of the whole verse is read: **And he made two cherubim of gold, of beaten work; and you shall make them from the two corners of the Ark.** <note>original: wa-gabara 2 kirubel za-warq fāḥqo wa-təgabromu ʼəm 2 maʼəzanti-hu la-tābotu; Ge'ez: ወገበር፡ ፪ ኪሩቤል፡ ዘወርቅ፡ ፋህቆ፡ ወትገብሮሙ፡ እም ፪ መእዘንቲሁ፡ ለታቦቱ፡</note>
**Verse 19. with it** <note>original: məslaktā; Ge'ez: ምስለክታ፡</note>] **with it** <note>original: məslabātī; Ge'ez: ምስለባቲ፡</note> in Manuscripts C and G.
**Verse 20. In Manuscript C,** **cherubim** <note>original: kirubel; Ge'ez: ኪሩቤል፡</note> is of the masculine gender. Manuscript H: **they shall face each other** <note>original: yətnāṣarā; Ge'ez: ይትናጸራ፡</note> (first instance), likewise Manuscript G (second instance).
**Verse 21. and you shall beat it** <note>original: wa-taweqṭo; Ge'ez: ወትዌቅጦ፡</note>] **and it shall rest** <note>original: wa-tanabbər; Ge'ez: ወትነብር፡</note> in Manuscript C. **[ ]** omitted <note>indicated by ^</note> in Manuscripts F, G, and H.
**Verse 22. Manuscript C:** **from above** <note>original: ʼəmlāʻla; Ge'ez: እምላዕለ፡</note> omitting the following **from upon** <note>original: ʼəmdabe; Ge'ez: እምደቤ፡</note>. **tabernacle** <note>original: marṭulā; Ge'ez: መርጡላ፡</note>] Above in Verse 9, it was read as **marṭul** <note>Ge'ez: መርጡል፡</note>; Manuscripts F and H vary in this; Manuscripts C and G more consistently show **marṭul** <note>Ge'ez: መርጡል፡</note>. **[which]** <note>original: za; Ge'ez: ዘ</note>] omitted <note>indicated by ^</note> in Manuscripts F and H. **I have commanded you** <note>original: ʼazazkuka; Ge'ez: አዘዝኩከ፡</note>] **I shall command you** <note>original: ʼəʼazazkuka; Ge'ez: እአዘዝኩከ፡</note> in Manuscript C.
**Verse 23. of gold, 7 [cubits]** <note>original: za-warq 7; Ge'ez: ዘወርቅ፡ ፯፡</note>] **of wonderful [wood] which does not rot** <note>original: ʼəm-ʻəḍub za-ʼiyənäqqəz; Ge'ez: እምዕፁብ፡ ዘኢይነቅዝ፡</note> in Manuscript C (cf. the Hebrew text <note>referring to acacia wood</note>).
**Verse 24. 50 palm-breadths** <note>original: ṣəbz 50; Ge'ez: ፅብዝ፡ ፶</note>] Since the translator wished to respond to the Greek word for "palm-breadth" <note>Greek: παλαιστοῦ</note>, I personally think that **50 fingers** <note>original: ʼaṣābəʻ 50; Ge'ez: አጻብዕ፡ ፶</note> ought to be read; compare the same confusion between "fingers" <note>Greek: δακτύλων</note> and "fingers" <note>Greek: δακτύλων</note> in Verses 15, 26, and 27.
**Verse 26. rings** <note>original: ḥəlaqāta; Ge'ez: ሕለቃተ፡</note>] In Manuscript H, the spelling **ḥəlaqāt** <note>Ge'ez: ሕላቃት፡</note> is used; in Manuscripts C and G, **ḥəlaqātāta** <note>Ge'ez: ሕለቃታተ፡</note> is common wherever they show this word.

**And you shall place** <note>original: wa-ʼanbər; Ge'ez: ወአንብር፡</note>] + **into the fingers** <note>original: wəsta ʼaṣābəʻ; Ge'ez: ውስተ፡ አጻብዕ፡</note> in Manuscripts F and H (cf. Verse 15), which, since it is nonsensical, I have omitted. In Manuscript C, verses 24–27 are translated as follows: **And you shall plate it with pure gold <note>cf. Hebrew</note> and you shall make for it a molding around it; and you shall make for it a rim the size of 50 fingers around it; and you shall make 50 rings of gold and you shall place [them] in the 50 corners of the table upon its 50 legs; and the rings shall be near the rim for the table; and its rings shall be places for the poles which carry the table.**
**Verse 29. In place of** **coverings/dishes** <note>original: manṣafāt; Ge'ez: መንጸፋት፡</note>, Manuscript C substitutes **altars/plates** <note>original: maṣābəḥ; Ge'ez: መጻብሕ፡</note>, likewise **bowls** <note>original: mayāməḥ; Ge'ez: መያምሕ፡</note> in place of **place of the ladles** <note>original: beta mawāṣḥət; Ge'ez: ቤተ፡ መዋጽሕት፡</note>, and **ladle** <note>original: wāṣḥ; Ge'ez: ዋጽሕ፡</note> in place of **measures** <note>original: masafartāt; Ge'ez: መሰፈርታት፡</note>, according to the version of the translator in Isaiah 38:12. **with it** (second instance)] omitted in Manuscripts C and G.
**Verse 30. [ ]** omitted in Manuscripts F, G, and H. Manuscripts C and G: **table** <note>original: māʼəda; Ge'ez: ማእደ፡</note>.
**Verse 31. Manuscripts C and G:** **lampstand** <note>original: māḫtot; Ge'ez: ማኅቶት፡</note> (first instance); likewise Manuscript C (second instance) and in Verses 32 and 34. Manuscripts C and G: **its handles** <note>original: maʼāḫzəhā; Ge'ez: መኣኅዝሃ፡</note>, likewise in Verses 33 and 34, with Manuscript C prefixing **and** <note>original: wa-</note>. Manuscripts C and G: **and it surrounded/a circuit** <note>original: wa-kababa; Ge'ez: ወከበበ፡</note>, likewise in Verses 33, 35, and 36.
**Verse 32. Manuscript C:** **the other** <note>original: kāʼlə; Ge'ez: ካልእ፡</note> without **from** <note>original: ʼəm-</note>.
**Verse 33. with 4** <note>original: məsla 4; Ge'ez: ምስለ፡ ፬</note>] **with for the 4** <note>original: məsla la-4; Ge'ez: ምስለ፡ ለ ፬</note> in Manuscripts F and C.
**Verse 34. [and]** <note>original: wa; Ge'ez: ወ</note>] Drawn from Manuscript H; **[ ]** these are missing in all manuscripts and were supplied by me.
**Verse 35. in the midst of** <note>original: māʼkala; Ge'ez: ማእከለ፡</note>] **and under** <note>original: wa-təḥta; Ge'ez: ወትሕተ፡</note> in Manuscript C.

Verse 37. Manuscripts C and G: **And you shall make** <note>original: wa-tagabbər; Ge'ez: ወትገብር፡</note>; Manuscript C: **And you shall arrange** <note>original: wa-təśārʻu; Ge'ez: ወትሠርዑ፡</note>; Manuscript C: **And they shall shine** <note>original: wa-yabarrəhu; Ge'ez: ወየበርሁ፡</note> instead of **And they shall close** <note>original: wa-yaʻāḍəʼu; Ge'ez: ወየዐጽኡ፡</note>.
Verse 38. See Ludolf’s Lexicon <note>referring to Job Ludolf’s *Lexicon Aethiopico-Latinum*, 1661</note> page 506. — **Beaten work** <note>original: fāḥqo; Ge'ez: ፋሕቆ፡</note>] **a likeness** <note>original: məslēta; Ge'ez: ምስሌተ፡</note> in Manuscript G. Verses 38–40, since they are damaged in the original manuscripts <note>Latin: mutili sint</note>, have been corrected and supplemented in Manuscript C as follows: **And that which is behind it, and it itself... and its golden censers, you shall make a likeness of gold; and all these its vessels, make according to the pattern which I showed you on the mountain.**

->Chapter 26.<- Verse 1. **They thought** <note>original: halayu; Ge'ez: ሀለዩ፡</note>] **one** <note>original: ʼaʻhāda; Ge'ez: አዕሃደ፡</note> in Manuscript C. Verse 2. **4** [the second occurrence]] Manuscripts A, C, and G place this number before the noun. Verse 4. Manuscripts C and G instead of **...** <note>unclear Ge'ez phrase: ሞዖ ህዋ፡</note> display **loops** <note>original: malahwā; Ge'ez: መለህዋ፡</note>; see also Verses 5, 10, and 11. It is self-evident that Verse 4 is damaged, and so far from the gap being filled in Manuscripts C or G, even the phrase **into the second entrance** <note>original: wəsta dagam mabayaʼət; Ge'ez: ውስተ፡ ደገም፡ መበየእት፡</note> is cast out from them. Verse 5 is also shortened. Verse 6. Manuscripts C and G usually show **clasps** <note>original: ḫʷaʼāyāt; Ge'ez: ኈአያት፡</note>. Verse 7. **of sackcloth** <note>original: za-śa-qo; Ge'ez: ዘሠቆ፡</note>] Manuscript C adds **curtains** <note>original: ʼaʻyāya; Ge'ez: አዕያየ፡</note> before it. Verse 8. Manuscript C adds **for the tent** <note>original: la-nabaw; Ge'ez: ለነበው፡</note> at the end of the verse. Verse 9. [**8**] the manuscripts have either the letter **S** <note>the Ge’ez letter 'sā' represents the number 60, but here it likely refers to a specific numeral variant</note> or a numeral sign. Verse 12. **face** <note>original: gaṣṣa; Ge'ez: ገጸ፡</note>] ^ [omitted] in Manuscript C. **behind** <note>original: kawalā; Ge'ez: ከወላ፡</note>] **behind** (variant spelling) <note>original: kawālā; Ge'ez: ከዋላ፡</note> in Manuscripts C and G. Verse 13. Manuscripts H and C: **from its side** <note>original: ʼəm-gaboʼahā; Ge'ez: እምገቦአሃ፡</note>. Verse 14. Before **hyacinth-colored [skins]** <note>original: yākənta; Ge'ez: ያክንተ፡</note>, it is certain that **from its upper part** <note>original: ʼəm-ʻəsto; Ge'ez: እምዕስቶ፡</note> has been lost, followed by **hyacinth**; then, with that word lost, this was placed in the accusative case. Verse 16. **4 cubits** <note>original: həmādu 4; Ge'ez: ህመዱ፡ ፬</note>] **ten [cubits] was the height of his cubit** <note>original: qamu la-10 həmādo; Ge'ez: ቀሙ፡ ለ፲ህመዶ፡</note> in Manuscript C. Verse 17. **joint** <note>original: maskamat; Ge'ez: መስከመት፡</note>] **ornament** <note>original: məsləmāt; Ge'ez: ምስልማት፡</note> in Manuscript G, **support** <note>original: masmakat; Ge'ez: መስመክት፡</note> followed by **its roots/bases** <note>original: śərawihu; Ge'ez: ሥረዊሁ፡</note> in Manuscript C. **they are supported** <note>original: yəsak-kamu; Ge'ez: ይሰከሙ፡</note>] **they are fastened** <note>original: yəsām-manu; Ge'ez: ይሳመኑ፡</note> in Manuscripts C and G. **to the cubit** <note>original: la-hamadu; Ge'ez: ለሀመዱ፡</note>] **to each one** <note>original: ʼaʻhədu; Ge'ez: አዕህዱ፡</note> in Manuscripts C and G. Verse 18. **southward** <note>original: maʻwān; Ge'ez: መዕዋን፡</note>] **south** <note>original: ʼazēb; Ge'ez: አዜብ፡</note> in Manuscript C (compare the Hebrew). Verse 19. [**of silver** <note>original: za-səktat; Ge'ez: ዘስክትት፡</note>] omitted in Manuscripts F, G, and H, and has been supplied by us. In Manuscript C, instead of **silver** <note>original: səktat</note>, the word **casting** or **alloy** <note>original: maʻlayu; Ge'ez: መዕለዩ፡</note> is everywhere common; see Verses 25, 32, 37, and 27:10–15 of our text; however, in Manuscript G, that word **silver** is usually written. [**for your corners** <note>original: lakləkəhəmu; Ge'ez: ለክልክህሙ፡</note>] in the manuscripts: **in your corners** <note>original: baklākhun; Ge'ez: በክላክሁን፡</note>, but we have substituted the former so that the sense would conform to what follows. Verse 20. **Arabia** (mistranslated as South) <note>original: harabi; Ge'ez: ሀረቢ፡</note>] see 35:27 and 9; the translator did not understand the Greek **Noton** (South Wind) <note>Greek: Νότον</note>: for it follows from 27:9, where it has **Harb** <note>Ge'ez: ሀርብ፡</note>, that **Harabi** is not to be taken as the name of Arabia. The author of Manuscript C wrongly substituted **North** <note>original: samēn; Ge'ez: ሰሜን፡</note>, with which word he wished to render the Greek **Borrhan** (North Wind) <note>Greek: Βοῤῥᾶν</note> and the Hebrew **Tsaphon** <note>Hebrew: צפון; tsafon</note>; see the Hebrew and Verse 18 above, and 27:11 below. Verse 22. **face** (the second instance)] **toward** <note>original: mangala; Ge'ez: መንገለ፡</note> in Manuscript C. Verse 23. **corner** <note>original: māʼkan; Ge'ez: ማእከን፡</note>] Manuscripts G and C usually show **and a corner** <note>original: wa-ʼazan; Ge'ez: ወአዘን፡</note> or **corner** <note>original: mahazan; Ge'ez: መሀዘን፡</note>; however, see 25:26 above in Manuscript C. Verse 24. **they shall be equal** <note>original: ʻərayāta yەکuna; Ge'ez: ዕረያተ፡ ይኵና፡</note>] ^ [omitted] in Manuscript C. Verse 27. Instead of **side** or **rib** <note>original: mankaga; Ge'ez: መንከገ፡</note>, Manuscript C twice provides the plural **sides/ribs** <note>original: manākagat; Ge'ez: መናከገት፡</note>, while Manuscript G in this verse and C and G in Verse 28 provide the singular **side**. [**number** <note>original: ḫʷəl-qu; Ge'ez: ኍልቁ፡</note>] Manuscripts F, G, and H have **all** <note>original: kʷəl-lo; Ge'ez: ኵሎ፡</note>, which must certainly be a corruption of the former word.

### CHAPTER 27.
Verse 1. Manuscript C: **altar** instead of **the house of the altar**. Verse 2. **and I shall make the altar**] omitted in Manuscript C; it follows **and I shall make in it**] **and from it** in Manuscript C. Manuscripts C and G: **its horns**; the suffix **-homu** <note>a plural possessive suffix</note> determines the noun like an article. Verse 3. [**And**] omitted in Manuscript G, **E** in Manuscripts F and H; in Manuscript C this noun itself is missing, but in its place is inserted **and make the vessels for the altar, the shovels and the bowls**, (compare the Hebrew), with the following **and the fleshhooks** etc. Manuscripts F and H: **and he scraped**. Verse 4. <meta>This page transitions from the textual notes on Exodus to the beginning of the commentary on the Book of Leviticus. It establishes that the Ge'ez version of Leviticus is remarkably well-preserved compared to the previous two books, likely due to it being less frequently read and handled by medieval Ethiopian scribes.</meta>

## C) **Annotations on Leviticus.**

### 1. **Concerning the state of the text and the character of the version.**

The Book of Leviticus enjoys a greater integrity of text and is less infected by the stain of corruption—which gradually crept into manuscript codices over the centuries—than Genesis and Exodus. The reason for this seems obvious to me: this body of laws was read less diligently by the Christian people of Ethiopia than the historical books. Therefore, the manuscripts of Leviticus were less worn out by use and were less subject to the pointless alterations of readers or scribes than the others. Aside from the places where we have filled in gaps <note>term: lacunae; missing sections in a manuscript</note> (4:2; 8:24, 33; 9:14; 13:13; 14:4; 15:4, 7, 20; 19:3; 20:23; 22:18; 24:10, 11; 25:2; 26:7), there are a few others where, due to the carelessness of scribes or the damage of time, certain things seem to have been omitted or to have vanished: 

Specifically, 1:16 *beside the altar* <note>Greek: παρὰ τὸ θυσιαστήριον</note>; 2:13 *of the covenant* <note>Greek: διαθήκης</note>; 13:51 *it is unclean* <note>Greek: ἀκάθαρτός ἐστι</note>; 17:15 *and he shall be clean* <note>Greek: καὶ καθαρὸς ἔσται</note>; 18:14 *and you shall not go in to his wife* <note>Greek: καὶ πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ οὐκ εἰσελεύσῃ</note>; 15 *for she is [his wife]* <note>Greek: γυνὴ γὰρ - αὐτῆς</note>; 19:3 *and your Sabbaths* <note>Greek: καὶ τὰ σάββατα ὑμῶν</note> (some of which we have supplied from **Manuscript C**); 7 *on the third day* <note>Greek: τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ τρίτῃ</note>; 20:21 *it is impurity* <note>Greek: ἀκαθαρσία ἐστίν</note>; 22:5 *or regarding a man by whom he may be defiled* <note>Greek: ἢ ἐπ' ἀνθρώπῳ, ἐν ᾧ μιανεῖ αὐτόν</note>, due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>a scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar-looking word later in the text</note>; 13 *but she has no offspring* <note>Greek: σπέρμα δὲ μὴ ᾖ αὐτῇ</note>; 18 *for a burnt offering* <note>Greek: εἰς ὁλοκαύτωμα</note>; 23:18 *without blemish* <note>Greek: ἀμώμους</note> (the first instance); 34 *of the seventh [month]* <note>Greek: ἑβδόμου</note>; 25:9 *on the tenth of the month* <note>Greek: τῇ δεκάτῃ τοῦ μηνός</note>; 38 *your God* <note>Greek: ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν</note>; 46 *after you* <note>Greek: μεθ' ὑμᾶς</note>. 

In chapter 7:9–10 (according to the Greek numbering 6:39–40) there is a larger gap, for everything is missing from *in the oven* <note>Greek: ἐν τῷ κλιβάνῳ</note> up to *not mixed* <note>Greek: μὴ ἀναπεποιημένη</note>; and in 14:41 the entire verse is omitted (due to homoeoteleuton). Perhaps some of the places we have mentioned were shortened by the translator himself. Occasionally, single words or short phrases are found intruded into the context of the Ge'ez version without the authority of the Greek model, namely: 
9:15 **the covering** <note>original Ge'ez: maśwār</note>; 
11:16 (Greek verse 15) **and all that is like it** <note>original Ge'ez: wa-kʷellu zamaysalo</note>; 
13:44 **the leprosy which is in his temple** <note>original Ge'ez: lamṣ ’anta westu senklātu</note>; 
16:29 **and** <note>original Ge'ez: wa</note> before **who was** <note>original Ge'ez: zahalawa</note>, and **of** <note>original Ge'ez: ’e</note> after it; 
21:3 **if** <note>original Ge'ez: ’emma</note> (the second instance); 
23:14 **and he shall purge** <note>original Ge'ez: wayāṣḥet</note>; — **to your God** <note>original Ge'ez: la’amlākekemu</note> (the first instance); 
25:11 **without** <note>original Ge'ez: ’enbala</note>; 
some other things we have enclosed in parentheses in 16:21, 22:9, 25:11. 

The order of certain names or sentences is inverted in 8:35, 11:14, 29, 30, 18:9, 20:27, and perhaps also 14:6–7 and 16:22. The persons of pronouns and verbs have been changed in 22:8, 9, 33; 25:44, 46; 27:33. Places where the text seems corrupt are 10:18, 15:3, 25:37, 47, 48, 51, 53 (see also the note on 4:7). Misread vowels occur in 15:3 and 19:15 (see also the emendations in 11:38, 21:2, 28:40, and others). If we set aside these errors we have listed, we shall judge the genuine text of the ancient version to be well-preserved. It also seems relevant to note here that the number of places where the text of **Manuscripts F and H** required correction from **Manuscripts C and G** is smaller in Leviticus than in Genesis and Exodus.

As for the translation itself, which we have just seen to be quite well-preserved in the manuscripts, it was well-executed by the translator and is worthy of all praise...

But all these things were omitted without any loss of meaning and are easily spared; nor do we blame the translator, who thus satisfied his passion for brevity, described above on page 19. Even in certain places where he did not strictly follow the words of the Greek text—specifically 1:15 and 5:8 (**he shall wring off its head** <note>original Greek: ἀποκνίσει τὴν κεφαλήν</note>), 11:23, 13:33, 55, 14:35, 56, 15:17, 19:7 (**it is unfit for sacrifice** <note>original Greek: ἄθυτόν ἐστιν</note>), 19:35, 21:19, 22:27—he certainly did not harm the sense of the text. Nor is the text corrupted by the additions found in 5:22, 6:2, 15:16, 19:3, 25:10, and 25:11 (provided they were added by the translator and not by later scribes). In the passages 15:25 **not in** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐν</note>, 19:20 **inquiry/visitation** <note>original Greek: ἐπισκοπή</note>, 19:28 **for a soul** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ ψυχῇ; referring to the dead</note>, 7:35 **anointing** <note>original Greek: χρίσις</note>, and 10:6 **you shall [not] uncover [your heads]** <note>original Greek: ἀποκιδαρώσετε; referring to the removal of the priestly turban</note>, he translates very well, although in the latter two places it seems to me that he followed a certain interpretative explanation <note>term: gloss; a marginal or interlinear note that clarifies a word</note>. I would also like you to notice passage 26:25, where he expressed in Ge'ez a double reading <note>term: doublet; when a translator includes two different ways of translating the same phrase</note> that he had found. Therefore, all these things we have enumerated confirm the translator’s merit rather than diminish it.

However, other things occur by which the excellence of the version is indeed somewhat detracted. The reader is most offended by the confusion of the names *olah* <note>original Hebrew: עוֹלָה; burnt offering</note>, *minchah* <note>original Hebrew: מִנְחָה; grain offering</note>, and *korban* <note>original Hebrew: קָרְבָּን; offering or gift</note>. Just as this confusion appears in certain other places in the Ethiopic Pentateuch <note>term: Pentateuch; the first five books of the Bible</note>, it is especially conspicuous in the Ethiopic version of Leviticus. For since the "Seventy" <note>term: Septuagint; the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> had translated those names differently in different places—using the terms **burnt offering**, **offering**, **gift**, **sacrifice**, and **whole offering** <note>original Greek: ὁλοκαύτωμα, κάρπωμα, δῶρον, προσφορά, θυσία, ὁλοκάρπωμα</note> with little consistency—it happened that the Ethiopic translator himself used **ቍርባን፡** <note>English: qwerban; offering/gift</note> and **መሥዋዕት፡** <note>English: maswa'et; sacrifice</note> indiscriminately. He thus completely removed the distinction that exists between those names. I must admit, however, that another cause contributed to this matter: namely, that the Ge'ez language suffers from a lack of various synonymous names to signify different types of sacrifice.

Equally, and for the same reasons, the difference between a **heave offering** <note>original Hebrew: תְּרוּמָה; terumah</note> and a **wave offering** <note>original Hebrew: תְּנוּפָה; tenufah</note> (rendered in Greek as *separation*, *imposition*, or *removal* <note>original Greek: ἀφόρισμα, ἐπίθεμα, ἀφαίρεμα</note>) is plainly abolished in the Ethiopic version. Furthermore, the meaning of the word **assembly/convocation** <note>original Hebrew: מִקְרָא; miqra; Greek: κλητή</note> in Chapter 23 and...

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Ge'ez (Ethiopic) translation of Leviticus. The previous page listed specific phrases the translator omitted; this page focuses on words that were lost, misunderstood, or substituted due to linguistic limitations or human error.</meta>

The word **Azazel** <note>Hebrew: עֲזָאזֵל; Greek: *apopompaios* or *apopompē*, referring to the "scapegoat" or "sending away"</note> in Chapter 16 has completely disappeared. In other places as well, most notably in Chapter 25, the Greek version is sometimes very obscure. As a result, even in the Ethiopic translation, several verses (such as 25:15, 33, and 47–53) were translated incorrectly and against the intended meaning of the Hebrew text.

While errors of this kind arose from the faulty state of the Greek source text, a certain lack of vocabulary in **Ge'ez** <note>the classical liturgical language of Ethiopia</note> also had an effect. Because of this, the translator often handled rare Greek names found in Leviticus in one of two ways: he either retained the Greek word without translating it into Ethiopic (especially in the list of clean and unclean animals in Chapter 11, and also in 2:4, 5 and 6:14; though he acted differently in 7:12 and 8:26), or he used names with a similar, but not identical, meaning (as seen in Chapters 11; 22:22–24; 21:18–20, and others).

However, the translator also made certain other mistakes where there was no obstacle in the Greek version or in the nature of the subject itself. He translated the following with less than ideal accuracy:
*   1:16 **the crop** <note>Greek: *ton prolobon*, the digestive organ of a bird</note>
*   3:14 **he shall offer** <note>Greek: *anoisei*</note>
*   4:7 **of the mixture** <note>Greek: *tēs syntheseōs*; though this is translated better elsewhere</note>
*   8:6 **he brought forward** <note>Greek: *prosēnenke*</note>
*   8:7 **according to** <note>Greek: *kata*</note>
*   10:3 **he was stunned** <note>Greek: *katenychthē*, meaning silenced or pierced with grief</note>
*   10:4 **of the sanctuary** <note>Greek: *tōn hagiōn*, literally "of the holy things"</note>
*   13:3 (and following) and 14:37 (and following), the words **lowly**, **hollow**, and **deeper** <note>Greek: *tapeinos*, *koilos*, *enkoiloteros*</note>
*   13:30 (and following) and 14:54 (and following), the word **eruption** or **fragment** <note>Greek: *thrausma*; rendered in Ethiopic as <gloss>sign</gloss> <note>Ge'ez: ትእምርት፡</note> or <gloss>color</gloss> <note>Ge'ez: ሕብር፡</note></note>
*   13:28 **mark** <note>Greek: *charaktēr*</note>
*   13:55 **it is fixed** <note>Greek: *estēriktai*</note>
*   16:7 **he shall take** <note>Greek: *lēpsetai*</note>
*   16:13 **of the testimonies** <note>Greek: *tōn martyrōn*</note>
*   18:17 **you shall not take** <note>Greek: *ou lēpsē*</note>
*   20 **to be defiled with her** <note>Greek: *ekmianthēnai pros autēn*</note>
*   23:4 **in their appointed times** <note>Greek: *en tois kairois autōn*</note>
*   26:16 **distress** <note>Greek: *aporia*</note>
*   26:23 **you are disciplined** <note>Greek: *paideuthēte*</note>
*   26:30 **carcasses** <note>Greek: *kōla*, literally "limbs"</note>

Sometimes he failed to understand the Greek words at all, or understood them differently than they were written: in 2:1, he read "soul" in the wrong grammatical case; in 15:10, he read **seeing** instead of **lifting**; and in 22:23, he read **seal** instead of **sacrifices**. In 2:14, he rendered the word for **roasted grain** <note>Greek: *chidra*</note> with the word <gloss>pure</gloss> <note>Ge'ez: ንጹሕ፡</note>, but in 2:16 he omitted it entirely. He also translated poorly the words **gift** (6:13), **all** (6:15), **acceptable to you** (19:5 and 22:19), and **you shall not practice divination** (19:26; see also Genesis 44:5, 15). He substituted a different meaning for the words in 11:34 and the phrase **whatever is inside** in 11:33, as well as the phrase **in abundance** in 25:36. In 13:33, 44, and 21:9, he seems to have misread and mistranslated the Greek. In 14:37, he omitted the word for **hollows**, which he seems not to have understood. In 22:3, he mistook the verb **they said** for a first-person form ("I said"), and in 25:14–15, he mistook the verbs for third-person singulars. In 16:44, he attributed the act of **scattering** to the people rather than to God. In 13:10–11, 17:2, 23:16–17, and 25:8–9, he followed a different word punctuation than what is established in the standard text. However, regarding the passages in 10:18 and 27:20 and 29, it seems doubtful to me whether they were translated incorrectly by the author or corrupted by later scribes. These are all the points I wish to note as being less than well translated in this book; the rest of the version is worthy of all praise.

Up to this point, we have not discussed the identity of the translator himself; for we have assumed, and continue to assume, that the translator of Leviticus is the same person who translated Genesis and Exodus. Indeed, nothing stands in the way of this opinion; the method of translation and the style reveal the same author. No small argument for this opinion is contained in the fact that those technical names, which pertain to the sacred rites of the Israelites—

## 2. Survey of readings which the translator had in his Greek manuscript, differing from the received Greek text.

<note>This section lists specific differences between the standard Greek Septuagint and the manuscript used by the Ethiopic translator. The symbol "+" indicates an addition, "^" indicates an omission, and "instead of" indicates a word substitution.</note>

**1**, 3 + **it** <note>Greek: *auto*</note> after **he shall bring** <note>Greek: *prosaxei*</note>. 8 ^ **the** <note>Greek: *ta*</note> before **on** <note>Greek: *epi*</note> (perhaps he read Wherever we have placed a question mark after individual readings in this overview, there is doubt as to whether that reading was received into the Ethiopic text by the translator himself, or by later scribes from other versions or by conjecture. Furthermore, many places are found where, in the Ethiopic version, either a <term>suffix pronoun</term> <note>a short pronoun form attached to the end of a word, common in Semitic languages</note> (for example, after **hands**, **finger**, **garments**, or **neighbor** in 3:2, 8, 13, 29, 30, 33, 34; 5:12, 21; 8:24; 9:9, etc.) or the conjunction **that** <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> (in passages 19:31, 32; 21:15; 22:3, 8, 31; 23:3, 36; 25:17, 38; 26:1, 2, 13, and others) is read as an intrusion. However, it seems probable to me that the translator did not have a different Greek reading in his exemplar in these places, but rather added those elements himself according to the laws and natural spirit of his own language. The same thing may be observed in many passages throughout the rest of the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>the first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical comparison of manuscript variations for the Book of Leviticus. Having finished the instructions regarding the priests' conduct in Chapter 10, the text now transitions into the dietary laws of Chapter 11. The translator continues to note differences between the primary manuscripts (labeled C, F, H, and G) and compares the Ge’ez (Old Ethiopic) text to the Greek Septuagint version.</meta>

For **he commanded** <note>Ge'ez: *azaza*</note> and **for Moses**, Manuscript C has **he commanded me** <note>Ge'ez: *azazanni*</note>. **Verse 16.** For **in this...** Manuscript C has a variation in the phrasing. The second mention of **Moses** is omitted <note>indicated by the symbol ʌ</note> in Manuscript C. **Verse 18.** The phrase **to the place** in Manuscripts F and H is written as **[lazaa] haba**, which is without sense. **holy things:]** **sanctuary:** Manuscript C. **[Te] Ta** Manuscripts F and H. **Verse 19.** **[P] Yi** Manuscripts F, G, and H.

### Chapter 11.

**Verse 3. all:]** **all:** <note>a minor grammatical case change in Ge'ez</note> Manuscript C. For **chews the cud** Manuscript C presents **ruminate** <note>Ge'ez: *yimasekwe'u*</note>; likewise in verses 4–7 and 26. **Verse 4.** Manuscript G: **camel** <note>original Greek: *ton kamēlon*</note>. **hare:]** **hare:** <note>spelling variation</note> Manuscripts F and H; likewise in verses 5 and 6 (before **its hoof**). **Verse 6. [hi] hi** <note>a particle</note> Manuscripts F and H. Manuscript C has this concerning the hare: **"Because the hare has a hoof and its claw is divided, but it does not chew the cud"**; this is an emendation by the author, who did not like the idea of the hare ruminating; a part of this same correction is already found in the accepted text of the Septuagint <note>Historically, the hare was categorized as a ruminant in the Bible, which the scribe of Manuscript C likely corrected based on observation.</note>.

The names of the animals in verses 29 and 30 are listed in a different order than in the Greek text: for the scribes placed the local <note>vernacular</note> names before the foreign ones, which is why the meanings of some have become doubtful and obscure. To me, it seems that the "land crocodile" <note>original Greek: *ho krokodeilos ho chersaios*</note> was translated as if they were two names, **lizard** and **crocodile** (Manuscripts C and G: **and crocodile**); the Greek *mygalē* <note>shrew-mouse</note> as **latseqt**, and the Greek *saura* <note>lizard</note> as **hangēga** (Manuscripts C and G: **hangwegw**); while **hantsan** (Manuscript G: **hantsan**) appears to be a corruption of the Greek *chalabōtēs* <note>a type of lizard or gecko</note>. **Verse 33.** Manuscripts C and G: **they shall break it**, subjunctive mood, see verse 25. **Verse 34. and all:]** **and all:** <note>case change</note> Manuscripts G and H. **is poured:]** **which is poured:** Manuscripts C and G, followed by **water** (in the accusative case). **Verse 35. and unclean:]** <insert>ʌ</insert> Manuscripts C and G <note>omitted</note>. **36. and whoever touches—it is:]** <insert>ʌ</insert> Manuscript C <note>omitted</note>. **Verse 37.** Manuscripts F and H: **which one sows**, see Genesis 1:11. **Verse 38. ## **D) Notes on the Book of Numbers.**

### **1. On the condition of the text and the character of the version.**

Our manuscripts have provided a fairly well-preserved text of the Book of Numbers. A significant number of damaged passages were indeed found in manuscripts **F** and **H**, but we were able to supply most of those gaps—and the largest ones—from manuscripts **C** and **G**. Only in a few places have we ourselves attempted to restore lost words without the authority of the manuscripts; therefore, words supplied from **C** and **G** or restored by us can be read in the passages **1, 32. 50. 2, 16. 31. 7, 24. 29. 35 (41. 53. 65. 77. 83). 10, 9. 11, 21. 28. 35. 12, 16. 13, 24. 30. 14, 22. 15, 5. 39. 16, 11. 28. 19, 21. 25. 4, 26. 34. 51. 64. 65. 27, 19. 28, 27. 28. 31, 7. 35, 5**; I would especially like you to note **6, 5. 13, 3. 15, 5. 28, 12. 13. 29, 6. 31, 44. 45. 34, 8. 9. 36, 6**, where the gaps were more extensive. 

There remain some passages where individual words or sentences are missing and desired; for the following are absent due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>A common scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar-looking word further down, resulting in the omission of the text in between.</note>: 
**3, 8** **all things** <note>original Greek: "πάντα"</note>. 
**9, 18** **the children of Israel shall encamp and by the command of the Lord** <note>original Greek: "παρεμβαλοῦσιν οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ διὰ προστάγματος Κυρίου"</note> due to homoeoteleuton. 
**10, 9** **in your land** <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῇ γῇ ὑμῶν"</note>. 
**11, 30** **Moses** <note>original Greek: "Μωυσῆς"</note>. 
**34** **there** <note>original Greek: "ἐκεῖ"</note>. 
**12, 5** **and the three went out to the Tabernacle of Witness** <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐξῆλθον οἱ τρεῖς εἰς τὴν σκηνὴν τοῦ μαρτυρίου"</note> due to homoeoteleuton. 
**13, 32 (33)** **in it** <note>original Greek: "ἐν αὐτῇ"</note>. 
**14, 33** **and they shall bear your unfaithfulness, until your carcasses are consumed in the wilderness** <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἀνοίσουσι τὴν πορνείαν ὑμῶν, ἕως ἂν ἀναλωθῇ τὰ κῶλα ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ"</note> due to homoeoteleuton. 
**15, 41** **I am the Lord your God** <note>original Greek: "ἐγὼ Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῶν"</note> for the first time, due to homoeoteleuton. 
**18, 1** **of the sanctuary, and you and your sons shall bear the sins** <note>original Greek: "τῶν ἁγίων καὶ σὺ καὶ οἱ υἱοί σου λήψεσθε τὰς ἁμαρτίας"</note> due to homoeoteleuton. 
**21** **all** <note>original Greek: "πᾶν"</note>. 
**20, 13** **and he was sanctified among them** <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἡγιάσθη ἐν αὐτοῖς"</note>. 
**22, 19** **and I will know** <note>original Greek: "καὶ γνώσομαι"</note>. 
**27** **and Balaam was angered** <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐθυμώθη Βαλαάμ"</note>. 
**23, 22** (compare **24, 8**) **to him** <note>original Greek: "αὐτῷ"</note>. 
**27** the entire verse. 
**28, 7** **strong drink** <note>original Greek: "σίκερα"</note>. 
**30, 11** **with an oath** <note>original Greek: "μεθ' ὅρκου"</note>. 
**31, 21** **the priest** <note>original Greek: "ὁ ἱερεύς"</note>. 
**30** **of all** <note>original Greek: "πάντων"</note>. 
**54** **before the Lord** <note>original Greek: "ἔναντι Κυρίου"</note>. 
**32, 8** **Barnea** <note>The site Kadesh Barnea.</note>. 
**21 and 22** **until his enemy be destroyed from before his face and the land be subdued before the Lord** <note>original Greek: "ἕως ἂν ἐκτριβῇ ὁ ἐχθρὸς αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ προσώπου αὐτοῦ καὶ κατακυριευθῇ ἡ γῆ ἔναντι Κυρίου"</note> due to homoeoteleuton. 
**29** **the land** <note>original Greek: "τὴν γῆν"</note>. 
**34, 11** **from the east to the springs** and **the borders of Bela** <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ἐπὶ πηγὰς" and "τὰ ὅρια Βηλά"</note>. 
**35, 19** **he shall kill the murderer when he meets him** <note>original Greek: "ἀποκτενεῖ τὸν φονεύσαντα ὅταν συναντήσῃ αὐτῷ οὗτος"</note> due to homoeoteleuton. 
**21** **or in enmity he smote him with his hand and he die** <note>original Greek: "ἢ διὰ μῆνιν ἐπάταξεν αὐτὸν τῇ χειρὶ καὶ ἀποθάνῃ"</note> due to homoeoteleuton. 

In certain other places, gaps seem to have arisen for us rather through the error of the translator or a defect in the Greek manuscript, namely in **Chapters 3, 13. 47. 14, 45. 16, 5. 21, 15. 22, 18. 24, 16. 17**, concerning which you may see what we shall say below. There occur very few places where certain additions—nearly all of them minor—have intruded into the Ethiopic version, namely in **Chapters 3, 12. 7, 3. 19, 2. 28, 5. 29, 36**; only one was added against the authority of the Greek in **Chapters 26, 40. 28, 17. 29, 9. 31, 4 (three times)**; moreover, what was added in **Chapter 27, 18**—**holy** <note>original Ge'ez: "ቅዱስ፡" (qedus)</note>—fits well (from the aforementioned places, we have included the additions in parentheses in **Chapters 3, 12. 19, 2. 26, 40. 28, 17. 29, 9**). Finally, in many places the manuscripts—sometimes all, sometimes individual ones—provided readings corrupted either by the decay of letters or the exchange of vowels, namely in **Chapters 3, 38. 47. 4, 27 (and 47?). 5, 25. 26. 30. 6, 13. 8, 26. 10, 6. 31. 13, 33. 15, 26. 29. 16, 32. 18, 7. 15. 24. 19, 12. 13. 20, 5. 23, 7. 18. 19. 24, 3.**

<meta>This page continues the textual analysis of the Book of Numbers, moving from specific omissions to a broader discussion of the translation's authorship and linguistic style within the Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Bible.</meta>

**15, 16. 20—24. 25, 13. 27, 4. 12. 19. 28, 6. 21. 29. 29, 4. 10. 15. 30, 9. 15. 31, 3. 33, 56.** Regarding all these passages, you may consult what we have noted in the catalogue of variant readings. We pass over proper names and corrupted numerical signs in this section, as it would be a lengthy task to review them all.

Concerning the author of the Ethiopic version of Numbers, we do not have even the slightest doubt that the same person who translated Genesis, the greater part of Exodus, and Leviticus also interpreted this book into Ethiopic <note>The ancient Semitic language of Ethiopia, also known as Ge'ez</note>. To be sure, there are certain individual words in the Book of Numbers that are translated differently than in the previous books. For example:

*   In Chapter **4, 9**, he translates "the tongs" <note>original Greek: "τὴν λαβίδα"</note> with the word *guṭat* <note>original Ge'ez: "ጉጠት"</note>, whereas it is translated differently in **Exodus 38, 17**.
*   In **19, 6** and **24, 6**, he translates "cedar" and "made of cedar" <note>original Greek: "κέδρον" and "κέድρινον"</note> with the word *ʿeḍ* <note>meaning "wood" or "tree"; original Ge'ez: "ዕፅ"</note>, which differs from **Leviticus 14, 4. 6**.
*   The phrase "to be gathered to his people" <note>original Greek: "προστίθεσθαι πρὸς τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ"; a biblical idiom for death</note> is translated differently in **20, 24. 26; 27, 13; 31, 2** than it is in **Genesis 25, 8. 17; 35, 29; 49, 33** (compare also the readings for these passages in Genesis).
*   He translates "commanders of thousands" and "commanders of hundreds" <note>original Greek: "χιλιάρχους" and "ἑκατοντάρχους"</note> in **31, 14. 31, 48. 52. 54** differently than in **Exodus 18, 25**.

However, variations of this kind seem to stem from the inconsistency and liberty of the translator, a fault we have frequently criticized before ¹). There is little weight in these variations to refute our opinion, especially when weighed against the gravity of the opposing arguments. Indeed, the entire character of the translation in this book is the same as in the preceding ones. The same Greek words and phrases are almost everywhere translated with the same Ethiopic words that we read in the other books of the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses</note>. 

You will find excellent examples of this if you read the sacrificial laws of Numbers alongside similar sections in the earlier books; likewise, compare the names of the sacred vessels and the individual parts of the sacred Tabernacle found in **Numbers 4, 6—16. 25. 26. 31. 32; 8, 2—4** and elsewhere with the parallel passages in Leviticus and Exodus, and reconsider what we discussed above on page 63. Furthermore, I would like you to notice the translation of individual words, such as:

*   "Salt" or "Salty" <note>original Greek: "ἁλυκὴ"</note> in **Num. 34, 3. 12; Gen. 14, 3; Deut. 3, 17**.
*   "Covenant" <note>original Greek: "διαθήκη"</note> in **Num. 25, 12. 13**.
*   "Called" or "Convocation" <note>original Greek: "κλητὴ" or "ἐπίκλητος"</note> in **Num. 29, 1. 7. 12; Lev. 23; Ex. 12, 16**.
*   "Servile work" <note>original Greek: "ἔργον λατρευτὸν"</note> in **Num. 28, 18** ff.; **Ex. 12, 16** (though different in **Lev. 23**).
*   "Throughout your generations" <note>original Greek: "ἐν ταῖς γενεαῖς ὑμῶν"</note> in **Num. 10, 8; 15, 15. 21. 23; 18, 23; 35, 29; Gen. 17, 12; Ex. 12, 14**, and very often in Leviticus (though different in some middle passages of Exodus).
*   "Possession" <note>original Greek: "κατάσχεσις"</note> in **Num. 13, 2 (3); 27, 12; Lev. 25, 24; Gen. 47, 11 (Gen. 48, 4)**.

Regarding the actual quality of the version produced by the translator for this book, one may judge it in almost the same way as we noted above concerning the interpretation of the other books.

*   "Pillar" <note>original Greek: "στήλην"</note> in **21, 28; 22, 41;** and **33, 52**.
*   "Opposite" <note>original Greek: "ἐναντίοι"</note> in **1, 53** and **2, 2**.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Ethiopic (Ge'ez) translation of the Book of Numbers, focusing on places where the translator deviated from the Greek Septuagint source due to misunderstanding or manuscript corruption.</meta>

There are quite many places in which the author, either because the Greek text was poorly read or wrongly understood, translated individual words poorly, or at least with little accuracy. He mistranslates the words "to take down" <note>original Greek: καθαιρεῖν</note> and "to set up" <note>original Greek: ἀνιστάναι</note> in **1:51**; "unclean because of a soul" <note>referring to a corpse; original Greek: ἀκάθαρτον ἐπὶ ψυχῇ</note> in **5:2, 9:6, 7, 10** (though it is better in **Leviticus 19:28**); "and she be not taken" <note>original Greek: καὶ αὐτὴ μὴ ᾖ συνειλημμένη</note> in **5:13**; "boiled" <note>original Greek: ἑφθὸν</note> in **6:19**; "and beyond" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐπέκεινα</note> in **15:23**; "as a privilege" <note>original Greek: εἰς γέρας</note> in **18:8**; "is added" <note>original Greek: πρόσκειται</note> in **21:15**; "of the hewn stone" <note>original Greek: τοῦ λελαξευμένου</note> in **21:10** (better in **23:14**); "I have been taken" <note>original Greek: παρειλήμμαι</note> and "I will turn away" <note>original Greek: ἀποστρέψω</note> in **23:20**; "having encamped" <note>original Greek: ἐστρατοπεδευκότα</note> in **24:2**; "was initiated" <note>original Greek: ἐτελέσθη</note> in **25:8** (better in verse 5); "to afflict the soul" <note>original Greek: κακῶσαι ψυχὴν</note> in **30:14**; "to take the total" <note>original Greek: τὸ κεφάλαιον λαβεῖν</note> in **31:26, 49** (better in **4:2**); and "to be missing" <note>original Greek: διαφωνεῖν</note> in **31:49** (which the translator of **Exodus 24:11** himself also did not understand). He also poorly translates "departure" <note>original Greek: ἔξοδον</note> in **29:35**. In **Chapter 30**, because he wrongly interpreted the words "to refuse" <note>original Greek: ἀνανεύειν</note> in verses 6, 9, 12 and "to take away" <note>original Greek: περιαιρεῖν</note> in verses 13, 14, 16, he distorted the entire meaning of this law. Various errors are also present in the version of the passages in **21:29, 30** and **35:33**.

Sometimes he seems to have followed a corrupt reading of his Greek manuscript or to have misread a good reading through carelessness. For instance, in **Chapter 7:15, 21, 27, 33, 39, 45, 51**, he translates "blameless" <note>original Greek: ἄμωμον</note> instead of "lamb" <note>original Greek: ἀμνόν</note>; in **13:32 (33)**, "holding fast" <note>original Greek: κατέχουσα</note> instead of "devouring" <note>original Greek: κατέσθουσα</note>; in **14:37**, "in a good land" <note>original Greek: γῇ δὲ ἀγαθῇ</note> or something similar instead of "in the plague" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ πληγῇ</note>; in **21:4**, "outside the mountain" <note>original Greek: ἔξω τοῦ ὄρους</note> instead of "from Mount Hor" <note>original Greek: ἐξ Ὤρ τοῦ ὄρους</note>; in **21:13**, "pouring out" <note>original Greek: ἐκχέον</note> instead of "protruding" <note>original Greek: ἐξέχον</note> and "of the mountains" <note>original Greek: ὄρεων</note> instead of "of the borders" <note>original Greek: ὁρίων</note>; in **23:7**, "of the borders" <note>original Greek: ὁρίων</note> instead of "of the mountains" <note>original Greek: ὀρέων</note>; in **24:21**, "wickedness" <note>original Greek: κακία</note> instead of "dwelling" <note>original Greek: κατοικία</note>; in **27:11**, "in the house" <note>original Greek: οἴκῳ</note> instead of "to his relative" <note>original Greek: οἰκείῳ</note>; and in **35:5**, "similar things" <note>original Greek: ὅμοια</note> instead of "neighboring things" <note>original Greek: ὅμορα</note>. In **14:25**, he was deluded into thinking the word "tomorrow" <note>original Greek: αὔριον</note> was the proper name of some place. In **Chapter 21:27**, since he did not know how to translate the word "riddlers" <note>or "proverb-speakers"; original Greek: αἰνιγματισταὶ</note>, he adopted the Greek word into his own text. In **Chapter 9:7**, he thought the interrogative particle <note>original Greek: μὴ</note> was a negative; in **14:12**, he rendered an entire statement as an interrogation; in **16:5**, he gave an optative sense to the words "he has visited and known" <note>original Greek: ἐπέσκεπται καὶ ἔγνω</note>; and in **25:12**, he thought "they said" <note>original Greek: εἶπον</note> was the first person singular of the indicative. However, the fact that he translates the name "Graves (of Craving)" <note>original Greek: μνήματα τῆς ἐπιθυμίας</note> in **Chapters 11:34, 35; 33:16** with the word *tēyēs* <note>original Ge'ez: ⲧⲏⲏⲥ; compare Exodus 14:11</note> does not seem absurd, nor should it be attributed to an error by the translator; for in another place where there is no ambiguity in that name, he translates "grave" <note>original Greek: μνῆμα</note> well, namely in **Chapter 19:16, 18**.

But he also interpreted many other things with less accuracy than he ought to have. I have noted: in **Chapter 1:5**, "they shall stand by" <note>original Greek: παραστήσονται</note>; in **3:28, 18:5**, "of the holy things/places" <note>original Greek: ἁγίων; see Leviticus 10:4</note>; in **6:9, 12**, "the head of the vow" <note>original Greek: κεφαλὴν εὐχῆς; differently in verse 18</note>; in **10:14, 18, 22, 25**, the word "rank/division" <note>original Greek: τάγμα</note>; in **10:31**, "you shall be" <note>original Greek: ἔσῃ</note>; in **13:20 (21)**, "those who persisted" <note>original Greek: προσκαρτερήσαντες</note>; in **17:3, 4 (16:38, 39)**, "covering" <note>original Greek: περίθεμα</note>; in **17:7 (16:42)**, "they rushed" <note>original Greek: ὥρμησαν</note>; in **24:6**, "wooded valleys" <note>original Greek: νάπαι</note>; in **27:21**, "of the manifest things" <note>original Greek: τῶν δήλων</note>; in **31:17**, "provisions/baggage" <note>original Greek: ἀπαρτία; compare verse 18</note>; in **33:52**, "lookouts" <note>original Greek: σκοπιὰς</note>; and finally in **34:7** and following, "to measure out" <note>original Greek: καταμετρεῖν; better in verse 29 and 35:4 and following</note>, as well as in the passages **18:30** and **19:22**. Other things, which he attempted to translate according to the sense rather than the sound of the words, he expressed better—for example, in **1:52, 2:25, 4:28, 33, 5:7, 8:2, 18:19, 23:14, 26:53, 32:25, 27, 31, 33:2**. Changes of person and number in verbs ¹) (**1:5, 5:3, 10:4, 14:34, 15:5, 7, 16:7, 18:24, 22:6, 35:30**) and transpositions of words...

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the Ethiopic (Ge'ez) translation of the Book of Numbers. The previous page discussed specific instances where the translator misinterpreted the Greek source text. This page shifts to discussing intentional omissions for brevity and provides a detailed list of textual variants where the translator’s Greek manuscript likely differed from the standard Greek Bible (the Septuagint).</meta>

I do not know whether the positions <note>referring to the placement of certain verses; original Latin: "positiones"</note> (14:27, 15:30, 27:17, 32:35, 36:11, 12) were introduced by the translator or by readers and scribes. For the sake of brevity, he occasionally omitted translating certain words of the Greek text which he considered superfluous: 2:2 "following" <note>original Greek: ἐχόμενος</note>. 5:10 several words; 5:24 several words, because the same are repeated in verse 26; 15:19 "and it shall be" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἔσται</note>. 16:17 "upon them" <note>original Greek: ἐπ’ αὐτά</note>. 17:27 "saying" <note>original Greek: λέγοντες</note>. 21:5 "the people" <note>original Greek: ὁ λαός</note>. 21:18 "in their ruling over them" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ κυριεῦσαι αὐτῶν</note>. 22:6 "this people" <note>original Greek: τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον</note>. (24:17 "man"? <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπος</note>) 25:14 "who was struck with the Midianite woman" <note>original Greek: ὃς ἐπλήγη μετὰ τῆς Μαδιανίτιδος</note>. 31:32 several words; 27:11 "his things" <note>original Greek: τὰ αὐτοῦ</note>. 27:23 "to Moses" <note>original Greek: τῷ Μωυσῇ</note>. 28:19 "burnt offerings" <note>original Greek: ὁλοκαυτώματα</note>. 28:25, 26 "called" or "summoned" <note>original Greek: κλητὴ or ἐπίκλητος; translated differently in 29:1, 7, 12; compare Leviticus 23</note>; 31:17, 18, 35 "bed" <note>original Greek: κοίτην</note>. 34:2 "land of the Canaanites" <note>original Greek: γῆ Χαναναίων</note>. 35:4 "of the wall" <note>original Greek: τείχους</note> and others; 35:23 several words; 35:28 "the one who killed" <note>original Greek: ὁ φονεύσας</note>. 36:4 "their inheritance" <note>original Greek: ἡ κληρονομία αὐτῶν</note>. In Chapter 31:50, he condensed "bracelet and armlet" <note>original Greek: περιδέξιον καὶ ἐμπλόκιον</note> into one; in 7:3 he omitted the word "covered wagon" <note>original Greek: λαμπηνικός</note> and in 11:12 the word "nursing father" <note>original Greek: τιθηνός</note>, because they are not entirely necessary and in the <term>Geez</term> <note>The ancient liturgical language of Ethiopia</note> language, simple words that correspond to these Greek terms are lacking. But in Chapter 16:17, he seems to have omitted "two hundred and fifty censers, and you and Aaron each his censer" <note>original Greek: πεντήκοντα καὶ διακόσια πυρεῖα, καὶ σὺ καὶ Ἀαρὼν ἕκαστος τὸ πυρεῖον αὐτοῦ</note> due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>A common scribal error where a writer's eye skips from one word to a similar-looking word further down the page, causing them to leave out the text in between</note>; likewise, the passage 18:29 was greatly mutilated by him.

In passages 4:6, 8, 10, 12, 14; 8:21 and others, the translator seems to have added suffix pronouns not based on the authority of the Greek original, but according to the grammatical rules of his own language <note>Ge'ez/Ethiopic</note>.

Finally, in several places, he followed a different word punctuation than the standard version, namely in 1:47, 3:49-50, 6:6-7, 14:28-29, 22:38, 24:24, 26:55-56, 28:17, 31:23, and 32:29.

### E) Annotations on Deuteronomy.

#### 1. On the nature of the version and the condition of the text.

We are indeed persuaded that the translation of Deuteronomy was composed by the same author who translated the other books of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>, or at least the greatest part of them. Readers who examine the books more carefully will observe various arguments for this opinion on their own; for this reason, we will consider it sufficient to note here certain indications of the same thing drawn from the translation of several words or phrases that occur more rarely.

For although various phrases in this book occur translated differently than in the others (for example: "breadth" <note>original Greek: εὖρος (euros)</note> in Deut. 3:11; "accursed thing" <note>original Greek: ἀνάθεμα (anathema)</note> in Deut. 7:26, 13:16, 18; "wild scab" <note>original Greek: ψώρα ἀγρία (psora agria)</note> in Deut. 28:27 and Lev. 21:20; "manifestations" <note>original Greek: δῆλοι (deloi)</note> in Deut. 33:8, compare Num. 27:21; "one who is castrated" <note>original Greek: θላድίας (thladias)</note> in Deut. 23:2 and Lev. 22:24; "to be added to his people" <note>original Greek: προστίθεስθαι πρὸς τὸν λαὸን αὐቶው (prostithesthai pros ton laon autou)</note> in Deut. 32:50, see what we noted on page 120; "to suffer from decay" <note>original Greek: σፋክεሊዜይን (sphakelizein)</note> in Deut. 28:32 and Lev. 26:16; "south-west wind" <note>original Greek: λίβα (liba)</note> in 33:23, which is most often translated differently in Genesis and elsewhere), nevertheless, much more frequently the author preferred to present the same translation of the same words as he did in the other books.

You may therefore compare, if you wish, how he translated "taking alive" <note>original Greek: ζωግρία (zogria)</note> in Deut. 2:34 and Num. 21:35; "to seize" <note>original Greek: κρατεῖን (kratein)</note> and "to be overtaken" <note>original Greek: καταλαμβάνεσθαι (katalambanesthai)</note> in Deut. 2:34 and Num. 21:32 (differently in Deut. 3:4); "salt" <note>original Greek: ἁλυκῆς (halukes)</note> in Deut. 3:17, Num. 34:3, 12, and Gen. 14:3; "let it suffice" <note>original Greek: ἱካνούስθω (hikanoustho)</note> in Deut. 2:3 and 3:26, and Num. 16:3, 7 (differently in Deut. 1:6); "hewn" <note>original Greek: λεላξευμένος (lelaxeumenos)</note> and...

Regarding the method of translation used, beyond those things which we have noted for the other books, we have almost nothing to add in general. Except for certain places—not so many, which we will soon review—the translator has rendered both the words and the sense of this book well into his own language. When intending to interpret the Song contained in Deuteronomy 32, he cared little for the actual sound of the words, but he imitated the rhythms and the meaning of the poem well, and sometimes even elegantly. He expressed an elegant [**play on words** <term>paronomasia: a rhetorical device using words that sound alike but have different meanings</term>] in Chapter 21:20. However, he approached the Blessing of Moses in Chapter 33 with little success; nor will you wonder much at this, if you consider that the Greek text of this chapter very often suffers from obscurity, and is not infrequently devoid of all sense. In the catalog of clean and unclean animals in Chapter 14, since local names for them were lacking, he adopted most of the Greek names intact, just as he did in Leviticus. The places (besides Chapters 32 and 33) in which he must be judged to have translated the Greek words less accurately are not so many; for example: 4:19 [**allotted** <note>original: ἀπένειμε</note>], 4:23 [**commanded** <note>original: συνέταξε</note>], 7:16 [**stumbling block** <note>original: σκῶλον</note>], 7:20 [**wasps** <note>original: σφηкίας</note>], 8:7 [**springs of the depths** <note>original: πηγαὶ ἀβύσσων</note>], 8:9 [**to mine/dig** <note>original: μεταλλεύειν</note>], 11:16 [**be enlarged** <note>original: πλατυንθῇ</note>], 11:30 [**oak** <note>original: δρῦς</note>], 14:1 [**baldness** <note>original: φαλάкρωμα</note>], 13:17 [**spoils** <note>original: σκῦλα</note>], 28:7 [**before your face** <note>original: πρὸ προσώπου σου</note>], 28:56 [**baldness** <note>original: φαλάкρωμα</note>], 28:59 [**and faithful/lasting** <note>original: καὶ πιστάς</note>], 31:20 [**they shall be satisfied** <note>original: κορήσουσι</note>], 33:13 [**of the seasons/hours** <note>original: ὡрῶν</note>] (differing in verses 14 and 16), 33:11 [**crush the loins** <note>original: κάταξον ὀσφῦν</note>], 33:14 [**coming together/harvest** <note>original: σύνοδος</note>], 34:10 [**knew** <note>original: ἔγνω</note>]—these he rendered less consistently in Ethiopic; <meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Ethiopic (Ge'ez) Old Testament, specifically the Book of Deuteronomy. Moses—given that he is distinguished by a certain rhetorical richness and abundance of words, as well as the very frequent repetition of the same or only slightly varied phrases in different places—naturally invites readers and scribes to make slight alterations to individual passages.

Not a few passages occur where larger or smaller additions have been joined to the genuine words of the text. Sometimes, where the meaning of the passages seemed transformed or made more difficult by such <term>glosses</term> <note>marginal or interlinear explanations that sometimes crept into the main text</note>, we have enclosed them in parentheses—for example, in Chapters 3:8, 10; 19:18; 25:9; 27:3; 28:31, 36, 37; 60—or in other places where, contrary to the meaning of the Greek text, the particle <term>and</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ወ (wa)</note> and similar words had been inserted, such as 1:29; 2:10; 6:8; 7:25; 12:7, 25; 13:19; 16:18; 21:6; 31:8; 32:8. 25:9 <term>that city</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ይእቲ፡ ሀገር፡ (ye'eti hagar)</note>; 26:7 <term>the Lord saw</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ርአየ፡ እግዚአብሔር፡ (ra'aya Egziabeher)</note>; verse 8 <term>great</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ዐቢይ፡ (abiy)</note> before <term>sign</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ተአምር፡ (ta'amer)</note>; 28:4 <term>may your blessing be upon us</term> <note>original Ge'ez: በረከከ፡ ይከውነን፡ (barakaka yekawnan)</note>; verse 60 <term>upon them</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ላዕሌሆሙ፡ (la'elehomu)</note>; verse 61 <term>and until you are destroyed</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ወእስከ፡ ትደመሰሱ፡ (wa-eska tedamasasu)</note>; 30:3 <term>all</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ኵሉ፡ (kwallu)</note>; 31:12 <term>so that they may hear</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ከመ፡ ይክመው፡ (kama yekma'u)</note>.

Perhaps even in the phrase <term>priests and Levites</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ካህናት፡ ወሌዋውያን፡ (kahnat wa-lewawyan)</note>, that "and" <note>original Ge'ez: ወ (wa)</note> is spurious; it is already found in many places in the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> and was carried from there into the Ethiopic version, having been added by readers and scribes as consistently as it is now read. Furthermore, because the Hebrew speaker himself was somewhat inconsistent in his use of grammatical person and number when using pronouns, it easily happened that the person and number of pronouns were frequently changed and confused in both the Greek and the Ethiopic versions—for example, in 1:25; 4:12, 30, 40; 6:3, 18; 7:11, 19; 8:19; 10:21; 11:10; 12:7; 13:16; 16:17, 18; 17:1, 2; 20:10, 11, 18; 21:2; 26:16; 30:18, 19; 31:17.

Then, as in other books, many <term>lacunae</term> <note>missing sections or gaps in the text</note> gradually arose in this one as well. We have filled many of these—including some very significant ones—from manuscripts C or G, or occasionally without manuscript authority: 1:21, 24; 2:14, 24; 4:26; 5:5, 8, 24; 6:7, 21; 7:5; 9:2; 10:1, 20; 12:4; 15:18; 17:2; 18:22, 23, 5; 24:5; 25:15; 28:1, 7, 66; 30:13, 16; 31:18, 19, 29; 32:1, 8, 47; 33:4; 34:4; and especially 11:28; 12:5; 14:25, 23, 18; 26:18, 19; 27:17, 23. The remaining gaps, which we have not filled, are as follows: missing in 1:8 is [**having entered, inherit the land** <note>original: εἰσπορευθέντες κληρονομήσατε τὴν γῆν</note>] due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>a common scribal error where the eye jumps between two words with similar endings, skipping the text in between</note>; in 2:23 certain things (see notes); in 3:26 [**on your account** <note>original: ἕνεκεν ὑμῶν</note>] (compare 1:37); in 4:2 [**which I command you today** <note>original: ἃς ἐγὼ ἐντέλλομαι ὑμῖν σήμερον</note>]; in 9:2 [**and many** <note>original: καὶ πολὺν</note>] and [**and you have heard, who shall stand against the face of the sons of Enak?** <note>original: καὶ σὺ ἀκήκοας, τίς ἀντιστήσεται κατὰ πρόσωπον υἱῶν Ἐνάκ</note>]; in 21 [**and I burned it** <note>original: καὶ κατέκαυσα αὐτὸν</note>].

Finally, some other changes to the text, whether minor or more significant, occur. Individual words are found relocated from their original positions to others in **12:20; 14:12, 13; 22:29; 28:3, 16, 42; 29:5, 6; 30:9, 16; 31:12; 32:14.** Beyond the many corrupt passages which we corrected in our edition (following manuscripts C or G) and enclosed in brackets, certain others should be mentioned here: specifically **1:14; 28:34; 14:8** where, instead of the word "as" <note>Greek: ὡς (hōs)</note>, the word <term>they are</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ሀለው (halaw)</note> was introduced into the text; **15:12** where (due to a misreading of numerical signs) <term>I drew away</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ሰያሕኩ (sayahku)</note> was substituted for <term>I praised</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ሰባሕኩ (sabahku)</note>; **25:12** where, contrary to the Hebrew and Greek, the plural <term>her hands</term> <note>original Ge'ez: አደዋሃ (adawaha)</note> is read; **29:6** where <term>and to her</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ዋልሃ (walha)</note> was intruded in place of the word <term>but</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ባሕቱ (bahtu)</note>; and finally **16:16** where the original and literal translation of the words "festival of unleavened bread" <note>Greek: ἑορτὴ τῶν ἀζύμων (heortē tōn azymōn)</note> was lost and replaced by the words <term>Festival of the Law Hallelujah</term> <note>original Ge'ez: በዓለ:ሕጎ:ሃሌሉያ (Ba'ala Higgs Hallelujah)</note>, which pertain to Christian sacred matters. Individual names and verbs have been somewhat corrupted by a poor reading of vowels; see, besides many proper names, the passages **1:14; 2:25; 3:14; 6:8, 17; 15:17; 29:21** and what we have noted for them; other examples of this kind occur elsewhere, such as **17:16 <term>Ethiopia</term>** <note>original Ge'ez: ኢትዮጵያ (Ityopya)</note> instead of <term>Ethiopia</term> <note>the author is noting a subtle variation in the Ge'ez spelling or vowel markers</note>; **33:2 <term>and he appeared to me</term>** <note>original Ge'ez: ወለአስተርአየኒ (wa-la'astara'ayani)</note> instead of <term>and to us</term> <note>original Ge'ez: ወለ“ኒ (wa-la...ni)</note>.

### CHAPTER 32

Just as with the hymn in Exodus 15, this Song of Moses (32:1–43) was also printed in Job Ludolf’s edition of the *Ethiopic Psalms* <note>Ludolf was a 17th-century German scholar considered the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe</note>, pages 321–325 (compare the notes we made above on page 74). Its text agrees most closely with Manuscript G. In Codex C, a corrector—who was more concerned with accurately expressing the meaning of the Greek words than with preserving the poetic rhythm—altered many passages of the song for the worse. For this reason, we have chosen not to list all of those corrections here. Furthermore, the Ethiopians have somewhat awkwardly divided this song into two separate hymns for their church services: the first covers verses 1–21, and the second covers verses 22–43. Even in our Manuscripts C and G, the beginning of a new chapter is marked at Verse 22.

This word **we'eyu** <note>original: ውእዩ፡</note> or **wa-we'eyu** <note>original: ወእዩ፡</note> is an <term>obsolete particle</term> (unknown even to the scholar Hiob Ludolf), which is why the later editors of Manuscripts C and G substituted the more common **in that place.** <note>original: በሀውያ፡</note> Manuscript H displays **at that.** <note>original: በውእቱ፡</note> Indeed, I have read this obsolete particle quite often in the Ethiopic <term>Book of Jubilees</term>; in <term>Amharic</term> <note>a modern language of Ethiopia</note> it sounds like **wada** <note>original: ወደ፡</note> (which is the same as **mangala** <note>original: መንገለ፡</note> meaning "towards" or "in the direction of" in Ge'ez). It seems to me to be related to the same root from which the nouns **gaba** and **eya** are derived, and it signifies nothing other than the Hebrew terms **ba-derek** or **la-derek** <note>meaning "in the way" or "by way of"</note>. Compare also the Ethiopic **eya.** **[Heth]** The name **Sinai** <note>original: ሲና፡</note> appears in the manuscripts.
