### 3. Regarding the names by which the individual books of the Pentateuch are called, and concerning the punctuation of the text and the division into chapters found in our manuscript codices.

The names we have assigned to the individual books of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> are either the most ancient or the most commonly used; but certain other names are also found here and there, which it is helpful to note here. Just as in the biblical text the names **Law** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ (Orit)</note> and **Creation** <note>original: ፍጥረት፡ (Fitrat)</note> are substituted for one another, so for the book of Genesis, besides the title **The Law of Birth** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ ዘልደት፡ (Orit Zaldet)</note>, the title **The Law of Creation** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ ዘፍጥረት፡ (Orit Zafitrat)</note> is also given (for example, in a certain section of the book *Fatha-Nagast* <note>The "Law of the Kings," a traditional Ethiopian legal code.</note>), and it is also called the **Holy Law** <note>original: ቅዱስ፡ ኦሪት፡</note>, according to Hiob Ludolf <note>A 17th-century German scholar and the father of Ethiopian studies in Europe.</note> (History of Ethiopia, Book III, 4, 17). In the *Fatha-Nagast*, I have indeed read the title for the third book as **The Law of the Levites** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ ዘሌዋውያን፡</note>, and for the fourth, **The Law of the Children of Israel** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ ዘደቀቆ፡ እስራኤል፡</note>. The fifth book in manuscripts F and G is titled **The Repeated Law** <note>original: ደግሞ፡ ኦሪት፡</note> (compare Deuteronomy 17:18), but so that the title would conform more closely to the names of the other books, it has been changed by most into **The Second Law** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ ዘዳግም፡ (Orit Zadagem), commonly known as Deuteronomy</note> (also in manuscripts C and H); according to Hiob Ludolf (in the place cited), this book is also called **The Law of the Tabernacle** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ ዘደብተራ፡</note>, which I myself do not remember ever reading. So much for this.

Now concerning the division of the text. Individual sentences and the larger parts of a speech are distinguished in all the books we have read by a few punctuation marks: in manuscripts C and G, the mark for minor punctuation is **፡**, and for major punctuation is **፨**; in manuscript F, the minor is **፡**, the major is **፨ ፨**, and also **። ═ ።** is commonly used, and in such a way that (in manuscript F) a new line always begins after the last two marks, but only rarely after the first. But one should be careful not to think that the biblical text was divided by the Ethiopians into a fixed number of members and verses in a manner similar to that of the Hebrew Masoretes <note>Jewish scholars who standardized the pronunciation and verse divisions of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, or that the major punctuation marks are used uniformly and in the same places across various manuscripts.

<summary>This page lists specific corrections for the Ge'ez text of Deuteronomy and discusses the various traditional Ethiopian titles for the books of the Pentateuch, as well as the inconsistency of punctuation marks across manuscripts compared to the Hebrew Masoretic tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Pentateuch, Deuteronomy, Genesis, Fatha-Nagast, Hiob Ludolf, Ge'ez, Masoretic Text, punctuation, manuscript variants</keywords>

--- Page 660 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the philological features of Ethiopian manuscripts, specifically focusing on the lack of a standardized punctuation system and the history of chapter divisions in the Old and New Testaments.</meta>

No traces occur of a fixed and established system of punctuation <note>original: "certae rataeque distinctionis"</note> that has been accepted by the whole church and transmitted or preserved through every manuscript. Indeed, it frequently happens—especially where the sense of the passage itself demands it—that the scribes of various manuscripts agree on the punctuation of the text; however, they more often disagree. For the most part, each scribe <note>original: "librarii," referring to the professional copyists of the manuscripts.</note> followed his own judgment or his own particular style of interpreting the text and connecting the flow of speech. The scribe of Codex G <note>A specific manuscript used for this study.</note> punctuated most poorly and, in countless places, quite foolishly; the author of Codex F acted more prudently and diligently. One will not be surprised by such a difference between manuscripts if one considers the lack of cultivation <note>original: "ruditatem"</note> among the Abyssinians <note>A historical term for people of the Ethiopian Highlands.</note>, which has become increasingly burdensome over these last few centuries.

It seems we must judge differently regarding the distribution of the text into sections or chapters <term>capitula</term> <note>Small divisions of text used in ancient and medieval manuscripts, often different from modern chapter numbering.</note>, which we find in the manuscript books. It is proved by various arguments that among the Ethiopians, just as among other nations, a certain division of the text into chapters—though not sufficiently consistent—was established through all or most of the books of Holy Scripture. The Ethiopians could not easily do without such a division for the ecclesiastical use of the Bible, and it is well known among all scholars that the chapters of the New Testament were translated from the Greeks to the Abyssinians in antiquity. But even the Old Testament required a similar division for church use: in lectionaries <note>Books containing scripture readings appointed for Christian worship.</note>, the chapters of the books of this Testament are sometimes cited, and indeed the older division of individual books has been handed down through the manuscript codices almost entirely to our own day. 

However, several causes have combined to make it difficult for us to extract the ancient and genuine division of most books from the manuscripts as accurately as we ought. First, among the ancient Ethiopians themselves, at least in certain individual books, various methods of carving the text into chapters (whether handed down from the Greeks or devised by themselves) seem to have been established; as the centuries passed, these were mixed with one another as the manuscripts were written. Secondly, many scribes altogether omitted to write or note this division into chapters, perhaps because they remembered it was a relatively recent addition to the sacred letters. Added to this is the fact that scribes easily made errors in noting these chapters—since they were much smaller than our modern chapters and therefore more numerous—and they even changed things according to their own judgment. Thus, after some time, a corruption and confusion of the division set in, similar to what we find in the variant readings of the text itself. Finally, in these most recent centuries—especially, as I believe, after the printed Bibles of the Greeks and others became known to the Abyssinians—our own method of dividing the text (or rather, that of the Greeks) was introduced among them, accepted, and written into many manuscripts produced in this recent age. Thus it happens that in such manuscript books, either no traces or only rare traces of the older division are found.

<vocab>Aethiopes (Ethiopians), Abyssini (Abyssinians), codices (manuscript books), capitula (chapters/sections), interpunctio (punctuation), Biblia (Bible), lectionaria (lectionaries), Graeci (Greeks)</vocab>

However, because of these circumstances, we have not been able to accurately reconstruct the older system of division from the three or four manuscripts <term>codices</term> <note>Plural of codex; ancient or medieval handwritten books.</note> we consulted. <meta>This page continues the analysis of manuscript chapter divisions, transitioning from the specific lists in Codex G and F to a broader discussion of how Ethiopic scribes organized the text of the Pentateuch based on divine speech, while comparing these to European and Masoretic standards.</meta>

page 163
signature 23

We will rightly judge that a portion of the text, according to the number of sayings that God spoke to Moses, was once distributed among the Abyssinians <term>Abyssinians</term> <note>A historical term for people from the Ethiopian Empire.</note> into a certain number of chapters¹). The truth of this observation seems to me to be confirmed by a certain note which the scribe of Codex F wrote at the end of Deuteronomy: **"The words which God spoke to Moses, 570 were counted"** <note>original Ge'ez: ዘነበበ፡ እግዚአብሔር፡ ለሙሴ፡ ፭፻፸ ዘተኰለቈ፡</note>; for even if I would hardly believe that all these 570 sayings of God were once equally marked in the Ethiopic manuscripts and that either the history of Moses or the Law was distributed into 570 chapters according to their number, yet it seems proven from this that they preferred to begin their chapters at the start of the words of God spoken to Moses. However, in Exodus and Leviticus, the scribe of Codex F seems to have omitted this method of marking the most significant sayings of God, either due to some inconsistency or due to a defect in the original model.

In Codex H, as it was derived from copies transcribed in Europe, the ancient chapter divisions have been abolished and have given way to modern chapter and verse numbers.

Even in Codex C, although it was written in Abyssinia itself, our modern division of the text into chapters is inscribed (see above, page 8): numbers are assigned to individual chapters (**Chapter 44** <note>original Ge'ez: ምዕራፍ፡ ፵፬፡</note>). Sometimes these inscribed chapter beginnings differ by one or more verses from our own or from the Greek. The chapters whose beginnings differ from the chapters of our edition are these: in Genesis, its chapter 11 begins from our text's 11:2, and its chapter 32 from our 32:2 (just like the Greek); but chapters 3, 6, and 37 agree with our text against the Greek. In Exodus, following the Greeks, the scribe began chapter 8 from our 7:26 and chapter 22 from our 21:37, but from chapter 36 onward, he followed the Hebrew order, except that in place of Exodus 36:35–38 he inscribed the number **Chapter 42** <note>original Ge'ez: ምዕራፍ፡ ፵፪</note>, from which it follows that he numbered forty-one chapters of Exodus rather than forty. In Leviticus and Numbers, since he mixed in another kind of division, he erred considerably in numbering and noting the chapters (see what we will mention below); finally, in Deuteronomy, its chapters 2:1, 13:1, 23:1, and 29:1 correspond to our 2:2, 13:2, 23:2, and 28:69; it began chapter 14 from the words **"And you shall not shave..."** <note>original Ge'ez: ወአትትላጸዩ፡; refers to Deuteronomy 14:1 regarding mourning rituals.</note>, and it extended chapter 32 up to 32:21, and chapter 33 from 32:22 up to 33:29. But even the author of this manuscript, although he undertook to substitute the modern division for the older one, nevertheless preserved certain remains of that older division in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. He intended to mark the beginnings of these ancient chapters not with attached numbers but only by writing the initial words in red ink <term>rubrics</term>, but in Leviticus and Numbers it happened that, with modern and ancient chapters mixed, he assigned numbers sometimes to the former and sometimes to the latter. In Exodus, therefore, there are only the chapters at 30:11, 17, and 22.

It remains for us to say something about the <term>pericopes</term> <note>Passages of Scripture appointed to be read during public worship services.</note> to be read in church, which are noted here and there in Codex F (see above, page 4) as well as in Codex H. Since Codex F was produced for the use of a specific church, the scribe intended to indicate the passages to be read for individual services. The method for indicating them is as follows. Next to the words where the reading begins, **HP** (here!) <note>original Latin: "hic!"</note> is written in red in the margin; in the upper margin, the day or hour when it is to be read is found noted; finally, sometimes next to the last words of the pericope, the siglum <image-desc>ornamental siglum resembling a cross with a looped top and base, similar to a stylized 'phi' or 'ankh'</image-desc> (= **stop!** <note>original Ge'ez: ቀሞ (qamo) or ቆሞ (qomo); original Latin: siste!</note>) is applied. It is regrettable that several of the annotations and sigla have been erased. Many of them are also preserved in Codex H; but since the scribes did not understand their meaning, they quite foolishly included both the annotations and the sigla within the text of the prayer itself. It is regrettable that several of the annotations and sigla <note>Special symbols or abbreviations used in manuscripts.</note> have been erased. Many of them are also preserved in Codex H; but since the scribes did not understand their meaning, they quite foolishly included both the annotations and the sigla within the text of the prayer itself. # 1. Annotations on the Book of Joshua.

## 1. Concerning the manuscript books from which our edition was drawn.

Just as in the preparation of the edition of the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy).</note>, so too for the edition of **Joshua** we have utilized four manuscript books. These correspond in number, general type, and the nature of the text they contain with those four sources we used for the Pentateuch.

The first place among these is held by **Codex F**, in which the Book of Joshua is contained on folios 228 to 253. Since this manuscript is entirely consistent in all its characteristics with what we noted above on pages 4–6, it seems nothing further needs to be discussed regarding it here.

Regarding the **Halle Codex H**, which we described above on pages 6 and 7, we stated there that it contained nothing but the Pentateuch. However, in that same library in Halle where that codex is kept, there exists another volume, derived from the same source as the Pentateuch, which includes the Book of Joshua. It is a <term>paper codex</term> <note>original Latin: "codex chartaceus"</note> in <term>quarto format</term> <note>A book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice, creating four leaves.</note>, consisting of 78 folios, and it contains:
1. "The Book of Joshua, transcribed from the copy of Dr. J. H. Michaelis <note>Johann Heinrich Michaelis (1668–1738), a German pietist and biblical scholar.</note> at Halle in Saxony in the year 1731."
2. Certain fragments of the Ethiopic Bible from the books of Judges, Samuel, Kings, Isaiah, Habakkuk, and the fourth book of Esdras; <margin>the margin contains several corrections of letters and notes.</margin>

From the notes written at the end of the Book of Joshua, we have learned that this book was derived from the copy of **J. Ludolf** <note>Job Ludolf (1624–1704), a German orientalist and the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe.</note>, which he had transcribed from the codex of **Ludovicus Piques** of Paris (see Ludolf’s preface to the *Ethiopic Lexicon* and his *Commentary on the History of Ethiopia*, page 298). We further know that the Piques codex was transcribed in Rome in the year 1666 by **J. M. Wansleben** <note>Johann Michael Wansleben (1635–1679), a traveler and linguist who collected manuscripts for the French king.</note> from an original manuscript which **Mahtzenta-Maryam** <note>An Ethiopian monk whose name means "Refuge of Mary."</note>, of Mand-Amba, brought from Jerusalem to Rome in 1638. It was brought so that it might be printed, and once the printing was completed, the final work was to be returned to Jerusalem.

Now indeed, there can be no doubt that this "Jerusalem-Roman" codex contained not only the Book of Joshua but also that Wansleben-Piques Pentateuch from which the Halle Pentateuch codex was derived. The text of the Book of Joshua provided in this codex is linked by the same very close kinship with the text of **Codex F** as we observed between F and H in the Pentateuch. Many errors, as well as gaps and variations in individual letters, are found in the Halle codex where it departs from Codex F; however, variations of this kind seem more attributable to the carelessness and mistakes of European scribes than to a different version of the text. The places where it truly shows variant readings are very rare, and in the passages of Chapter 1:8, 6:22, 7,

At 18:9, 1:14, 13:21, 34:24, and 29, there are certain small gaps <note>original Latin: "exiguas quasdam lacunas"</note> found in **Codex F**—or at least in our transcript of it—which can be successfully filled from that volume [Codex H]. Since this is the case, the two Halle codices of the Pentateuch and Joshua appear to be two volumes of the same work; for this reason, we shall designate this Joshua codex with the same **siglum** <note>A letter or symbol used by scholars to identify a specific manuscript; original Latin: "siglo".</note> **H** with which we marked the previous volume, the Pentateuch codex.

The third source we used in the edition of the Pentateuch, the Rüppellian **Codex C**, also contains the Book of Joshua, as we already mentioned above on page 8. The fourth of our codices, **G**, is the third volume of the Bruce Bibles, which are preserved in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. It is a parchment volume of large quarto size <note>A book size where the paper is folded twice to create four leaves.</note> consisting of 127 folios; it contains the books of Joshua (folios 1–15), Judges, Ruth, Chronicles, and 1–4 Kings. ¹) The text of the Book of Joshua provided by this volume is of the same type and maintains the same relationship to the text of **Codices F, H,** and **C** as we outlined above in the description of the Bruce Pentateuch on pages 8–10.

In compiling our edition, we have followed exactly the same method that we explained above on pages 10 and 11.

### 2. Concerning the nature of the version, the condition of the text, and the division of the book.

It was an ancient custom among the Greeks to bind the books of Joshua, Judges, and Ruth more closely with the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note> and to separate this body of ancient historical records—known by the name **Octateuch** <note>Meaning "Eight Books"; original Latin: "Octateuchi".</note>—from the Books of Kings. Many proofs of this custom still survive in the older Greek manuscript Bibles, as well as in biblical commentaries and **catenae** <note>A form of biblical commentary consisting of a "chain" of interpretations from various Church Fathers; original Latin: "catenisque".</note>. ²) The Ethiopians received this custom as passed down from the Greeks, but they substituted the title **The Law** <note>original Ge'ez: "ኦሪት" (Orit); original Hebrew: "תּוֹርָה" (Torah).</note> for the name Octateuch. Although this title was taken from the Pentateuch (the primary part of the Octateuch) and is applied to the books of Judges and Ruth with some degree of impropriety, it fits the Book of Joshua perfectly. For the things that Moses and Joshua either commanded, established, or performed in founding and organizing the public affairs of the Israelites are bound together by the closest links and are easily and most aptly encompassed by the common name "The Law," or "the fundamental precepts, institutions, and acts." 

It is because of this custom of binding together the first eight books of Holy Scripture that the Ethiopians very often give the Book of Joshua the title **The Law of Joshua** <note>original Ge'ez: "ኦሪት፡ ዘኢየሱስ" (Orit za-Iyasus), also appearing as "ዘአየሱስ" (za-Ayasus) or "ዘሀቤሁ" (za-Habehu).</note>; even in our **Codices C** and **G**, the book bears this title. But no less frequent is the title **The Book of Joshua son of Nun** <note>original Ge'ez: "መጽሐፈ፡ ኢየሱስ፡ ወልደ፡ ነዌ" (Mats'hafa Iyasus Walda Nawe).</note> (for example, in the book *Fátha-Nagást* <note>The "Law of the Kings," a traditional Ethiopian legal code.</note>) and the shorter **Of Joshua** <note>original Ge'ez: "ዘአየሱስ" (za-Ayasus) or "ዘየቤሁ" (za-Yabehu).</note>, which is the name prefixed to the Book of Joshua in our **Codex F**.

How well the earlier internal churches were aware of the close necessity by which the Pentateuch and the Book of Joshua were joined together seems to me to appear from that very title, **The Law of Joshua**, <note>original Ge'ez: **ኦሪት፡ ዘኢያሱ፡** (*Orit Ze-Iyasun*). The term "Orit" (Law) usually refers strictly to the Pentateuch; its use here suggests Joshua was viewed as an integral continuation of the Torah.</note> which this book carries among the Ethiopians. Now, indeed, we seek another argument for this same point: that the same man whom we saw above to have been the principal translator of the Pentateuch also translated the Book of Joshua from the Greek language into Ge'ez. I shall now attempt to demonstrate this more extensively. For although a few expressions and words are found here and there in the Ethiopic Joshua that seem to contradict our opinion, nevertheless, the abundance of those expressions used by the translator in Joshua, just as in the Pentateuch, is so great that I am personally most strongly convinced that the Ethiopic translator of both books was the same.

He translates the terms "ark of the covenant" (e.g., Joshua 3:3, 6, 7), "tabernacle of testimony" (18:1, 19:51), "peace offering" (22:23, 27, 29), "camp" and "congregation" (e.g., 6:23, 9:16, 25), "a land flowing with milk and honey" (Joshua 5:6), "the good land" (**good/beautiful**, Joshua 23:13, 15; compare Deuteronomy 1:35, 3:25, 4:22, 8:7, 10, etc.), "native-born" (Joshua 8:35), "every breathing thing" (Joshua 10:28), "the diviner" (13:22; compare Numbers 23:23, Deuteronomy 18:10, 14), "house of bondage," and "anathema" <note>A thing devoted to destruction or a curse.</note> (translated sometimes as **he devoted/prohibited** in 6:17, 18, 7:1; and sometimes as **cursed** in 7:12), and "cities of refuge" using plainly the same words that are customary in the Pentateuch.

Just as in the Pentateuch, he everywhere translates "servant of the Lord" as **child/servant**, "slave" as **servant**, and "to overlook" in Joshua 1:5 as **he disregarded** (compare Leviticus 20:4, 26:37, 40, Numbers 22:30, Deuteronomy 22:3). The phrase "be strong and courageous" (1:6, 7, 9, 18, 10:25, Deuteronomy 31:6, 7, 23) becomes **be strong and be brave**. "Beast of burden" becomes **donkey** (6:21; compare what we noted above on pages 59 and 140), "elders" becomes **leaders** (7:23 and others), and "possessions" or "money" (e.g., 7:24, 22:8) becomes **goods**. "Burning anger" (7:26, 9:18, 22:20, Numbers 25:4, Deuteronomy 29:23) is rendered as **wrath of wrath** or as **plague** (Joshua 22:18). "Other gods" (e.g., 23:16) is **strange gods** or **gods of another**, and "foreign gods" (Joshua 24:14, 23) is **alien gods**.

Further examples include: "to survey/visit" (8:10, Numbers 13:2, 16, 17) rendered as **he saw**; "spies" (Joshua 2 and others) as **those who scouted there**; "survivor" (10:28, 30, 33, 11:8, Deuteronomy 2:34, Numbers 21:35) as **survivors**; "into the ears" (8:37, Deuteronomy 31:28, 30) as **he made them hear**; "to encamp to fight" (11:5—8, 11—Genesis 14:8, Exodus 17:9) as **he encamped to battle**; "advanced in days" (13:1, 23:1, 2, Genesis 18:11, 24:1) as **one whose days have passed**; "giants" (12:4, 13:12, Genesis 6:4, 10:9, 14:5, Numbers 13:33, Deuteronomy 1:28) as **those who are giants**; "to mistreat" (Joshua 24:4; compare Exodus and Deuteronomy) as **he neglected/harmed**; "for judgment" (Joshua 20, Deuteronomy 25:2) as **requital and lamentation so that they might be humbled**; "woodcutter" (Joshua 9:21, Deuteronomy 29:10) as **cutter of wood**; "water carrier" (Joshua 9:25, Deuteronomy 29:10); "in the last days" (Joshua 24:27, Deuteronomy 8:16) as **in the latter days**; "since yesterday and the third day" (3:4, 4:18, Genesis 28:19, 31:2, Exodus 4:10, 5:7, 14) as **yesterday**; and "Enakim" <note>The Anakim, a race of giants mentioned in the Bible.</note> (11:21, 22, Deuteronomy 2:10, 11, 21) as **those who are in Akem**; **people**...

He interpreted [the word] as **established** <note>original Ge'ez: **ሐ፡ አቈመ፡** (*ha aqwama*)</note> (Joshua 14:12). For the Greek words for **salt** and **salts** <note>original Greek: ἁλὸς and ἁλῶν</note> (Joshua 3:16, 12:3, 18:19; Genesis 14:3), and **saline/briny** <note>original Greek: ἁλυκὴν</note> (Joshua 15:2, 5; Genesis 14:3; Numbers 34:3, 12; Deuteronomy 3:17), and **maritime/by the sea** <note>original Greek: παράልιος</note> (Joshua 11:3, 13:21; Deuteronomy 1:7, 33:19; though he translates this word differently in Joshua 8:30 and Genesis 49:13), as well as **Lebanon** and **Libal** <note>original Ge'ez: **ሊባኖስ** and **ሊባል**</note> (Joshua 15:2, 3, 10; Deuteronomy 33:23; elsewhere he translates this as **Akeb** <note>original Ge'ez: **አኬብ፡**</note>, for example, Joshua 15:1, 4, 7, 11, 17:9, 19:8), and the **terebinth tree** <note>original Greek: τεሬብින්θος</note> (Joshua 17:9, 24:26; Genesis 14:6, 43:11), and **wooded vale** <note>original Greek: νάπην</note> (Joshua 18:16; Numbers 21:20; elsewhere he uses other terms, see Deuteronomy 3:29, Numbers 24:6)—just as in the Pentateuch, he did not provide an Ethiopic translation for these, but preserved the Greek words in his version.

Just like the translator of the Pentateuch, he had a particular fondness for the terms **Yelkel**, **Syud**, and **Abha** <note>original Ge'ez: **የልከል፡**, **ስዩድ፡**, **አብሐ፡**</note> (Joshua 10:19, 19:47), and the word **portion** <note>original Ge'ez: **ሕብር፡** (*hibr*), used for the Greek μέρος (*meros*)</note> (e.g., Joshua 12:2, 13:27, and others). Certain other expressions he used occur here and there in the Pentateuch, though less consistently, namely: **to be divided/spread** <note>original Ge'ez: **ተበዛ፡**</note> (Joshua 4:7, 5:1; Exodus 7:15, 21), **before/in front of** <note>original Ge'ez: **ፈጸመ፡**, used for the Greek ἔμπροσθεν</note> (Joshua 6:9, 8:10; Exodus 16:14; Numbers 1:53, 32:17; Deuteronomy 20:4), **to rest/abide** <note>original Ge'ez: **ነወተ፡**</note> (Joshua 6:10; Exodus 24:14), **armed/ready for battle** <note>original Ge'ez: **ርኵይ፡**</note> (Joshua 4:12, 3:17; Numbers 31:3, 5; though also **girded** <note>original Ge'ez: **ቀኑት፡**</note> in Joshua 4:13), **to do early in the morning** <note>original Ge'ez: **አኝገሀ፡**</note> (Joshua 7:4; Leviticus 26:8), **tunic/garment** <note>original Ge'ez: **ህህቆ፡**</note> (Joshua 7:21; Genesis 37:3, 23; Exodus 37:21), **he stretched out his hand** <note>original Ge'ez: **አልሀለ፡ እዳ፡**</note> (Joshua 8:18, 19; Genesis 14:22; elsewhere **he spread out** <note>original Ge'ez: **ሰፋሐ፡**</note> in Exodus 7:5, 19; Numbers 14:30), **on this side and that** <note>original Ge'ez: **ለፌ፡ ወለፌ፡**</note> (Joshua 8:20, 22; Exodus 2, 12), **to swear an oath** <note>original Ge'ez: **ተወሐለ፡ ወሐላ፡**</note> (Joshua 9:4, 5, 11, 13, 14; Exodus 34:12, 15; Genesis 26:28, 21:31, 31:44; elsewhere **to make a covenant** <note>original Ge'ez: **ተሤያየ፡ ኪዳነ፡**</note>, for example, Deuteronomy 7:2), **to border/surround** <note>original Ge'ez: **ሀቀበ፡**</note> (Joshua 18:17; Numbers 34:4; but also **ascent** <note>original Ge'ez: **ምዕረገ፡**</note> in Joshua 10:10), **to encamp** <note>original Ge'ez: **ገሀዘ፡**, for the Greek καταστራቶペεύειν</note> (Joshua 4:19; Exodus 14:10; Deuteronomy 1:40), **to delay and tarry** <note>original Ge'ez: **ጉንደየ፡ ወዮአለ፡**</note> (Joshua 11:19; Exodus 14:3), **thicket/grove** <note>original Ge'ez: **አው፡**, for the Greek δρυμὸς</note> (Joshua 17:15; Deuteronomy 20:19; the word for grove is translated differently in Joshua 17:18 and Deuteronomy 19:5), **near/neighboring** <note>original Ge'ez: **ምእዝዘ**</note> (Joshua 12:9; Deuteronomy 11:30; Numbers 34:3), and **to capture a city** <note>original Ge'ez: **አስተጋብአ፡**, for the Greek λαβεῖν πόλιν</note> (Joshua 15:16; Deuteronomy 3:4 and others; but translated differently in Joshua 1:11, 6:20, 8:19, 21). Just as in Deuteronomy (compare the notes on page 142), so too in Joshua 21:4, he inserted the conjunction **and** between the terms **priests** and **Levites**.

From such a great and constant agreement in the translation of individual words and phrases, it seems to me that it should be rightly conjectured that the same primary translator of the Pentateuch also translated this Book of Joshua. It is of no great importance in this matter that a few Greek words are rendered by different Ethiopic terms than those usually employed in the Pentateuch; for we have observed more than once above that even within one and the same book, the translator was not always consistent with himself in rendering individual words. The variations of this kind that I have noted in the Book of Joshua are roughly these: the word **to fail/cease** <note>original Greek: ἐκλείπειν</note> he translates as **dried up** <note>original Ge'ez: **ነጸፈ፡**</note> (Joshua 3:13, 16, 4:7); **to occupy** or **to take** as **found** <note>original Ge'ez: **ረከበ፡**</note> (Joshua 1:11, 6:20, 8:19, 21, though also **captured** <note>original Ge'ez: **አስተጋብአ፡**</note> in 15:16, as in the Pentateuch); **booty/plunder** or other synonymous words as **pillaged** <note>original Ge'ez: **በርበረ፡**, which is rarer in the Pentateuch than the word **ምህርካ፡**</note>; for **valley** (Joshua 8:11 ff.) he uses **rocky place/cleft** <note>original Ge'ez: **ጸጸት፡**, not the usual **ቈላ፡**</note>, by which name he later renders **suburbs/pasture lands** in Chapter 21; for **near** (Joshua 8:35) he uses the word **beside** <note>original Ge'ez: **ጠቃ፡**</note>, which a later translator of Exodus used in Exodus 24:4, 29:12 and others (but elsewhere he has **near...** <note>original Ge'ez: **ምእ** - *catchword for the next page*</note>)

[...captured] <note>original Ge’ez: **ኃዘ** (*haza*)</note>), the Greek phrase for **the rear** <note>original Greek: τὰ ὀπίσω (*ta opisō*)</note> with the word **behind** <note>original Ge’ez: **ከዋላ** (*kawala*)</note> in Joshua 8:2, 4, 14 (compare the use by the second translator of Exodus in Exodus 26:12, but also in the Book of Joshua 6:9, where **behind** <note>original Ge’ez: **ከዋላ**</note> represents the Greek for **bringing up the rear** <note>original Greek: οὐραγεῖν (*ouragein*)</note>). The word for **wasps** <note>original Greek: Σφηκία (*sphēkia*)</note> in Joshua 24:12 is rendered differently than in Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20, though in none of these three places was that word translated particularly well. The term for **farmsteads** <note>original Greek: 'Επαύλεις (*epauleis*)</note> was translated one way in Numbers 32:16 and another in Joshua 15:30, 36 (compare Joshua 13:28), but for no other reason than he wished to use the word **enclosures** <note>original Ge’ez: **አዕጻዳት** (*a’tsadat*)</note>—which he had used in Numbers 32—to represent the Greek word for **villages** <note>original Greek: κώμας (*kōmas*)</note> in Joshua 15 and elsewhere. The Hebrew formula **until this day** <note>original Hebrew: עַד־הַיּוֹም הַዘֶּה (*ad-hayyom hazzeh*)</note> in the Book of Joshua is mostly (though not always) translated as **until today and until this day** <note>original Ge’ez: **እስከ፡ ዮም፡ ወእስከ፡ ዛቲ፡ ዕለት** (*eska yom wa-eska zati elat*)</note>; in the Pentateuch, it appears as **until today** <note>original Ge’ez: **እስከ፡ ዮም**</note> in Genesis 19:38, 26:33, 35:20, 47:26, and as **until this day** <note>original Ge’ez: **እስከ፡ ዛቲ፡ ዕለት**</note> in Genesis 32:33, 47:26, and Deuteronomy 2:22, 3:14, 34:6. However, the reason for this difference lies in the fact that the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> in the Book of Joshua more frequently interpreted that formula as "until today’s day" <note>original Greek: ἕως τῆς σήμερον ἡμέρας</note> rather than simply "until today" <note>original Greek: ἕως σήμερον</note> or "until this day" <note>original Greek: ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ταύτης</note>. The word **keep yourselves** <note>original Greek: φυλάξεሰθε (*phylaxesthe*)</note> in Joshua 6:18 and 9:5 is expressed solely by **watch** <note>original Ge’ez: **ዑቁ** (*uqu*)</note>, whereas in the Pentateuch, a fuller expression—**watch yourselves** or **keep yourselves** <note>original Ge’ez: **ዑቁ፡ ርእሰክሙ** or **ዕቀቡ፡ ርእሰክሙ**</note>—is usually found. It follows that some of these variations were made with good reason, while others have parallels in the Pentateuch; thus, no argument presented in the Book of Joshua is serious enough to suggest that a new author should be assigned to this book.

We judge that the Book of Joshua was well and accurately translated by our interpreter. Almost everywhere he successfully imitated the Greek words and their sense. He omitted certain individual words which he considered less necessary for the sake of brevity: in 1:8 **and you shall prosper**; in 1:16 **all**; in 7:3 **about**; in 8:29 **body**; in 17:13 **and it happened and when** and **the Canaanites**. In a few places, he chose to depart slightly from the Greek words: for example, in 1:3 **footprint** <note>original Greek: ἴχνος</note>, 2:9 **has fallen upon** <note>original Greek: ἐπιπέпτωκε</note>, etc., 2:19 **he shall be guilty to himself**, 3:3 **and they commanded**, etc., 8:15 **and he saw**, 22:32 **and they answered them the words**—these were not expressed word-for-word. Likewise in 6:10 and 9:5; in the passages 2:6 **flax-stalks** <note>original Ge’ez: **ሊኖካላሜን** (a transliteration of the Greek λινοκαλάμη)</note>, 7:22 **messengers**, 15:2 and 15:5 **ridge** <note>original Greek: λοφिάν</note>, 15:7 **ascent**, 23:4 **allotted**, he translated less accurately than he ought to have. Sometimes he followed a different punctuation of the text than the one now accepted (for example, in 3:4 he joined **the way** with **approach**, not with **know**; he joined the words of 15:20 with verse 19 rather than verse 21), or, due to the ambiguity of certain Greek words, he strayed slightly from the true meaning: for example, in 4:19 in the translation of the word for **to encamp** <note>original Greek: καταστρατοπεδεύειν (compare Deuteronomy 1:40, Exodus 14:10)</note>, 4:5 **bring forward**, 8:11 **they encamped**, 13:22 **suddenly**, 14:1 **having inherited**. The sense of the phrases **from the sea of Gai** (8:9, 12, 13) and **in all the land** (3:11, 13; better in 4:7) he did not express very clearly. In translating the word for **people** or **clan** <note>original Greek: δῆμος</note> he was less consistent, as seen especially in chapter 13:23 and following. The phrase **as the days of the wheat harvest** (3:15) was translated in such a way as to help the understanding of Ethiopian readers; also, in translating the word for **mother city** <note>original Greek: μητρόπολις</note>, he seems to have considered the settlement customs used in Ethiopia (14:15, 15:13, 21:11; though differently in 10:2). The translator either read or understood the Greek vocabulary incorrectly, namely: 4:3 **ready** <note>original Greek: ἕτοιμοι (*hetoimoi*)</note>, 8:29 **heap** <note>original Greek: σωρὸν (*sōron*)</note>, 10:13 **of the straight** <note>original Greek: τοῦ εὐθοῦς (*tou euthoūs*)</note>, 11:13 **colored** <note>original Greek: κεχρωματισμένους (*kechrōmatismenous*)</note>, 18:13 **boundaries** <note>original Greek: ὅρια (*horia*)</note>, 24:12 **wasps** <note>original Greek: σφηκία (*sphēkia*); **compare Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20**</note>; in 21:4 he prefixed the particle **and** <note>original Greek: καὶ (*kai*)</note> before **Levites** <note>original Greek: Λευίτας (*Leuitas*)</note>, just as in Deuteronomy. Certain Greek names were taken whole into his version, either because he rashly thought they were proper nouns, or because he had no accurately corresponding names in his own language: **javelin** <note>original Greek: γαισῷ (*gaisō*)</note> at 8:19, 19, 26; **salt** and **of salts** <note>original Greek: ἁλὸς (*halos*) and ἁλῶν (*halōn*)</note> at 3:16, 12:3, 18:19; **salt marsh** <note>original Greek: ἀλυκὴν (*alukēn*)</note> at 15:2, 5; **coastal** <note>original Greek: παράλιος (*paralios*)</note> at 11:3, 13:21 (otherwise at 8:30); **terebinth tree** <note>original Greek: τερέμινθος (*tereminthus*)</note> at 17:9, 24:26; **the South** <note>original Greek: Λίβα (*Liba*)</note> at 15:2, 3, 10; **North** <note>original Greek: βοῤῥᾶ (*borrha*)</note> at 15:6 (elsewhere better); **of the sun** <note>original Greek: ἡλίου (*hēliou*)</note> at 15:7, 10; **stone** <note>original Greek: λίθον (*lithon*)</note> at 15:6; **of the glen** <note>original Greek: νάπης (*napēs*)</note> at 18:16. The version of Joshua which the translator composed seems to be fairly well preserved in our manuscripts <note>The author uses 'codices' to refer to the specific Ethiopic manuscript copies he consulted</note>. But one assists another, and by comparing the readings of the individual manuscripts, it was possible to repair the greatest part of the damage. Whether these [errors] were made by the translator's own mistake, it is hardly possible to decide. The additions, which were thrust in by readers or scribes without the authority of the Greek original <note>original: "Graeci exemplaris"</note>, are neither many nor great; they occur in 5, 4; 7, 21; 8, 37; 11, 2, 8; 13, 20, 23; 19, 29; 20, 8; 21, 5, 16, 34; 22, 14, 25, where we have enclosed them in parentheses. Furthermore, you will note the words:
**in Gadero** <note>Ge'ez: በገደሮ፡ (ba-Gadero)</note> 8, 19;
**those who were in them** <note>Ge'ez: እለ፡ ውስቴቶሙ፡ (ella wastētomu)</note> 13, 13;
**city** <note>Ge'ez: ሀገር፡ (hagar)</note> 18, 28;
**children of** <note>Ge'ez: ደቂቀ፡ (daqiqa)</note> 21, 4,
which rest on no authority of the Greek version. Regarding the corrupt passages found in manuscripts F and H, we have corrected most of them according to the authority of manuscripts C and G, and have enclosed the corrected parts in brackets, especially in 3, 11; 4, 13; 5, 9; 6, 22, 26; 8, 21; 10, 2, 18, 33; 13, 13, 21; 17, 10, 16; 19, 48, 50; 22, 20, 28. For other passages under heavy suspicion of similar corruption, such as 1, 3; 8, 29, 36; 13, 6; 22, 30; 24, 27, see the annotations for each individual chapter. Such corruptions of single letters or vowels are most conspicuous in proper names—of which a huge multitude is contained in this book—and the individual manuscripts vary greatly in writing them. However, we have corrected only the most serious and frequent ones or noted them among the variant readings; the rest, as they were not worth the effort, we have omitted from correction.

It remains for us to add something regarding the division of this book into sections and chapters. In manuscripts C and G, just as throughout the individual books of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>, so also through the whole book of Joshua, those **chapters** <note>Ge'ez: ምዕራፍ፡ (*me’eraf*)</note> into which the text is commonly distributed today among Europeans are written and numbered, and no other traces of division are found in them. The same applies to manuscript H, as it was produced in Europe. In manuscript F, the scribe who wrote it included no section titles; he seems to have intended to indicate the beginnings of new sections by line spacing at times: 2, 15; 3, 1; 4, 11; 6, 10; 7, 1; 8, 29 (**And when the sun was [setting]**) <note>Ge'ez: ወሶበ፡ሀለወት፡ፀሐይ፡ (wa-soba hallawat tsehāy)</note>; 9, 12; 10, 1, 31, 33, 34; 11, 13; 12, 1; 13, 1; 14, 1; 16, 1; 18, 1; 19, 32; 21, 1; 23, 1; 24, 1, 19, 33. Furthermore, just as the words of God spoken to Moses are marked in the Pentateuch, so also in the book of Joshua, the words of God spoken to Joshua are distinguished by line intervals and by having the initial words written in red ink <note>A practice known as rubrication</note> in eleven places, namely: 3, 7; 4, 1 (middle); 4, 15; 5, 9; 6, 2; 7, 10; 8, 1; 8, 18; 10, 8; 11, 6; 20, 1.

The passages <note>term: *Pericopae*—assigned readings for church services</note> to be read in the church were either never written in manuscript F or have been erased. But in manuscript H, three ecclesiastical readings are noted: 1, 1 **at the prayer of the Cross** <note>Ge'ez: በምህላ፡መስቀል፡ (ba-mehlā masqal)</note>; 3, 17 (**and all the children of Israel [passed] over**) in manuscripts H and P: **at the washing of feet** <note>Ge'ez: በኀፀበተ፡እግር፡ (ba-hatsabata eger)</note>; 5, 10 (**and the children of Israel made [Passover]**) in H and P: (the name of the feast day is missing).

# Chapter 10

**Verse 1.** The manuscript groups CG, both in this chapter and in Judges 1, show **Aynzeka** <note>original: አይንዜቃ</note>. **They uprooted** <note>original: ወሠረዋ</note> is replaced by **and he destroyed** <note>original: ወአዋፋአ</note> in CG.

**Verse 2.** **And they feared** <note>original: ወፈረሁ</note> is written as **they feared** <note>original: ፈረሁ</note> in CG. CG reads: **he knows [the kingdom]**; FH reads: **the mountain which he established** <note>original: ደብር፡ ዘሠወተ</note>, which seems to be a corrupted reading of **capital of the kingdom** <note>original: ደ“፡ ዘመንግሥት</note>. Compare how he translated the term <term>metropolis</term> <note>original Greek: μητρόπολιν, meaning "mother city" or capital</note> in Joshua 14:15, 15:13, and 21:11. CG has **his kingdom** <note>original: መንግሥቱ</note> instead of **capital of the kingdom**.

**Verse 3.** **Almo** <note>original: አልሞ</note> is found in CH. CG has **Ayaremut** <note>original: አያረሙት</note>; this is also found in verses 5 and 23. **Ayufata** <note>original: አዩፋታ</note> is **Yafata** <note>original: ያፋታ</note> in CG. **Debit** <note>original: ደቢት</note> is **Mountain** <note>original: ደብር (Debir)</note> in CG. CG has **Aylam** <note>original: አይላም</note> here, as well as in verses 5, 23, and elsewhere.

**Verse 4.** **Ascend** <note>original: ዕረጉአ</note> is omitted in CG.

**Verse 5.** It is helpful to note that in the FH manuscripts, where the letter "a" <note>the Ethiopic suffix አ</note> is attached to individual words of this speech, **to me** <note>original: ኀቤ</note> is written as **towards me** <note>original: ኀቤአ</note> when joined with that "a"; compare the note on Numbers 20:19. [ ] Omitted in FH. **Jebusites** <note>original: ኢየቡሴዎን</note> is **Awareon** <note>original: አዋሬዎን</note> in CG.

**Verse 6.** [**Phaturu**] <note>original: ፋጡሩ</note> is omitted in FH. [**And Ayosine**] <note>original: ወአዮሢነ</note> is omitted in FH.

**Verse 10.** **The Lord God** <note>original: እግዚ“፡ ዩ“</note> is omitted in CG.

**Verse 11.** [**And**] <note>original: ወ</note> is omitted in FH, but they later include **and** before the word **inside** <note>original: በውስጥ</note>.

**Verse 12.** **Or destroyed... before the face of Israel** <note>original: አው፡ ቀጥ“፡ —— ገጾሙ፡ ለእስራኤል</note> — all these words are omitted in CG.

**Verse 13.** **This** <note>original: ዛቲ</note> is omitted in CG. **Harab** <note>original: ሀረብ</note> is **West** <note>original: ምዕራብ (Me’rab)</note> in CG.

**Verse 14.** **Which like** <note>original: እንተ፡ ከመ</note> is **Like which** <note>original: ከመ፡ እንተ</note> in CG.

**Verse 15.** Omitted in CG.

[ ] Manuscripts F and H have the following: **And his boundary was Asel and they take it...** <note>original: ወደቦ፡ ኢያሴል፡ ወይነሥአወ፡ አንተ፡ መክዕ፡ ወለይሰር</note> + **its sunrise** <note>original: ጸባሖሁ</note> in F; which words, since they are clearly corrupt and nonsensical, I have deleted. **Verse 11.** **And Tohen** <note>original: ወቶሔን</note>] Manuscripts C and G omit **and** <note>original: ወ</note>. ## 2. Notes on the Book of Judges.

### 1. On the condition of the text, the nature and author of the version, and the division of the book.

The Book of Judges among the Ethiopians is titled **Of the Judges** <note>original: ዘመሳፍንት (Ze-masafint)</note> (in manuscript F), **Book of Judges** <note>original: መጽሐፈ፡ መሳፍንት (Matshafa Masafint)</note> (for example, in the *Fátha Nagást* <note>The "Law of the Kings," a traditional Ethiopian legal code</note>), and **The Law of the Judges** <note>original: ኦሪት፡ ዘመሳፍንት (Orit Ze-masafint)</note> (in manuscripts C and G). We have already explained the significance of the last of these titles above on page 168.

The text of the book, as edited by us, was drawn from three manuscripts—F, C, and G—which we described more fully above. We have closely followed Manuscript F wherever possible, as it preserves a faithful version by the ancient translator. However, where we noticed the text provided by F was incomplete or corrupt, we corrected it based on the authority of the more recent manuscripts C and G. These later manuscripts offer a text that was revised and altered by a later author. We have no doubt that our edition accurately reflects the ancient version. In the passages 1:1, 17; 3:31; 4:7; 6:2, 6, 25, 27; 8:8, 15; 9:18, 26; 11:14; 13:21; 14:7, 19; 15:7; 17:6; 18:9, 24, 26; 20:7; and 21:12 <gloss>1)</gloss> after we filled larger or smaller gaps from manuscripts C and G, only a few places remain where some words of the ancient version seem to have dropped out. The following are missing: 1:9 "toward the south and the lowland" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὸν νότον καὶ τὴν πεδεινήν</note>; 1:17 "and they called the name of the city *Anathema*" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐκάλεσαν τὸ ὄνομα τῆς πόλεως Ἀνάθεμα; 'Anathema' refers to something devoted to destruction</note>; 1:22 and 23 "and the Lord was with them. And they encamped and scouted out Bethel" <note>original Greek: καὶ Κύριος ἦν μετ' αὐτῶν. Καὶ παρενέβαλον καὶ κατεσκέψαντο Βαιθήλ</note> omitted due to *homoeoteleuton* <note>A common scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar-looking word later in the text</note>; 7:4 "and everyone of whom I say to you, 'this one shall not go with you,' he himself shall not go with you" <note>original Greek: καὶ πᾶς, ὃς ἐὰν εἴπω πρὸς σέ, οὗτος οὐ πορεύσεται μεትὰ σοῦ, αὐτὸς οὐ πορεύσεται μετὰ σοῦ</note> also due to *homoeoteleuton*; 7:21 "and they fled" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἔφυγον</note>; 8:33 "and behold, he and the people with him are coming out against you, and you shall do to him whatever your hand finds [to do]" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἰδοὺ αὐτὸς καὶ ὁ λαὸς ὁ μετ' αὐτοῦ ἐκπορεύονται πρὸς σέ, καὶ ποιήσεις αὐτῷ, ὅσα ἂν εὕርῃ ἡ χείር σου</note>; 9:45 "and he demolished the city" <note>original Greek: καὶ τὴν πόλιν καθεῖλε</note>; 10:8 "at that time, eighteen years in all" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ ὀκτωκαίδεκα ἔτη (τοὺς) πάντας</note>; 12:13 "son of Hillel" <note>original Greek: υἱὸς Ἑλλήλ</note>; 13:16 "because Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the Lord" <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐκ ἔγνω Μανወέ, ὅτι ἄγγελος Κυρίου αὐτός</note>; 16:23 "great" <note>original Greek: μέጋ</note> and "Dagon" <note>original Greek: Δαγών</note>; 19:16 "in the evening" <note>original Greek: ἐν ἑስπέρᾳ</note>; 20:1 "to the Lord" <note>original Greek: πρὸς Κύሪον</note>; 20:26 "on that day" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ</note> (found in CG); 20:27 "of the covenant" <note>original Greek: τῆς διαθήκης</note>; 20:37 "and the ambush rushed and spread out toward Gibeah" <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸ ἔነድρον ὥρμησε καὶ ἐξεχύθησαν πρὸς τὴν Γαባά</note>; 21:3 "O God of Israel" <note>original Greek: Θεὲ Ἰσραήλ</note>. We have corrected certain corrupt readings of manuscript F using C or G in Chapters 2:22; 3:19; 4:17; 5:3, 4, 14, 19, 23, 24; 6:35 (comparing 7:24, 9:31, 11:12); 8:2, 3; 9:34; 15:8; 16:31; 18:11, 12; 19:5, 6, 17, and we have indicated these corrected passages by adding brackets. In 8:17, 22; 11:16, 37, we have adopted better readings from CG into the text and noted the readings of manuscript F in the annotations for those places. There remain passages in 8:10, 26; 10:18; 17:10; 19:4; 20:13, 25, 31 where we were unwilling to correct the distorted readings that almost all manuscripts provide; regarding these, one may consult the specific annotations for those locations. --- Page 693 ---
<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Ethiopic translation of the Book of Judges, specifically focusing on how the ancient translator handled the Greek source text (the Septuagint). It evaluates the accuracy, style, and specific instances where the translator added, omitted, or modified words to better suit the Ge'ez language or his own interpretive choices.</meta>

The marks <note>brackets or signs used to indicate editorial insertions</note> we have included in this book are very rare; they are found primarily in 4:3. In the passages 1:35, 5:14, 5:29, 6:10, and 9:28, the single particle **Φ** <note>the Greek letter Phi, likely used as a scribal mark</note> was incorrectly inserted by the scribes.

If you compare this Ethiopic version of the Book of Judges with the Greek text, you will see that the greatest part of the book has been well and clearly rendered by the Ethiopian translator. There are indeed places in this book where we might judge the Ethiopian’s words to be somewhat obscure or entirely lacking sense—for example, in Chapter 1:15, 1:19, and 18:7, and especially in the Song of Deborah in Judges 5 (verses 7, 8, and 10) and elsewhere. However, this should not be blamed on the Ethiopian translator, but rather on the Greek translators <note>referring to the Septuagint</note>, who frequently interpreted the Hebrew words very poorly. Wherever the Greek version is not burdened by this kind of obscurity, the Ethiopian has also translated most things correctly.

He followed the Greek words faithfully almost everywhere. Where he preferred to deviate from the literal sound of the Greek words, he certainly expressed their meaning well. For example, in his translation of the words:
* "and it came to pass" <note>Greek: καὶ ἐγένετο</note> in 3:4.
* "secret" <note>Greek: κρύφιος</note> in 3:19.
* "he took" <note>Greek: ἔλαβε</note> in 3:21.
* "at his feet" <note>Greek: κατὰ πόδας αὐτοῦ</note> and "he cried out" <note>Greek: ἐβόησε</note> in 4:10.
* "he called" <note>Greek: ἐκάለσε</note> in 4:13.
* "I will stay" <note>Greek: καθίσομαι</note> in 6:18.
* "empty and cowardly" <note>Greek: κενοὺς καὶ δειλοὺς</note> in 9:4.
* "Elloulim" <note>Greek: Ἐλλουλίμ; a transliteration of the Hebrew for 'revelry' or a festival</note> in 9:27.
* "of the web" <note>Greek: τοῦ ὑφάσματος; referring to fabric on a loom</note> in 16:14.
* "and the house of Micah etc." <note>Greek: καὶ ὁ οἶκος Μιχαία</note> in 17:5.
* "they will add" <note>Greek: προσθήσουσι</note> in 18:25.
* "having begun" <note>Greek: ἀρξάμενος</note> in 19:6.
* "strengthening the heart" <note>Greek: στηρίζων τὴν καρδίαν</note> in 19:8.
* "the day has declined" <note>Greek: κέክλικεν ἡ ἡμέρα</note> in 19:8, 9, 11.
* "he himself dwelt" <note>Greek: αὐτὸς παρῴκει</note> in 19:16.
* "door" <note>Greek: θύραν</note> in 19:26.

Likewise, he departed significantly from the Greek words in 4:21, 6:38, 8:3, 20:8–9, and at the beginning of 21:21; he translated less accurately in 3:22 and at the end of 17:4. 

At times, he seems to have added certain words without any Greek authority, namely: 
* "to those" <note>Ge'ez: ለእነ፡ (la-ella)</note> in 1:1.
* "in it" <note>Ge'ez: ቦቱ፡ (botu)</note> in 6:26 and 6:28.
* "only" <note>Ge'ez: ባሕቲቱ፡ (bahtitu)</note> in 7:10.
* "to her" <note>Ge'ez: ለቲ፡ (lati)</note> in 9:2.
* "with the end" <note>Ge'ez: ምስለ፡ ኅልቁ፡ (misla helqu)</note> in 11:38.
* "standing" <note>Ge'ez: ቆሞ፡ (qomo)</note> in 18:17.

In other places, he omitted several words from the Greek text that seemed superfluous or less necessary, such as:
* "the tip" <note>Greek: τὸ ἄκρον</note> and "of that in the hand" <note>Greek: τῆς ἐν τῇ χειρί</note> in 6:21.
* "of the grove" <note>Greek: τοῦ ἄλσους</note> in 6:26.
* "let me test once more with the fleece" <note>Greek: πειράσω δὴ καί γε ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐν τῷ πόκῳ</note> in 6:39.
* "in the ears" <note>Greek: ἐν ὠσί</note> in 7:3 and 9:2–3.
* "this one shall go with you" <note>Greek: οὗτος πορεύσεται σὺν σοὶ</note> in 7:4.
* "a cake" <note>Greek: μαγίς</note> in 7:13.
* "to Gideon" <note>Greek: πρὸς Γεδεών</note> in 8:1.
* "and they passed by" <note>Greek: καὶ παρῆλθον</note> in 9:26.
* "I will add/repeat" <note>Greek: προσθήσω</note> in 10:13.
* "all" <note>Greek: πάντα</note> in 11:20.
* "into their hands" <note>Greek: εἰς χεῖρας αὐτῶν</note> in 14:9.
* "in me" <note>Greek: ἐν ἐμοί</note> in 15:8 (though he includes it in 6:13 and 6:15).
* "with the warp" <note>Greek: σὺν τῷ διάσματι</note> in 16:13.
* "behold" <note>Greek: ἰδού</note> in 19:16.
* "this" <note>Greek: τοῦτον</note> in 19:23.
* "the sons of Israel" <note>Greek: οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραήλ</note> twice in 20:45.
* "into a man's bed" <note>Greek: εἰς κοίτην ἄρσενος</note> in 21:12.
* "at that time" <note>Greek: ἐν τῷ καιርῷ ἐκείνῳ</note> in 21:24.

The words in 17:2 were considerably shortened by him. In the Song of Deborah, however, he indulged in this liberty more than a good translator should; by cutting off many parts of the speech, he often distorted the style of the poetic rhythm. For this reason, all the observations we made on pages 20 and 140 regarding the version of Genesis 49 and Deuteronomy 33 apply to Judges 5 as well.

Furthermore, in certain places the translator substituted more specific Ethiopic terms for more general Greek expressions:
* 2:14 "to deliver into hands" <note>Greek: ἀποδιδόναι ἐν χερσί</note> became "to deliver into his hand" <note>Ge'ez: ለእቶ፡ ውስተ፡ እዴሁ፡ (la-eto westa edehu)</note>.
* 2:19 "practices" <note>Greek: ἐπιτηδεύματα</note> became "evil" <note>Ge'ez: አከይ፡ (akay)</note>, and "stubborn" <note>Greek: σκληρὸς</note> became "evil" <note>Ge'ez: አከይ፡ (akay)</note>.
* 3:19 "of the carvings/idols" <note>Greek: τῶν γλυπτῶν</note> became "house of gods/temple" <note>Ge'ez: ቤት፡ አማልክት፡ (bet amalkt)</note>.
* 6:27 "to do" <note>Greek: ποιῆσαι</note> became "having entered" <note>Ge'ez: በዊኦ፡ (ba-wi'o)</note>.
* 9:23 "spirit" <note>Greek: πνεῦμα</note> became "demon" <note>Ge'ez: ጋኔን፡ (ganen)</note>.
* 16:29 "to take hold of" <note>Greek: κρατεῖν</note> became "to lean/shake" <note>Ge'ez: ንሂሀ፡ (nehiha)</note>.

Or vice versa, he strayed more broadly from the stricter sense of the Greek words:
* 3:3 "satrapies" <note>Greek: σατραπείαι</note> [translated as] "nations" <note>Ge'ez: አሕ... (ah...) - the word is likely 'ahzab', meaning nations/peoples</note>

<summary>This page evaluates the quality of the Ethiopic translation of Judges, noting that while generally faithful to the Greek Septuagint, the translator often simplified poetic sections or substituted specific Ge'ez terms for broad Greek ones.</summary>

### Lexical Comparisons and Translation Choices

To; 4:21 **hammer** <note>original Greek: σφύρα</note> was rendered as **stone** <note>original Ge'ez: እብን፡ ('ebn)</note>; 
5:22 **they were hindered** <note>original Greek: ἐνεποδίσθησαν</note> was rendered as **they resisted** <note>original Ge'ez: ተቃዋወሙ፡ (taqawawamu)</note>; 
6:19 **an ephah of flour** <note>original Greek: οἰφὶ ἀλεύρου</note> was rendered as **yofant** <note>original Ge'ez: ዮፋንት፡; a transliteration of the Greek 'oiphi'</note>; 
6:37, 38 **a fleece of wool** <note>original Greek: πόκον τῶν ἐρίφων</note> was rendered as **wool** <note>original Ge'ez: ፀምር፡ (tsämr)</note>; 
7:8 **to prevail** <note>original Greek: κατισχύειν</note> was rendered as **he established** <note>original Ge'ez: አቀመ፡ (aqämä)</note>; 
10:4, 12:14 **colt** <note>original Greek: πῶλος</note> was rendered as **donkey** <note>original Ge'ez: አየጥ፡ (ayät)</note>; 
11:3 **empty men** <note>original Greek: κενοὶ</note> was rendered as **worthless** <note>original Ge'ez: ኒየያት፡ (niyayāt)</note>; 
14:5 **a lion’s cub** <note>original Greek: σκυμνὸς λέοντος</note> was rendered as **lion** <note>original Ge'ez: አንበሳ፡ (anbäsa)</note>; 
14:10 **he made a feast** <note>original Greek: ἐποίησε πότον</note> was rendered as **he arranged** <note>original Ge'ez: ሠርዐ፡ (šär'a)</note>; 
15:8 **tow** <note>original Greek: στυпπίον; the coarse part of flax</note> was rendered as **chaff** <note>original Ge'ez: ሐሠር፡ (ḥäšär)</note>; 
16:7, 8 **moist/fresh** <note>original Greek: ὑγρός</note> was rendered as **new** <note>original Ge'ez: ሐዲስ፡ (ḥaddis)</note>; 
18:3 **to turn aside** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλίνει</note> was rendered as **he entered** <note>original Ge'ez: ቦአ፡ (bo'a)</note>; 
18:16 **to be stationed** <note>original Greek: στηλοῦσθαι</note> was rendered as **they gathered** <note>original Ge'ez: ተጋብአ፡ (tägab'a)</note>; 
21:11 **to devote to destruction** <note>original Greek: ἀναθεματίζειν</note> was rendered as **to kill** <note>original Ge'ez: ቀተለ፡ (qätälä)</note>; 
21:11, 11:34 **dances** <note>original Greek: χόροις</note> was rendered as **harps** <note>original Ge'ez: መሳንቆ፡ (mäsanqo)</note>; 
21:23 **to dance** <note>original Greek: χορεύειν</note> was rendered as **to play/frolic** <note>original Ge'ez: ተወነየ፡ (täwänäyä)</note>.

The translator rendered the following words with little accuracy in his version: **cloak** <note>original Greek: μανδύας</note> (3:16); **skull** <note>original Greek: κράνιον</note> (9:53; compare 4:21, 22; 5:26); **battle-line** <note>original Greek: παράταξις</note> (6:25); **lookout** <note>original Greek: σκοпιά</note> (11:29); and **they went up** <note>original Greek: ἀνέβησαν</note> (20:3). 

He mistakenly believed that the nouns **sacred grove** <note>original Greek: ἄλσος, 'alsos,' often referring to the goddess Asherah</note> and **Ephod** <note>original Greek: Ἐφὼδ</note> signified images of gods, and he interpreted them as **image/idol** <note>original Ge'ez: ምስል፡ (misil)</note> in passages 3:7, 6:25, 28, 30; 8:27, 17:5, 18:14–20.

Because precise corresponding terms were lacking in Ge'ez, he retained several Greek words as if they were proper names: **oak** <note>original Greek: βαλάνῳ</note> in 9:6 (compare Genesis 35:8); **bramble** <note>original Greek: ῥάμνον</note> in 9:14 and following; **broth** <note>original Greek: ζωμόν</note> in 6:19, 20; and **linen garments** <note>original Greek: σινδόνας</note> in 14:12, 13. He did the same for **weeping** <note>original Greek: κλαυθμὸν</note> in 2:1 (though he translated it differently in verse 5) and **palms** <note>original Greek: φοινίκων</note> in 3:13 and 4:5 (compare Deuteronomy 34:3).

Certain other things, which he understood less well or even wrongly, he interpreted incorrectly: 1:15 **lofty** and **lowly** <note>original Greek: μετεώρων and ταπεινῶν</note>; 3:20 **in the summer parlor** <note>original Greek: τῷ θερινῷ</note>; 5:2 **to begin** <note>original Greek: ἄρχεσθαι</note>; 8:2 **the gleaning/small leaves** <note>original Greek: ἐμφυλλίς</note>; 12:6 **password/signal** <note>original Greek: σύνθημα</note>; 20:31 **they were emptied out/drawn away** <note>original Greek: ἐξεκενώθησαν</note>. Regarding the translation of the words in 8:7, you should consult the annotation for that specific place. 

In various places, he also erred in reading the Greek words: in 1:36, he read **boundary** <note>original Greek: ὅριον</note> as **mountain** <note>original Greek: ὄρος</note> (?); in 4:9, **your advantage** <note>original Greek: τὸ προτέρημά σου</note> as **your former word** <note>original Greek: τὸ πρότερον ῥῆμά σου</note>; in 7:21, **they signaled** <note>original Greek: ἐσήማναν</note> as **they rotted** <note>original Greek: ἐσάπησαν</note> (?); in 8:30, **thighs** <note>original Greek: μηρῶν</note> as **parts** <note>original Greek: μερῶν</note>; and in 16:3, **bar** <note>original Greek: μόχλος</note> as **crowd** <note>original Greek: ὄχλος</note>. 

In several places, he followed a different word punctuation than the accepted one, namely in 5:25, 9:15, and 24. He thought the words **he was cut off** etc. <note>original Greek: ἐξεκόπη κ. τ. λ.</note> in 21:6 were an interrogative statement. He also joined the beginnings of verses 2:15, 5:13, 21, 11:16, 26, 13:20, and 18:3 with the immediately preceding verses, and connected the end of verse 18:15 with the 16th verse. Remarkable is his translation of **they went down** as **they went up** <note>original Ge'ez: ዐርጉ፡ ('ärgu)</note> in 14:7; **to go on the way** as **his house** <note>original Ge'ez: ቤቶ፡ (beto)</note> in 17:8; and **they hastened** as **they were gathered together** <note>original Ge'ez: ተወሃለኡ፡ (täwähalä'u)</note> in 20:41.

### Analysis of the Author's Identity

Now that the character of the translation has been described, let us express what we think of its author. There are certain phrases found in this book that are less common in the Pentateuch <note>the first five books of the Bible</note> and Joshua; for example, **fortress** and **to take refuge** <note>original Ge'ez: ጸወን፡ and ተጸወነ፡</note> in 9:46–51; **to bestow/grant** <note>original Ge'ez: ጸገወ፡</note> in 1:14; **by lot/rope** <note>original Ge'ez: በሐበለ፡</note> in 3:22; **with him** <note>original Ge'ez: ምስሌሁ፡</note> in 7:16, 19, 20. Phrases such as **to be gathered to his fathers** (2:10) and **to fill the hand/consecrate** (17:5, 12) are translated differently here than in the Pentateuch. Even the translation of the terms *alsos* and *Ephod* (mentioned above) seems relevant here, although it is clear the translator was led by sufficient reasons to vary the translation.

But in many other matters—and indeed in the most numerous ones—the translation of this book agrees wonderfully with the version of the Pentateuch and Joshua. In Judges 1 and 2, everything, even the rarer words, is rendered in the same way as in Joshua. You will particularly note the translation of the words **surrounding areas** (1:16), **for tribute** (1:28–35), **descent** (1:16), **at the entrance** (1:14), **city of letters/scribes** (1:11, 12), **the former/before** (1:10, 11, 23), and others. Just like the translator of Joshua, the translator of Judges used words like **to arrive**, **having gone**, **to blow**, **to cast**, **to be silent**, **to permit**, **to be enough**, **to gather together**...

Next, one may compare several terms from the <term>Pentateuch</term> <note>the first five books of the Bible</note>:

* Genesis 21:22 and 26:26 match **መጋቤ፡ መርዔት** <note>original Ge'ez: magābe mar’ēt; chief of the flock/steward</note> in Judges 14:20.
* Leviticus 5:15 and elsewhere match **አስበለ** <note>original Ge'ez: asbala</note> in Judges 21:22.
* Deuteronomy 21:4 matches **መብእካ** <note>original Ge'ez: mab’eka; a valley or watercourse</note> in Judges 5:6.
* Deuteronomy 32:6 matches **ገፋትኤ** <note>original Ge'ez: gafāt’ē</note> in Judges 5:6.
* Genesis 17:14, Leviticus 26:15, and others match **ኀደገ፡ ኪዳነ** <note>original Ge'ez: ḫadaga kidāna</note> for the phrase *to break a covenant* <note>Greek: διασκεδάζειν διαθήκην</note> in Judges 2:1.
* Exodus 10:7 matches **ሀውየ** <note>original Ge'ez: hawya</note> for the word *booty* or *snare* <note>Greek: σκῦλον</note> in Judges 11:35 (though different in 8:27).
* Exodus 5:17 matches **ሀረረ** <note>original Ge'ez: harara; to be lazy or idle</note> in Judges 18:7.
* Genesis 40:20 matches **በሀል** <note>original Ge'ez: bahal</note> for the word *drinking feast* <note>Greek: πότος</note> in Judges 14:17.

Furthermore, the following words: **ማኅበር** <note>original Ge'ez: māḫbar; assembly. Greek: ἐκκλησία, συναγωγή</note> (20, 1 seq., 21, 5—16); **ትዕይንት** <note>original Ge'ez: te’eyent; camp. Greek: παρεμβολή</note> (4, 15, 16, 21, 12); **አገበረ** <note>original Ge'ez: agabara; to make serve/enslave</note> (13, 15); **ጎወደ** <note>original Ge'ez: gowada; to flow</note> (15, 1); **ትውልድ** <note>original Ge'ez: tewled; generation. Greek: γενεὰ</note> (2, 10, 3, 2); **አዝማድ** <note>original Ge'ez: azmād; relatives/kindred. Greek: συγγένεια</note> (1, 25, 9, 1); **ተቃየደ፡ ኪዳነ** <note>original Ge'ez: taqāyada kidāna; to make a covenant</note> (2, 2, 8, 33); **ሀገር** <note>original Ge'ez: hagar; city</note> (3, 9, 15, 4, 3, 6, 6, 10, 10); **ሀለቀ** <note>original Ge'ez: halaqa; to perish/end</note> (2, 15, 4, 3, 6, 9, 10, 8); **አስጠመወ** <note>original Ge'ez: asṭamawa; to dip/immerse</note> (4, 3); **አጠወቀ** <note>original Ge'ez: aṭawaqa; to press/oppress</note> (1, 34); **ተቀንየ** <note>original Ge'ez: taqanya; to serve/be enslaved</note> (2, 7, 3, 8, 14, 10, 6); **ቤተ፡ ቅኔት** <note>original Ge'ez: bēta qenēt; house of bondage</note> (6, 8); **ጎሕር** <note>original Ge'ez: goḥer; pit/cistern</note> (4, 19); **ሀውየ** <note>original Ge'ez: hawya</note> used in various senses (6, 11, 32, 37); **ባሕር** <note>original Ge'ez: bāḥer; sea</note> (6, 19); **መቅደስ** <note>original Ge'ez: maqdas; sanctuary</note> (ibid.); **ዐጸረ** <note>original Ge'ez: ‘atṣara; to press/squeeze</note> (6, 38); **ሕብስት** <note>original Ge'ez: ḫebest; bread</note> (8, 26); **መፍትው** <note>original Ge'ez: maftew; fitting/proper</note> (19, 19); **ሐዊር** <note>original Ge'ez: ḫawir; to go/walk</note> used in an obscene sense (19, 22); **ጐየየ** <note>original Ge'ez: gwayaya; to flee</note> (9, 48); **ሀለቀ** <note>original Ge'ez: halaqa</note> (5, 30); **መጠው** <note>original Ge'ez: maṭaw; to deliver</note> (6, 34, 35, 14) and **አውጻወ** <note>original Ge'ez: awtsāwa; to bring out</note> (7, 23, 24, 18, 12); **ሕብር** <note>original Ge'ez: ḫeber</note> for *part* <note>Greek: μέρος</note> (7, 11, 19, 1) and many other words are used very frequently in the Book of Judges just as they are in the Pentateuch and Joshua.

Similarly, throughout the Pentateuch, the word *behold* <note>Greek: ἰδοὺ</note> is translated by **ረበበ** <note>original Ge'ez: rababa</note> (3, 24, 25, 4, 22, 6, 28, 19, 27); the word *to see/know* <note>Greek: ἰδεῖν</note> by **አእመረ** <note>original Ge'ez: a’mara</note> (6, 22, 16, 18); and *to lift up the voice* <note>Greek: ἐπᾶραι τὴν φωνὴν</note> by **ጸርጎ** <note>original Ge'ez: tsargo</note> (2, 4, 9, 7, 21, 2). The translation of *to rise early* <note>Greek: ὀρθρίζειν</note> as **ነቅሀ** <note>original Ge'ez: naqha</note> (19, 5, 8), *to be assembled* <note>Greek: ἐκκλησιάζεσθαι</note> as **አንገላገ** <note>original Ge'ez: angalāga</note> (20, 1; see Numbers 16, 11), and *pure* <note>Greek: ἁγνὸς</note> as **ሀለየ፡ ወፋር** <note>original Ge'ez: halaya wafar</note> (1, 14) is also unique to the Book of Judges itself; otherwise, the translator uses the words **ገሠ** <note>original Ge'ez: gaśa</note> (7, 1, 9, 33, 19, 9, 21, 4), **ተጋብአ** <note>original Ge'ez: tagāb’a</note>, and **ገራህት** <note>original Ge'ez: garāht</note> or **ሐቀል** <note>original Ge'ez: ḥaqal</note> just as the translator of the Pentateuch and Joshua does.

Having duly considered these similarities we have listed, as well as the close relationship that exists between the translation of the Book of Judges and Joshua, and between Joshua and the Pentateuch, we are further led to conjecture that the translator of the Book of Judges was either using the most common Ethiopic Pentateuch and Joshua or was not at all different from the primary translator of the Pentateuch and Joshua. To me, at least, those unique expressions found here and there in the Book of Judges do not seem to stand in the way.

<meta>This page continues the philological comparison between the Ge'ez translation of the Book of Judges and other Old Testament books. The author concludes that the same translator was likely responsible for several books based on their shared stylistic quirks and errors, then discusses chapter divisions and specific textual variants compared to the Greek Septuagint.</meta>

...nothing prevents us from concluding that the same person translated all those books. The same general method of translation and the same lack of understanding regarding poetic style <note>original Latin: "styli poëtici ignorantia"</note> is evident in those books, specifically in Genesis 49, Deuteronomy 33, and Judges 5. However, it seems necessary to caution readers at this point not to form a final judgment on this matter until they have also compared the version used in the other historical books.

I do not know whether the Book of Judges was divided into chapters among the earlier Ethiopians; certainly, no traces of such divisions appear in our manuscripts. In <term>Codex F</term> <note>an early manuscript of the Ethiopic Bible</note>, the words **ይበ፡ እግዚአብሔር፡** <note>original Ge'ez: yibe 'egzi'abḥer; "The Lord said"</note> are marked in red ink at 2:2, 6:23, 7:2, 3, 4, 5, 7, and 9; no other type of division is indicated anywhere else in this manuscript. In the more recent <term>Codices</term> <note>ancient manuscript volumes</note> C and G, those 21 chapters that are read in our own editions of the Bible are inscribed and numbered. Chapter nineteen in Codex G begins from the word **ΦΥΛΦ** <note>likely a phonetic transcription of a Ge'ez word used as a marker</note> at the middle of 19:1, just as in the Greek editions of Judges.

### 2. A survey of readings where the translator’s Greek source differed from the standard Greek text.

1, 1: "in the Lord" <note>original Greek: ἐν Κυρίῳ</note> instead of "through the Lord" <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦ Κυρ.</note> (C). 4: "his" <note>original Greek: αὐτοῦ</note> instead of "theirs" <note>original Greek: αὐτῶν</note>. ibid. "they cut" <note>original Greek: ἔκοψαν</note> at the 2nd instance. 5: "they found" <note>original Greek: εὗρον</note> instead of "they overtook" <note>original Greek: κατέλαβον</note>. [at] "in Bezek" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ Βεζέκ</note>. 6: "they pursued" <note>original Greek: κατεδίωξαν</note> instead of "they overran" <note>original Greek: κατέδραμον</note>. ### CHAPTER 8.

**Verse 2. "Do I excel you?"** <note>original: እትኄይስኪ</note>**] "You excel me"** <note>original: ትኄይሱኒ</note> in the manuscripts, which is nonsensical. But even instead of the suffix **"me"** <note>original: ኒ</note> it is better to read it as the interrogative **"?"** <note>original: ኑ</note> [**"if"**] ① in Codex F. **Verse 3. [ ]** Omitted in Codex F. For although the word which corresponds to the Ethiopic **"he destroyed"** <note>original: አጥፋ</note> is not read in either the Greek or Hebrew text, Codex F nevertheless has the interrogative particle **"nu"** <note>original: ኑ</note> inserted after the phrase **"they were unable,"** <note>original: እይክለሙ</note> which, since it is nonsensical, I have replaced with the emendation from CG.

**Verse 4. "And with it, whoever"]** <note>original: ወበአእቱ፡ መኑኑ</note> **"and his twelve"** <note>original: ወአልባቱ፡ ፲፪</note> **in CG. Verse 7. "I will crucify"** <note>original: እሰቅል</note> and so on] The author <note>referring to the original translator or ancient editor</note> misinterpreted this sentence both here and in Verse 16. He hallucinated <note>The translator uses this strong term to indicate a significant scholarly error in the manuscript</note> that the word *akanthais* <note>Greek: thorns</note> or *akanbais* (for so he seems to have read it) was a proper name, just like *Barkeneim* <note>Greek: Βαρκηνηίμ, meaning briers</note>, and he assigned the meaning of "piercing" or "crucifying" to the verb *aloan* <note>Greek: to thresh</note> or *kataxainein* <note>Greek: to card/tear</note>. For *Barkeneim*, he had the reading *Barchomein*, and he poorly read and translated it as **"two akomehi"** <note>original: ፪ አኮመሂ</note>; he translated the same word better in Verse 16. Furthermore, the translation of the word *akanthais* <note>thorns</note> was corrupted by the scribes into **"waists"** <note>original: ሀቆባት</note>. No emendation occurs in CG.

### 3. Annotations on the Book of Ruth.

#### 1. Regarding the nature of the version and the condition of the text.

**T**he eighth small book of the <term>Octateuch</term> <note>The first eight books of the Old Testament</note> was edited in the year of Christ 1660 by Johann Georg Nisselius and printed at Leiden under the title: "The Book of Ruth, in Ethiopic, extracted from an ancient manuscript recently brought from the East and faithfully rendered into Latin." The text contained in this book agrees remarkably in almost all places with our **Codex F**, and it exhibits nearly all the same obsolete word forms and the same scribal errors for which **Codex F** is notable ¹). We shall designate Nisselius's book with the symbol **N.**

In addition to books **F** and **N**, we have used the more recent manuscripts **C** and **G** in compiling our edition; these contain the ancient version as corrected by another author and varied in many places by scribes. From these, we have filled gaps in 1:6, 2:11, and 4:13, 17, and we have corrected certain corrupted readings in 1:17, 2:3, 8, 16, 17, and 4:3, 8, 15. Others we have corrected ourselves, see 1:14 and 4:9. But some gaps remain which were not even filled in **Manuscripts C and G**, specifically in 1:12 where the words **"because I said, there is hope for me to belong to a man"** <note>Greek: ὅτι εἶπα, ὅτι ἐστί μοι ὑπόστασις τοῦ γεννηθῆναι με ἀνδρί</note> are missing (due to <term>homoeoteleuton</term> <note>a scribal error where the eye skips text between two similar words</note>); in 2:2 **"in his eyes"** <note>Greek: ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ</note>; in 2:3 **"by chance"** <note>Greek: περιπτώματι</note>; in 2:4 **"behold"** <note>Greek: ἰδού</note>; and in 2:13 **"O Lord"** <note>Greek: Κύሪε</note>; nor do I doubt that many of these words...

...already omitted in the ancient version. For if anyone considers the entire character of the translation, they will easily recognize that the translator of this book cared little for individual Greek words and accurately expressed only the general sense of many sentences or phrases—and in some cases, not even the sense. For example, "To visit" <note>original Greek: Ἐπισκέπτεσθαι</note> in 1:6 is translated not as "to visit/inspect" <note>original: ኀወጸ፡</note> but as "to show mercy/grace" <note>original: ተሣሀለ፡</note>; and "may he add these things" <note>original Greek: καὶ τάδε προσθείη</note> in 1:17 is rendered "he gave him to death" <note>original: ወሀቦ፡ ለሞት፡</note>; likewise in 1:17, "because death will separate me and you" <note>original Greek: ὅτι θάνατος διαስተለῖ ἀναμέσον ἐሞῦ καὶ σοῦ</note>. In 2:2, "to gather among the ears of grain" <note>original Greek: συνάγειν ἐν τοῖς στάχυσι</note>. In 2:7, "among the sheaves" <note>original Greek: ἐν τοῖς δράγμασι</note>. In 2:13, "to speak to the heart" <note>original Greek: λαለῖν ἐπὶ καρδίαን</note>. In 2:14, "morsel" <note>original Greek: ψωμός</note>. In 2:21, "until they finish" <note>original Greek: ἕως ἂν τελέσωσι</note> etc. In 3:10, "you have made good" <note>original Greek: ἠγάθυνας</note>. In 4:4, "there is no one besides you" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστι πάρεξ σοῦ</note> etc., are translated according to the sense rather than word-for-word. 

However, he translates less accurately than is proper in 1:16 "to meet" <note>original Greek: ἀπαντᾷν</note> (different in 2:22), 1:19 "if this is she," 2:3 "it happened by chance," 2:9 "to draw water," 2:10 "why is it that... you recognize me," 2:16 "and even dropping... from the bundles," 3:2 "he is winnowing the threshing floor... tonight," 3:7 "in the portion," 4:2 "he gave back," and 4:4 "acquire" (different in verses 8–10). He wrongly interpreted 3:10 "young men" <note>original Greek: νεανιῶν</note>. In 4:1, for "O hidden/anonymous one" <note>original Greek: κρύፍιε</note>, he rather rashly substituted the word "not spoken of" or "unnamed" <note>original: አትነገረ፡</note>. Finally, he thought the words "let me go now" etc. in 2:2 and "I am the kinsman-redeemer" in 4:4 were spoken as questions. Some slight additions are found, such as "helper/grace" <note>original: ረዴ፡</note> in 2:13 and "bird" <note>original: ዖፍ፡</note> in 3:2.

Regarding the author of the translation, it seems hardly anything certain can be determined due to the small size of the book. Nevertheless, I would recommend the reader observe the translation of individual words made by him, which are the same as those found in the Book of Judges and other parts of the Octateuch <note>The first eight books of the Bible</note>. "To lift up the voice" <note>original Greek: Ἐπᾶραι τὴν φωνὴν</note> he translates as "he shouted/cried out" <note>original: ጸርኃ፡</note> in 1:9, 14 (cf. Judges 2:4, 9:7, 21:2); "to be for a man" <note>meaning to marry; original Greek: εἶναι εἰς ἄνδρα</note> as "to marry/be wed" <note>original: አውሰቦ፡</note> in 1:11, 12, 13 (cf. Judges 15:9, 21:1, 7); "to grow up" <note>original Greek: ἁδርυνθῆναι</note> as "he grew up" <note>original: ለህቀ፡</note> in 1:13 (cf. Judges 11:2, 13:24); "kindred" <note>original Greek: συγγένεια</note> as "relative/kin" <note>original: ዘመድ፡ and አዝማድ፡</note> in 2:1, 3 (cf. Judges 1:25, 9:1); "yesterday and the third day" <note>meaning recently; original Greek: ἐχθὲስ καὶ τρίτης</note> as "yesterday" <note>original: ትማልት፡</note> in 2:11 (see above p. 169 and Judges 1:10, 11, 23); "threshing floor" <note>original Greek: ἅλων</note> as "threshing floor" <note>original: ዐውድ፡ ኰክለ፡</note> in 3:2–14 (cf. Judges 6:37); "the heart was made good" <note>original Greek: ἠγαθύνθη ἡ καρδία</note> as "the heart rejoiced" <note>original: ተፈሥሐ፡ ልብ፡</note> in 3:7 (cf. Judges 19:6, 9, 22; 18:20); "to turn aside" <note>original Greek: ἐκκλίνειν</note> as "he turned away" <note>original: ገሐሠ፡</note> in 4:1 (cf. Judges 4:18, 14:5 and elsewhere); "elders" <note>original Greek: πρεσβύτεροι</note> as "leaders/elders" <note>original: ሊቃናት፡</note> in 4:1; "field" <note>original Greek: ἀγρὸς</note> sometimes as "field" <note>original: ሐቅል፡</note> in 1:1, 2, 6, 22; 2:6; 4:3, and sometimes as "landed property/farm" <note>original: ገራህት፡</note> in 4:3, 5 (see p. 195); "neighbors" <note>original Greek: γείτονες</note> as "neighbors" <note>original: አጐርር፡</note> in 4:17 (Exodus 3:22); "as/about" <note>original Greek: ὡς</note> as "it amounts to/about" <note>original: የአክል፡</note> in 1:4 (see p. 170); "to humble" <note>original Greek: ταπεινοῦν</note> as "he brought low/shamed" <note>original: አሕሰረ፡</note> in 1:21 (Judges 19:24, 20:5; but different in Judges 16:5); "to treat badly/afflict" <note>original Greek: κακοῦν</note> as "he caused pain/grief" <note>original: አሕመመ፡</note> in 1:21 (Judges 4:3). Add certain other words frequently used by him, such as "to make/place" <note>original: ረሰየ፡</note>, "surety/protector" <note>original: ዋሕስ፡</note>, "he entered/returned" <note>original: አተወ፡</note>, and "he fled/turned" <note>original: ንየየ፡</note> etc. The term "to act as kinsman-redeemer" <note>original Greek: ἀγχιστεύειν</note> was required by the sense itself to be translated differently in this book than in the Pentateuch and Joshua. The noun "young man" <note>original Greek: παιδάሪον</note> was translated in our book not as "son/child" <note>original: ወልድ፡</note>, but as "youth" <note>original: ወሬዛ፡</note> and "servant/attendant" <note>original: ጸዋ፡</note> (2:5, 6, 9, 15).

The four chapters into which the Book of Ruth is divided among Europeans are also marked in Manuscripts C and G. In Manuscript F, no division of the book is noted; Nisselius also followed the modern division of the book in his edition. A note added at the beginning of the first chapter in Codex F indicates that a section to be read in the churches on the day of the end of winter (or the end of the year) is to be taken from the Book of Ruth: "To be read during the prayer on a winter's day" <note>original: በምህላ፡ ዕለተ፡ ክረምት፡ ዘይትነበብ፡</note>.
