## Postscript. <note>original Latin: Postscriptum</note>

With the completion of this third installment, we issue the first volume of the **Ethiopic Old Testament** <note>original: Veteris Testamenti Aethiopici</note>. There remain to be edited and printed four more volumes, which will encompass the remaining historical books, the poetic books, the prophetic books, and the apocryphal and pseudepigraphal works. However, although we possess the materials necessary for publishing these books, having collected them from various manuscript codices, the lack of funds required for their printing prevents these four volumes from being immediately submitted to the press. For the **German Oriental Society** <note>original: Orientalis Germanorum Societas; also known as the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft</note>, which most generously supported the publication of this first volume by providing half of the expenses, is in no way able to offer new subsidies for our edition due to the smallness of the annual income it receives. Furthermore, the assistance of others, though sought most eagerly, has for the present not been offered or found. Therefore, we yield to necessity and look forward to better times which—as the study of this literature becomes more widespread and flourishes more happily—will open a new opportunity for continuing and completing the work.

**Editor.**

Kiel <note>original: Kiliae</note>, February 1, 1855. <note>original: Calendis Februariis MDCCCLV</note>

# GREETINGS TO THE READER
<note>original Latin: S. L., likely an abbreviation for <term>Salutem Lectori</term>, a standard academic greeting of the era.</note>

About to publish once more a part of the Ethiopic Bible—the first part of the second volume—we must put forward a few words concerning the method used for this edition.

For after the bookseller who took care of the printing of the first volume refused to include the remaining parts, the German Oriental Society <note>The <term>Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft</term> (DMG), one of the oldest scholarly organizations dedicated to the study of Asia and the Orient.</note> wished to promote and increase the aid already very liberally supplied at the start of this work’s publication, so that it might take the remaining volumes into the number of books to be published under its own auspices and at its own expense. At the request of the Distinguished Man, H. Brockhaus <note>Hermann Brockhaus (1806–1877), a famous German Orientalist and professor at Leipzig.</note>, Professor at Leipzig, it was decreed by the members in the council held on the first of October in the year 1857 at Breslau <note>Now Wrocław, Poland.</note> that a certain definite sum of money from the Society’s funds should be expended each year from now on to finish our edition of the Bible (see: **Minutes of the General Assembly at Breslau in the Journal of the German Oriental Society. Vol. 12. 1858. p. 195**). As we profess ourselves to be bound by our innermost soul for such a great benefit bestowed upon our work, so we are convinced that all lovers of Ethiopic literature owe the greatest thanks to the directors and members of this most illustrious Society. Therefore, a new light now shines upon these Bibles, which were buried in a long night of oblivion, and one may hope not in vain that their edition will be brought to a conclusion in a time not so far off, if it pleases God. In intervals of single years, single parts <note>original: <term>fasciculi</term></note> will be issued; whether these intervals ought to be extended more or less will be committed to the power and judgment of the Society’s directors.

Readers will easily perceive that this volume differs somewhat in its external appearance from the first. This variation, although it may seem less convenient to some, could nevertheless hardly be avoided. For the Ludolfian types <note>The "Ludolfian types" were a specific font of Ethiopic characters based on the designs of Hiob Ludolf (1624–1704), the founder of Ethiopic studies in Europe.</note>, which we used in printing the first volume, although they are indeed clear, are rather large and require too much space. We were led by the very reason of economy to make the intervals between the single lines in the first volume too narrow, and the writing...

<summary>In this preface, August Dillmann explains that the German Oriental Society has taken over the funding and publication of the Ethiopic Bible after the previous publisher withdrew. He also notes a change in the physical appearance of the book, switching from the large "Ludolfian" font to save space and costs.</summary>

<keywords>August Dillmann, Ethiopic Bible, German Oriental Society, H. Brockhaus, Ludolfian types, scholarly publishing history, 19th-century philology</keywords>

--- Page 726 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface by August Dillmann for the second volume of the Ethiopic Old Testament. The previous page ended mid-word; this page completes the discussion on the administrative shift to the German Oriental Society and moves into technical improvements in printing and acknowledgments of manuscript sources.</meta>

...ture will acknowledge the same. We were previously printing the text in a continuous series across the entire width of the page. This practice was contrary both to the perpetual custom of the Abyssinians <note>A historical term for Ethiopians.</note> and the common rules of calligraphy. Therefore, after smaller and very beautiful Ge'ez <note>The ancient liturgical language of Ethiopia.</note> types—modeled after those grand ones made for d'Abbadie in Paris—were cast in the famous workshop of F. A. Brockhaus, we did not want to miss the opportunity to use them for our project. Trusting that we would be doing a great favor for our readers, we gladly agreed that the managers of the Society should hand over the volumes still to be published to this workshop. In this way, it was possible for the pages to be divided into two columns according to the Ethiopian custom, and for the wider intervals between lines—more suited to the rules of writing—to be restored, while also somewhat reducing the number of sheets required for printing. To achieve these advantages, we did not hesitate to slightly change the external appearance of the book.

Regarding the manuscript books, upon whose authority we compiled the biblical text included in this volume, we have discussed them more fully in the Critical Apparatus <note>The section of a scholarly work that compares different versions of a text to determine the most accurate reading.</note>, and there is no need to add more here. However, we must add praise for those distinguished and eminent men who, through their individual efforts, most kindly assisted our labors. Antoine d’Abbadie <note>1810–1897; a French explorer and scholar who amassed a massive collection of Ethiopian manuscripts.</note>—whose kindness in opening his treasures to us is already known to readers of our edition of the *Kufâlê* <note>The Ethiopic name for the **Book of Jubilees**.</note>—most generously shared all his Ethiopic manuscripts necessary for the preparation of this biblical volume and permitted us to use them for our work. Furthermore, the Rüppellian manuscripts <note>Manuscripts collected by Wilhelm Rüppell, a German naturalist and explorer of Northeast Africa.</note> kept in the public library at Frankfurt am Main were sent to us here in Kiel through the extraordinary kindness of the distinguished Dr. Böhmer. This was made possible by the authority most generously granted by the high Senate of the imperial city and the legal security provided by the most excellent Baron B. de Bülow, the envoy of the most August King of Denmark in Frankfurt. We most eagerly embrace this offered opportunity to publicly pay the thanks due to these highly revered men.

->Given at Kiel, on the Ides of January <note>January 13th</note>, 1861.<-

->**A. Dillmann.**<-

### Division 2
And Hannah said: "My heart <note>original: "ልብየ" (leb-ye). In Semitic thought, the heart is the seat of intellect and will.</note> rejoices in the Lord, and my horn <note>The "horn" is a common biblical metaphor for strength or dignity, derived from the power of a bull.</note> is exalted in my God (and my Savior); my mouth is enlarged over
<margin>2</margin> my enemies, and I have rejoiced in your salvation. For there is none holy like the Lord, and there is none righteous like our God, and there is

<margin>4</margin> deeds]. The bow of the mighty has been weakened, and He has girded the 
<margin>5</margin> weak with strength. Those who were full now lack bread, and the hungry are satisfied; for the barren woman has born seven children, but she who had many children has become a house of

<margin>7</margin> and brings up again. The Lord makes poor and makes
<margin>8</margin> rich; He humbles and He exalts. He raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dust, to seat them with the great ones of the nations and make them inherit a throne of glory."

"And He gives his prayer to him who prayed, and He has blessed the years <margin>9</margin> of the righteous; for a child of man is not strong by his own power. The <margin>10</margin> Lord makes the enemies of the Lord sick; He [alone] is holy. Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor let the mighty man boast in his strength, nor let the rich man boast in his riches. But in this let him who boasts glory: in understanding and knowing the Lord, and doing judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth. The Lord ascended to the heavens and thundered; He judges the ends of the earth, for He is righteous, and He gives strength to our kings and exalts the horn of His Messiah." <note>original: "መሢሑ" (Mesihu), meaning "His Anointed One." # The First Book of Kings

<margin>1</margin> Section 1. There was a certain man from Ramathaim-Zophim <note>original: "Am-Armatem Sifa"</note>, from the hill country of Ephraim <note>original: "Dabra Efrem"</note>. His name was Elkanah <note>original: "Helqana"</note>, the son of Jeroham <note>original: "Iyaremyal"</note>, son of Elihu <note>original: "Eli"</note>, son of Tohu <note>original: "Toqe"</note>, son of <margin>2</margin> Zuph <note>original: "Naseb"</note>, an Ephrathite. And he had two wives: the name of the one was Hannah <note>original: "Hanna"</note>, and the name of the second was Peninnah <note>original: "Fenana"</note>. Peninnah had children, but <margin>3</margin> Hannah had no children. And this man used to go up every year from his city, Ramathaim, to worship and sacrifice to the Lord <note>original: "Egziabher"</note> in Shiloh <note>original: "Selom"</note>. And Eli and his two sons, Hophni <note>original: "Afni"</note> and Phinehas <note>original: "Finhas"</note>, the priests of the Lord, were there. <margin>4</margin> Then, on a certain day, Elkanah offered a sacrifice and gave portions [of the meat] to Peninnah his wife and to her children. <margin>5</margin> And to Hannah he gave one portion <note>While some versions suggest a "double portion," the Ge'ez text emphasizes that he gave her a single portion because she had no children to share with, yet he loved her specifically.</note> because she had no children; however, Elkanah loved Hannah more than the others, <margin>6</margin> but the Lord had closed her womb. And the Lord did not give her children, according to

<column-break/>

her affliction and according to how she grieved with much sorrow and was troubled <margin>7</margin> because of this—because the Lord had closed her womb and did not give her children. And so he did every year: when they went up to the house of the Lord, she would be distressed and weep and would not eat. <margin>8</margin> And Elkanah her husband said to her—and she said, "Here I am, my lord"—and he said to her: “What is wrong with you? Why do you weep? Why do you not eat? And why is your heart troubled? - Saul: The first king of Israel.
- Samuel: The prophet and judge who anointed Saul.
- Amalek: A tribe traditionally seen as the archetypal enemy of Israel.
- Israel: The nation/people of the covenant.
- Agag: The king of the Amalekites.
- King: (Neguś) The sovereign ruler.
- Lord: (Egziabher) The Ethiopic name for God.
- Carmel: A geographical location (Mount Carmel).
- Gilgal: A significant cultic and political site for early Israel.
- Kenites: (Qenēwon) A group related to Moses' father-in-law, spared by Saul.
- Egypt: (Gəbṣ) The land of Israel's former captivity.

# 1 Kings 1 [1 Samuel] — Section 2, Page 37

[Ahi]melech the priest at Nob <note>original: 'ናባባ' (Nababa). A city of priests near Jerusalem.</note> was startled when David came to him. He said to him, "Why have you come alone, and no one is with you?"

<margin>፪</margin> David said to the priest, "The king has commanded me with a word today, saying to me: 'Let no one know anything of this matter for which I am sending you or what I have commanded you.' And as for my young men, I have directed them to a certain place where they are to keep the faith of the Lord. I have separated from them.

<margin>፫</margin> Now therefore, if you have anything at hand, even bread,

<margin>፬</margin> give it to me from what you have." The priest answered David and said to him, "I have no common bread with me, but only holy bread <note>term: 'ኅብስት ፡ ቅዱስ' (Holy Bread). Also known as the 'Bread of the Presence' or Shewbread, which was usually reserved only for priests.</note>; provided that the young men are pure from women, they may eat it."

### 2 Samuel (Second Kings) 6

They told him <note>original: "ይበልዎ" — referring to King David being informed</note>, “The Lord has blessed the house of Obed-Edom <note>original: "አቤዳራ" — Abedara; the Ge'ez rendering of Obed-Edom</note> and everything that belongs to him because of the Ark of God.” And David went and brought up the Ark of God from the house of Obed-Edom into the City of David with <margin>13</margin> great joy. And David played the harp <note>original: "ዕንዚራ" — Enzira; a traditional stringed instrument like a lyre or harp</note> before the Ark; and David was clothed in a striking garment <note>original: "ዘየሀይድ፡ ዐይን" — literally 'that which seizes the eye'; usually referring to the linen ephod worn by priests</note>. <margin>15</margin> And David and all the people of Israel brought up the Ark of the Lord with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet <margin>16</margin> <note>original: "ቀርን" — Qarn; a horn or shofar</note>. <sig>1 *</sig>

## A. NOTES ON THE FOUR BOOKS OF KINGS.

### I. Concerning the manuscripts, based on which this edition of the Books of Kings was made.

For the preparation of this edition of the Books of Kings, we have used eight manuscript codices <note>A "codex" is an ancient manuscript in book form rather than a scroll.</note>, two of which are kept in Britain, two in Frankfurt am Main, and four in the Abbadie library; these will be designated by us with the symbols **B, M, S, R, A, C, D,** and **E**.

1) **B** is the Bruce codex, kept in the Bodleian Library, described by us in the *Catalogue of Ethiopic Manuscripts of the Bodleian Library in Oxford*, Oxford 1848, pages 2–5 under No. III; it was written in the time of J. Bruce <note>James Bruce (1730–1794) was a Scottish explorer who brought many Ethiopian manuscripts to Europe.</note>.

2) **M** is British Museum codex No. I, of a more recent age, described by us in the *Catalogue of Ethiopic Manuscripts of the British Museum*, London 1847, page 1, in which the first and second books of Kings are complete, but of the third only Chapters I–II, 12 are contained.

**S** and **R** are vellum manuscripts from the Rüppell collection, kept in the Frankfurt library. 

3) **S** is of a larger quarto size <note>A "quarto" refers to the size of the book, where the printing sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>, containing 604 pages and composed of three parts: 
*   **a)** the first, pages 1–312, contains the four books of Kings; 
*   **b)** the second contains the twelve Minor Prophets, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Wisdom of Solomon, and Isaiah; 
*   **c)** the third contains the Apocalypse of Ezra and Daniel. 
It was copied in a more recent age, with the pages of the first and third parts divided into two columns, and those of the second part into three columns.

4) **R** is of a very large quarto size, containing 382 pages, in which are contained the four books of Kings (pages 1–151), the two books of Chronicles, the apocryphal Ezra, the canonical Ezra, Tobit, Judith, Esther, the Apocalypse of Ezra, and the *History of the Jews* <note>original Ge'ez: "ዜና፡ አይሁድ፡" (Zena Ayhudd) — This refers to a popular history often attributed to a "pseudo-Josephus."</note>; it is neatly written in a more recent age, with pages divided into three columns.

5) **A** is Abbadie No. 57, described by Antoine d'Abbadie in the *Catalogue of Ethiopian Manuscripts belonging to Antoine d'Abbadie*, Paris 1859, page 68; it is older, written by an Amharic scribe. The leaves of the bundles <note>original Latin: "fasciculorum" — refers to the gathered groups of pages that make up a manuscript.</note> of which it consists were incorrectly joined by the binder; their order should be restored as follows: folios 1–7, 60, 17–24, 8–16, 25–30, 59, 58, 51–57, 42–50, 35–41, 63, 31, 32, 61, 62, 33, 34, 64–118.

6) **C** is Abbadie No. 137, described in the same work <note>original Latin abbreviation: "l. c." (loco citato)</note> on page 153.

7) **D** is No. 197 in the same work, page 198.

8) **E** is No. 35 in the same work, page 42.

Of these eight codices, **A** is the oldest, having been written about four centuries ago; the others are more recent, copied during the last two centuries.

Now, however, we must inquire into the quality of the codices and the version of the text they contain. To explain this question, we believe three types of codices and three types of the version should be distinguished. 

1) **S** and **A** provide the *Ancient* <note>original Latin: "Antiquam"</note> or first version. For the first part of Codex **S**, which includes the books of Kings...

<summary>This page introduces the scholarly foundation for the edition of the Books of Kings, listing and describing eight key Ge'ez manuscripts from European collections used to reconstruct the text. It identifies the manuscripts by age, location, and scribe, and begins to categorize them into different historical versions of the biblical text.</summary>

<keywords>Ethiopic manuscripts, Books of Kings, Ge'ez, James Bruce, Antoine d'Abbadie, codicology, biblical versions, Bodleian Library, British Museum</keywords>

--- Page 864 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly description of the manuscripts used for the Books of Kings, moving from the physical description of Codex S to a comparative analysis of Codex S and Codex A, followed by a discussion of the "Vulgate" Ethiopian recension.</meta>

...although written in a more recent age, it was clearly produced for the use of a more significant church where it would be read publicly. This is evident from the large script as well as the titles frequently inscribed in the upper margins of the pages, which indicate the subject of the individual readings. Furthermore, this part of the codex was written with great diligence, at least from the beginning; toward the end of the book, errors become more frequent. The version contained within it agrees well with that provided by **A**.

Codex **A**, although several centuries older than **S**, is of inferior quality. It suffers from very many errors and gaps, and it contains many word forms that poorly suit the laws of grammar and the linguistic usage of the people of Tigray <note>The author distinguishes between the classical Ge'ez style, traditionally preserved better in the northern Tigray region, and the later Amharic-influenced style.</note>; it also displays very many words written in the manner of the Amharic speakers (such as **ይበል፡** <note>original: "yibäl" for "yibälhu"</note> for **ይበልሁ፡**, **አግቦ፡** <note>original: "agbo" for "agbǝ'o"</note> for **አግብኦ፡**, **ለኩ፡** <note>original: "läku" for "läläku"</note> for **ለለኩ፡**) and other singular styles of writing that shrink from the custom of the Tigrayans (such as **እከይት፡** or **እኪይት፡** <note>original: "ǝkäyt" or "ǝkiyt" for "ǝkit"</note> for **እኪት፡**, **የነቅሃ፡** <note>original: "yänäqha" for "yanäqha"</note> for **ያነቅሃ፡**, **ኢያውሥኦ፡** <note>original: "iyawśǝ'o" for "iyayawśǝ'o"</note> for **ኢያያውሥኦ፡** for **ኢከውሥኦ፡**). When these matters are rightly weighed, it seems one must conclude that this book was quite negligently transcribed by an Amharic man, who was less skilled in the Ge'ez language, from a sufficiently corrupt model. Nevertheless, it has provided us with outstanding assistance in recovering the ancient version. For, with the exception of the errors and corruptions by which **A** is deformed, its text agrees well with **S**. It rarely happens that **A**, and even more rarely that **S**, displays readings that diverge from the other codex and agree with a third version. Whether this happened because readings of a third version were mistakenly mixed into these codices, or because two recensions of the ancient version itself were once circulating among the Ethiopians, is indeed a question, but we lack the resources to solve it. Titles indicating the subject of the leaves and the readings are also written in red in the upper margin of codex **A**. However, the chapters and sub-chapters into which the Books of Kings are usually subdivided in other codices are found in neither **A** nor **S**.

2) The second place is held by **BCD MR**, which provide the *vulgata* <note>The "Vulgate" or common version currently used in Ethiopia.</note> or second version, which now circulates in Abyssinia <note>The historical name for Ethiopia.</note>. This *common* <note>original Greek: *κοινή* (koine)</note> version differs from the older version in almost the same way that the text of **G** differs from the text of **FH** in our edition of the Octateuch <note>The first eight books of the Old Testament.</note>. Its principal characteristics are these:

a) It relies on an emendation of the ancient version made by again inspecting and comparing it with a Greek model. For after the ancient version appeared to shrink more than was right from the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> version—the version thereafter read by the Greeks—whether because of the variety of Greek readings read by the first Ethiopian translator, or by the errors or license in interpreting taken by that first translator, or by the gaps, additions, or other changes that had gradually crept into almost all public and private copies through the negligence of scribes and the injury of time, the Abyssinians, having instituted a revision of their translation, took care to fill the gaps, delete additions, and emend various passages to conform them to the Greek *common* <note>original Greek: *τῆς κοινῆς* (tēs koinēs)</note> models. By whom or by which people, in what century, and by whose authority this revision was instituted is not yet established, but it cannot be denied that it was instituted. This revised version is contained in most of the codices that now circulate among the Abyssinians and are used in schools for instructing beginners.

b) The speech and diction are more polished and brought back to the rules of common speaking and writing usage as it obtained toward the end of the Middle Ages: archaisms are corrected here and there; the clarity of the sense and the continuity of the speech are better provided for by the translocation, addition, or omission of words, names, or particles; a certain consistency in translating individual words has been restored; obscure and more difficult words have been replaced by easier and more transparent ones (though not necessarily more accurate), some things omitted, and others added for the sake of illustration (one may see what we have explained more fully regarding these kinds of emendations in the latter part of Volume I, page 9).

c) The subdivision of the books into **ምዕራፍ፡** <note>original: "mǝ'rāf" (chapter)</note> or **ክፍል፡** <note>original: "kǝfl" (division/section)</note> in those which display the Vulgate version,

<summary>This page analyzes the linguistic quality of Codex A and S, noting the former's Amharic influence and errors. It also introduces the Ethiopian "Vulgate" version, a later revision of the Ge'ez text intended to align it more closely with Greek Septuagint models.</summary>

<keywords>Codex A, Codex S, Ge'ez, Amharic influence, Tigrayan usage, Vulgate version, Septuagint, manuscript revision, Ethiopian biblical translation</keywords>

--- Page 865 ---
<meta>This page continues the analysis of the different versions or "recensions" of the Ethiopic Bible found in various manuscripts. It specifically moves from the "Vulgate" (the common second version) to a scholarly third version corrected against Hebrew sources.</meta>

...is usually inscribed in the manuscripts. The manuscripts mentioned above provide this second version. However, it should not be overlooked that manuscripts **B** and **M** occasionally—and manuscript **D** very frequently—suggest readings from the first version and, much more often, from the third version. For this reason, I am inclined to say that **D** contains a "mixed" version rather than simply the second. Furthermore, like **A** and **S**, manuscript **D** did not originally show a distinction between chapters and sections, but the chapter numbers were later added in the margin by a different hand. Additionally, **D** and **M** occasionally display changes to the text and explanatory notes <gloss>glosses</gloss> which, being clearly reckless, we have chosen not to transcribe in our overview of variant readings.

3) Finally, **E** presents a *third* version, or rather a recension <note>A "recension" is a revised edition of a text based on critical study.</note> of the version, specifically one emended from the Hebrew. There are many places, both in other books and in these Books of Kings, where the Greek Septuagint <note>original: "LXX virorum"—the "Version of the Seventy," the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> differs significantly from the Hebrew text. This occurred either because the Seventy followed different Hebrew readings or a different edition of the books, or because they misinterpreted the Hebrew words, or because the Septuagint version itself was later corrupted in various ways.

Now, the teachers of the ancient Ethiopian Church were neither so isolated from contact with other nations nor so lacking in fervent study of the sacred scriptures that such discrepancies between the two texts could escape them or be ignored. Therefore, we are not at all surprised that they undertook a new revision of their version based on the Hebrew. It can be clearly proven from many passages that this revision was made directly from the Hebrew itself, without any intermediate version (one more closely adapted to the Hebrew) being used. Please compare, for example: 1 Kings <note>In the Ethiopian tradition, 1 and 2 Samuel are called 1 and 2 Kings. Thus, "Book I" here refers to 1 Samuel.</note> Chapter 1:1; 2:28; 7:12; 10:14–16; 14:50; 17:17, 32; 19:13; 20:20.¹)

It appears that the Ethiopic version they corrected from the Hebrew was the ancient one rather than the "Vulgate" <note>The "Vulgate" refers to the common, standardized version used in the church.</note>, because its readings agree much more frequently with the first version than with the second. This version, which we shall call the "Third" or "Hebrew-Ethiopic" version, is found in manuscript **E**. Aside from this codex, we have had no other resource for investigating this version, although it was mentioned above that other manuscripts of ours (especially **D**) occasionally display readings from this third version. However, because **E** was produced with the greatest care, it must be considered most trustworthy and can rightly be said to compensate for the lack of another copy.

Furthermore, this third version seems to have been unable to gain public authority in the Abyssinian <note>Ethiopian</note> Church, and was apparently consulted and used by scholars more than by the laity. This explains why a corrector of manuscript **E**, in almost every place where the third version differs from the second, erased the readings of the (first and) third and wrote the readings of the second either between the lines or in the margin (although the opposite also occurred in a few places: where the scribe of **E** had written a reading from the second version, the corrector noted the third version's reading in the margin or between the lines). For this reason, **E** is of great value, as it contains almost all the readings of both the third and second versions carefully inscribed. Similar to **A** and **S**, **E** also agrees in that no chapter distinction is noted within it; only the chapter numbers have been added in the margin by a different hand.

After the end of the fourth book of Kings in **S** (pages 308–311 and again on two leaves prefixed to the codex) and **A** (folios 118, 119), there is a survey of the kings, priests, and prophets who flourished in Israel from Samuel until the Exile. Additionally, in **S**, a short list <gloss>syllabus</gloss> of proper names found in the Bible is added, along with their interpretations. Both appendices, in a shortened form, are found in **D** and **C** near the end of the fourth book of Kings.

***

¹) Since this is the case, the question regarding the origin of the improved version of the Octateuch <note>The first eight books of the Old Testament: Genesis through Ruth.</note> (**C**), proposed in the latter part of Volume I, page 8, should be reconsidered. I suspect it should be resolved by stating that the version was made not from a Greek, Syriac, or Arabic-Hexaplar text, but from the Hebrew itself.

<meta>This page follows the discussion of the "third version" or Hebrew-corrected recension of the Ethiopic Bible. Equipped with these resources, we could not hesitate as to how we should prepare our edition. We have taken care to print the ancient version, following manuscripts **S** and **A**. Where they differ, we have mostly accepted the readings of **S**, and more rarely those of **A**, noting the alternative reading among the variants. However, we have omitted anything that seemed to rely on obvious errors by the scribes, so that the sea of variant readings would not grow excessively. There were very few places where it was necessary to repair the faults of both manuscripts using the others; we have made such emendations conspicuous, usually by placing them in square brackets [ ]. We have transcribed the readings of the second and third versions in the annotations—almost all of the third, and all of those from the second that seemed to be of any importance. We have used the symbol **E** for the third version (meaning Codex E), and the symbol **κ** <note>original: "κ" for "κοινή" (koine), meaning the "common" or standard version</note> for the second version, specifically where manuscripts **B**, **C**, **D**, **M**, and **R** agree. Where one manuscript differs, we have added "exc." <note>Latin "excepto," meaning "except for"</note> (for example, "except for C or D"); where several differ, we have used the symbols for the individual manuscripts.

In the case of the word *arrow* <note>original Greek: σχίζα (*schiza*), used in 20:20–22 and 36–38</note>, the translator treated it like a proper noun [just as the second translator did not know how to aptly translate the word for *cloak* <note>original Greek: μανδύας (*manduas*) in 18:4</note>, whereas the first translator in 17:38 had correctly translated it as **ልብስ** <note>original Ethiopic: *libs*, meaning "garment" or "clothing"</note>]. Aside from these instances, however, the Ethiopian’s prose is easy to understand and clear. Furthermore, if one considers the work as a whole, it should be regarded as a faithful and skillfully executed version, even if one must freely admit that in individual places the translator erred or rendered the Greek words with less than ideal accuracy.

The following terms were wrongly understood and translated by him: 
6:11 *the votive offering* <note>original Greek: θέμα (*thema*)</note>. 
9:4 *through the mountain* <note>original Greek: δι' ὄρους (*di' orous*), which he likely mistook for δι' ὁρίων (*di' horion*), "through the borders"</note>. 
9:20 *three days old* <note>original Greek: τριταίων (*tritaion*)</note>. 
14:6 *that there is no restraint for the Lord to save*. 
14:14 *with pebbles* <note>original Greek: κόχλαξι (*kokhlaxi*)</note>. 
14:47 *he was allotted the task*. 
15:23 *divination — they bring in teraphim* <note>The "teraphim" were household idols or cult objects</note>. 
16:3 *of the flutes* <note>original Greek: αὐλῶν (*aulon*), likely confused with "courtyards"</note>. 
17:6 *shield* <note>original Greek: ἀσπίς (*aspis*), which can also mean "asp" or "viper"</note>. 
20:20, 36, 37 *to hurl a javelin*. 
20:25 *he arrived first* <note>original Greek: προέφθασε (*proephthase*), perhaps confused with "he approached"</note>. 
20:38 *he gathered up*. 
20:41 *until a great end*. 
21:13 *to feign* and *spittle* and other words. 
23:24 *in the evening*. 
29:5 *they were leading* <note>original Greek: ἐξῆρχον (*exerkhon*), perhaps confused with "they went out"</note>. 
31:2 *they join together* [likewise in 17:20, the word *they changed* was wrongly translated by the second translator, whereas the first had translated it well in 17:52], although some of these errors may be easily excused by the obscurity or complexity of the Greek phrasing.

Many other things, while not translated perversely, were nonetheless rendered less correctly and with insufficient accuracy, such as: 
1:12 *he multiplied*. 
28 *I lend* and *loan* (compare 2:20). 
2:5 *they left the land*. 
2:33 *his eyes to fail and to waste away*. 
3:1 *distinguishing*. 
10:3 *the oak of Tabor*. 
5 and 10 *dance* <note>original Greek: χορός (*khoros*)</note>. 
8:17 *your flocks*. 
10:18 and 12:6 *I brought up*. 
14:8 *we cross over* and *we shall be rolled down*. 
20 *and behold — confusion*. 
29 *he has departed*. 
15:16 *wait* <note>original Greek: ἄνες (*anes*)</note>. 
25 and 26 *return with me* (different in verse 30). 
17:40 *shepherd's — a collection*. 
49 *through the helmet*. 
20:30 *of those deserting*. 
21:6 *the day took them*. 
24:1 *he arose from there*. 
8 *he persuaded with words*. 
25:6 *all that is yours*. 
31 *and this shall not be a loathing and a stumbling block to you*. 
29:4 and 10 *you did not station him there*. 
30:1 *toward the South and toward Sekelach*. 

There are very many places where he deviated slightly from the Greek words, such as 2:30 *it shall pass through*. 3:3 *he was sleeping*. 4:2 *and the battle turned*. 4 *of the seated cherubim*. 14 *the voice of this cry*. 6:3; 6:4 *golden*. 6:7, 10 *yoke [the kine]*. 13 *in the valley*. 17; 19 *they were glad*. 7:1 *they sanctified*. 9:19 *before me*. 24 *hindering* and *break off*. 10:4 *they shall ask you for peace*. 11:7 *amazement*. 12:14 *with the mouth*. 16 *see*. 19 *on behalf of your servants*. 13 *it has become vain for you*. 14:9 *we will stand by ourselves*. 30, 39 *if he answers*. 40 *to the man of Israel*. 42 *it prevailed*. 47 *he obtained the kingdom*. 15:17 *you are small* etc. 18 *until you finish them*. 19 *you rushed* etc. 16:7 *his great stature*. 11 *the young boys have failed*. 20 *an omer* <note>a biblical unit of dry measure</note>. 23 *in his hand*. 17:5, 6 [17 *an ephah*. 21] 36. 18:25 *foreskins*. 19:3; 20:12 *I will inquire — David*. 13, 17. 21:2 *I testify*. 22:2 *he was leading*. 9 *the one set over*. 13 *against me as an enemy*. 17 and 18 *to go to meet*. 23:1 *the threshing floors*. 6 *in his hand*. 13 *and he ceased from coming*. 21 *you have labored*. 26 *being covered*. 25:2 *and it happened in*. 3 *with understanding*. 14 *he turned away from them*. 17 *son*. 20 near the end. <meta>ink blot</meta> near the end. 26:3 *behind him*. 19 *he shall stir up* and *he might smell*. 20 *he pursues*. 21 *and I have been ignorant*. 28:24 *pastures*. 29:4 *he will be reconciled*. 7 *you shall not do*. 30:2 *onto the road*. 10, 22 *they pursued*. 24 *of the one going down*. 

The phrase *his ears shall tingle* was rendered in the same manner as in 3:11 and also Jeremiah 19:3; the word for *trespass* or *guilt* is also usually translated by the word **ኀጢአት** <note>original Ethiopic: *hati'at*, usually meaning "sin"</note>, although in 24:24 this translation is not very suitable. Once or twice he deviated from the Greek words in translating the phrases *and it came to pass* (**ወኮነ**) 1:4, 12, 20, 3:2 etc.; *and behold* (**ወናሁ**) (see the note at 4:13); *to uncover the ear* <note>an idiom meaning "to reveal a secret" or "whisper"</note> 20:13, 22:8, 17; *into the ears* 8:21, 11:4, 15:14; and the words *he leaped up* 20:34, 25:9; *ranks* 4:10, 15:4; *centurion and chiliarch* <note>captains of hundreds and thousands</note> 8:12, 18:13, 22:7; *mediums/spiritists*...

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Ethiopic translation of the Books of Samuel (referred to here as Kings). The previous page discussed specific errors; this page moves into a detailed comparison of the Ethiopic text against the Greek Septuagint, noting where the translator was successful, where he abbreviated, and where he likely had a different Greek source text.</meta>

28:3 and following; **angels** <note>original Greek: ἄγγελοι (*aggeloi*)</note> 19:11, 14, 20; 25:14; **young boy** <note>original Greek: παιδάριον (*paidarion*)</note> 4:17; 25:27; 30:17. Other things, although not word-for-word, he nevertheless translated well, such as: 1:26 **in me** <note>original Greek: ἐν ἐμοί (*en emoi*)</note>; 2:28 **to go up** <note>original Greek: ἀναβαίνειν (*anabainein*)</note>; 9:5 and 14:6 **he will do** <note>original Greek: ποιήσει (*poiesei*)</note>; 19 **bring the hands together** <note>original Greek: συνάγαγε τὰς χεῖρας (*synagage tas kheiras*)</note>; 15:22, 17:21, and 22:7 **sons** <note>original Greek: υἱοί (*huioi*)</note>; 15 **let him give** <note>original Greek: δότω (*doto*)</note>; 24:20 and 29:4 **conspirator** or **adversary** <note>original Greek: ἐπίβουλος (*epiboulos*)</note>; **I will deliver/give over** <note>original Greek: προσδῶ (*prosdo*)</note> 15:6; 27:1 (rendered less well in 25:22; compare 3:17). 

For the sake of brevity, he sometimes omitted words that seemed superfluous, such as: 4:19 **the message** <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀγγελίαν (*ten aggelian*)</note>; 5:2 **and they took** [the ark] of the Lord (compare 5:1); 7:12 **the name**; 14 **of the hand**; 8:8 **the works**; 9:8 **to answer**; 10:1 **not**; 3 **beyond**; 14:19 **going, he went and**; 20 **he went up and**; 28 **he answered and**; 20:18 **that he will be visited**; 26 **that he has not been purified**; 21:13 **of the gate**; 22:19 and 30:19 **from** and **to**; 23:22 **his foot**; 28:2 **chief-**; 30:6 **of each**; 24 **they shall divide according to the same**; 25 **commandment and**. 

Similarly, he everywhere omitted the words **as** and **as if** <note>original Greek: ὡς (*hos*) and ὡσεί (*hosei*)</note> when they were placed before numbers (except in 14:22): 9:22; 14:2, 14; 22:2; 23:13; 25:13, 38. 

Sometimes, for the sake of clarity, he seems to have added certain things or translated more wordily into his own language, such as: 1:11 from the beginning; 1:20 **in the course of time** <note>original Greek: τῷ καιρῷ τῶν ἡμερῶν (*to kairo ton hemeron*)</note>; 1:24 **she took** <note>original Ge'ez: ነሥአት፡ (*nes’at*)</note> (in), and **a measure** <note>original Ge'ez: ወስፈርተ፡ (*wesiferte*)</note>; 6:4 **that there is a fault among you** <note>original Greek: ὅτι πταῖσμα ἐν ὑμῖን (*hoti ptaisma en hymin*)</note>; 8:20 **our war**; 9:2 **mighty**; 13:2 **among those who** <note>original Ge'ez: በእለ፡ (*be’ele*)</note>; 14:22 **formerly** <note>original Ge'ez: ቀዳሚ፡ (*qedami*)</note>; 32 **as they found** <note>original Ge'ez: በከመ፡ ረከቡ፡ (*bekeme rekebu*)</note>; 37 **and he said** <note>original Ge'ez: ወይቤ፡ (*weyibe*)</note>; 15:4 **Israel** <note>original Ge'ez: እስራኤል፡</note>; 16:22 **let him stand**; [17:12 **Jesse**; 18:5 **he understood**]; 18:14 **being with**; 27:8 **in the country** <note>original Ge'ez: በሐረ፡ (*behare*)</note>; 28:2 **for all the days**; 8 **two** <note>original Ge'ez: ክልኤን፡ (*kil’en*)</note>; 13 **they weighed** <note>original Ge'ez: ደለሙ፡ (*delemu*)</note>; 29:3 **backwards** <note>original Ge'ez: ድኅሬተ፡ (*dihrete*)</note>; 6 **to the Philistines** <note>original Ge'ez: ለኢሎፍሊ፡ (*le’ilofli*)</note>; 30:22 **of the spoils**. 

Finally, a few places are to be noted where other words were substituted for the Greek words, either by the translator or by others, such as: 4:19 **she turned** <note>original Ge'ez: ወተመይጠት፡ (*wetemeytet*)</note> instead of **because they returned**; 10:5 **you shall find** <note>original Ge'ez: ትረክቡ፡ (*tirekbu*)</note> instead of **encounters**; 11:1 **Gilead** <note>original Ge'ez: ገላድ፡</note> instead of **Jabesh**; 11:12 **for Samuel** <note>original Ge'ez: ለሳሙኤል፡</note> instead of **to Samuel**; 12:23 **that he might show** <note>original Ge'ez: ያርኢ፡ (*yar’i*)</note> instead of **I will show**; 13:19 **for the Hebrews** <note>original Ge'ez: ለዕብራውያን፡</note> instead of **the Hebrews**; 14:34 **for all** <note>original Ge'ez: ለኵሉ፡</note> instead of **to them**; 14:36 **from here** <note>original Ge'ez: እምዝየ፡ (*emizye*)</note> instead of **here**; 15:6 **they shall kill you** <note>original Ge'ez: ይቅትሉከ፡ (*yiqtiluke*)</note> instead of **I will deliver** (1st person); 20 **because of this I heard** <note>original Ge'ez: በበይነ፡ ዝንቱ፡ ሰማዕኩ፡ (*bebeyne zintu sema’ku*)</note> instead of **because I heard**; 20:3 **is it not** <note>original Ge'ez: አኮኑ፡ (*akonu*)</note> instead of **not**; 21:14 **you did not bring him** <note>original Ge'ez: አያምጻእክምዎ፡ (*ayamts’aikimwo*)</note> instead of **you brought him**; 23:18 **so that they might be reconciled** <note>original Ge'ez: ከመ፡ ተንተሐሉ፡ (*keme tentehalu*)</note> instead of **and they made a covenant**; 27:1 **the King** <note>original Ge'ez: ንጉሥ፡</note> instead of **Saul**; 28:2 **tell me** <note>original Ge'ez: አይድየ፡ (*ayidye*)</note> instead of **you shall know** (or **make known**?); 30:9 **those who followed** <note>original Ge'ez: ወበአለ፡ (*webe’ele*)</note> instead of **the rest** (or **some**?).

### 2) Survey of the readings which the translator had in his Greek copy, which differ from the Holmesian Septuagint text.

1:1 **+ into** [original: *eis*] after **man**. **Eli** [original: *Eli*] instead of **Eliou**. **son of Nasib the Ephrathite**. 2 **to him** instead of **to this**. 3 **+ that** [original: *ekeinos*] after **man**. 4 **on one day**. 5 ∧ [omits] **the things concerning**. 6 **and he did not give**. ∧ [omits] **the things concerning**. 7 **and thus. him** instead of **her**. 8 **you strike your heart**. 9 **Hannah**. **+ he sat** after **priest**. 11 **of a man** or **a man** (instead of **of men**). ∧ [omits] **and** before **wine**. 13 **she** [nominative] instead of **this** [feminative]. 16 **of despondency** instead of **of loquacity**. 18 **+ Hannah** after **said. before** instead of **in the eyes of**. 19 **+ into** before **Armathaim**. 20 ∧ [omits] **of God**. 22 **+ with me** after **the child**. 23 **to the Lord** instead of **the Lord**. 25 **the child** [nominative] instead of **of the child** [genitive]. 2:8 **to him** instead of **to them**. 10 **+ being righteous** after **ends of the earth**. 14 **he let down** instead of **he struck. into the cauldron or into the great bronze vessel**. 15 ∧ [omits] **meat** before **boiled**. 16 **+ indeed** [original: *de*] before **first**. ∧ [omits] **that**. 18 **+ and there was** before **child**. ∧ [omits] **ephod**. 24 **+ not** after **children**. ∧ [omits] **for the reports which I hear are not good**. 25 **he shall pray** instead of **and they shall pray**. 26 ∧ [omits] **was** before **good**. 27 **+ to him** after **said**. 28 **of houses** instead of **of scepters. for food**. 29 **upon my sacrifice** and **upon my incense. in being blessed**. 30 ∧ [omits] **that** before **but rather. he shall be brought to nothing** instead of **he shall be dishonored**. 31 **+ and** before **behold**. 33 ∧ [omits] **to you**. 3:1 **+ and** before **there was not**. 4 **+ saying** after **Lord**. 5 **+ to him Eli** after **said**.

### CHAPTER 2. The Song of Hannah, Verses 1–10, is found in printed form in Job Ludolf's edition of the *Ethiopic Psalms*, pages 325–326; we will note its variant readings under the symbol L.

Verse 1. **And she said:**] Manuscripts E, C, M prefix **And Hannah prayed**. **And my savior:**] <meta>omission</meta> in Manuscript E. **Head:**] **and a head** in all manuscripts except S. **Above:**] [Manuscripts D, M, L] **Upon**. **In your salvation:**] [Ludolf's edition] **In your deliverance**.

Verse 2. **Besides you:**] [All manuscripts except S] add **O Lord**.

Verse 3. **Great things:**] [Manuscripts A, B, M, R] add **words**. **And let not — words:**] <meta>omission</meta> in Manuscript A. **And the Lord:**] <meta>omission</meta> in all manuscripts except S. **Prepared:**] Manuscripts A, M, L. **Work:**] [Manuscripts S, k, L] **Throne**; [Manuscript E] <margin>a throne</margin>; [Manuscript A] **a throne in the heavens**.

Verse 4. **And he made weak:**] <meta>omission</meta> of **and** in B, R, L.

Verse 5. **They lacked:**] [Manuscripts A, R, L] **They were hungry**. **And you — in her:**] [Manuscripts L, C] **And the child-bearer**.

Verse 6. **And he brings down:**] [Manuscripts D, L] **let him bring me down**; [Manuscripts k, E] **he brings me down**.

Verse 7. **He humbles and he**[<unclear>raises</unclear>]**:**] [Ludolf's edition] **He makes me small and he honors**.

Verse 8. **He raises him:**] [Manuscripts B, C, D, L] prefix **who**; [Manuscripts M, R] prefix **and**. **And he turns him:**] [Manuscript A] **and he changes him**; [Ludolf's edition] **and he makes him ripen**. **Great ones of the pe[ople]:**] [Manuscript S] **Great ones of the people**. **Glory:**] [Ludolf's edition] **and glory**.

Verse 9. **For the one who prayed:**] <meta>omission</meta> of **for the one who** in Manuscript S. **Their year for**] [Manuscripts k, L] **the year of**. **For the righteous:**] [Manuscripts C, D, R, L] **the righteous ones**. **But man**[<unclear>is</unclear>]**:**] [Manuscripts M, L] **man**; [Manuscript A] prefixes **man**.

Verse 10. **He makes them sick:**] [Manuscripts k, L] **He makes them weak**. **Those who — among:**] [Ludolf's edition] **And he who boasts, let him boast in the knowledge and understanding of the Lord, in doing justice and righteousness in the midst of**. **He:**] [Ludolf's edition] adds **righteous**. **Ends:**] [Manuscripts A, k, L] **unto the ends**. **Because he**[<unclear>ar</unclear>]**ose**] <meta>omission</meta> in Ludolf's edition.

To this verse, Manuscripts M, D, and C <margin>in the margin</margin> prefix: **And Elkanah went to his house in Ramathaim**. **And she left him:**] [Manuscript k] **And she left him**. **And she returned:**] [Manuscript S] adds **into**; [Manuscript D] adds **into her house**; [Manuscripts B, C, M, R] **And he returned into**; [Manuscript E] **And Elkanah and his wife went**. **Ramathaim:**] [Manuscript E] adds **into his house**.

## CHAPTER 13.

**Verse 1.** Manuscripts A, S, and E; the text is completed as: **"And Saul had been king for two years over Israel"** <note>original: "ወኮኑ፡ ሎቱ፡ ለሳኦል፡ ፪ ዓመተ፡ እምዘ፡ ነገሠ፡ ላዕለ፡ እስራኤል፡"</note> in Manuscript k and Manuscript E in the text. **Verse 2. [And all heard (version A):]** **"In order that he might be heard..."** in Manuscripts B and R; Manuscripts M, C, and D contain both readings, namely **"In order that he might be..."** and **"And all heard."** **[Saying:]** + **"this"** in Manuscript S; Manuscript E reads **"saying this word and they said."** **[Philistines:]** Manuscript S reads **"and the Ali-,"** Manuscript E reads **"those of the Philistines,"** and Manuscripts B, M, and R read **"Philistines."** **[And they shouted:]** Manuscripts A, S, C, D, and E have simply **"and"** (see also Chapter 11, Verse 7). **Verse 5. ### CHAPTER 14

**Verse 6. [Where he was]:** **"Where he was not"** <note>original: "ዘኢኰኖሌ፡ ኀበ፡ አሎ፡"</note> in Manuscript k. **[Because... he lived]:** **"Because God did not fail to save him"** <note>original: "እስመ፡ ኢይስሕና፡ ለእግዚአብሔር፡ አድኀኖ፡"</note> in Manuscript E.

### 4) Index of Chapters for Book I.

In ancient times, the Ethiopians had no division of the text for the four books <note>The "four books" refers to 1 & 2 Samuel and 1 & 2 Kings, often grouped together in the Ethiopic tradition</note>. For this reason, no distinctions of chapters or sections are inscribed in Manuscripts A and S, which represent the ancient version, nor were they originally noted in D and E. Later, the Ethiopians learned to divide the text into *sections* (**kəfəl** <note>original: ክፍል</note>). These are inscribed in Manuscripts B, C, M, and R. Finally, in these recent centuries, the method of dividing the text into *chapters* (**mə’əraf** <note>original: ምዕራፍ</note>) as established by Europeans was also adopted by the Ethiopians. These were inscribed into the text by the same scribes who copied Manuscripts B, C, and R, while in D and E they were added to the margin by a different hand. Where the beginnings of the traditional "sections" align with the beginnings of the modern "chapters," the scribes of those manuscripts containing both usually note only one or the other, rather than both. Furthermore, they are often quite negligent in numbering the sections. Consequently, the total number of sections cannot be determined with absolute certainty from our manuscripts. Their general breakdown is as follows: 1) 1:1. 2) 1:21. 3) 2:1. 4) 2:11. 5) 2:22. 6) 2:27. 7) 3:1. 8) 3:2. 9) 3:19. 10) 4:1. 11) 5:1 M. 12) 6:1. 13) 6:13. 14) 6:15. 15) 6:17. 16) 7:1. 17) 7:2. 18) 7:5. 19) 7:7. 20) 8:1. 21) 8:4. 22) 8:10. 23) 9:1. 24) 9:5. 25) 10:1 M. 26) 10:9. 27) 10:14. 28) 10:17. 29) 10:25. 30) 11:1 M. 31) 11:11. 32) 11:14. 33) 13:1. 34) 13:15. 35) 14:1. 36) 14:24. 37) 14:36.

### 1) Regarding the integrity of the text edited by us and the nature of the translation.

*In the text of the ancient version of this book, several words are found to be corrupt, primarily due to an incorrect reading of the vowels. *The translator omitted the translation of the words:* **of firstfruits** <note>original Greek: ἀπαρχῶν (aparchōn)</note> 1:21; **spring/fountain** <note>original: κρήνην (krēnēn)</note> 2:13 (compare 4:12); **Titans** <note>original: Τιτάνων (Titanōn)</note> 5:18, 22; **of weeping** <note>original: κλαυθμῶνος (klauthmōnos)</note> 5:23; **with a saw** <note>original: πρίονι (prioni)</note> and **of a brick** <note>original: πλινθίου (plinthiou)</note> 12:31; **frying pan** <note>original: τήγανον (tēganon)</note> 13:9; **nebel** <note>a harp or vessel, original: νέβελ</note> 16:1; **pledge** <note>original: ἀραβωνῶνα (arabōnōna)</note> 17:19; **cloak** <note>original: μανδύα (mandya)</note> 20:8 (although he had translated it at 10:4 and 1 Samuel 17:38; compare 1 Samuel 18:4); **club** <note>original: κορύνην (korynēn)</note> 21:16—*he left these untouched in his book as if they were proper names. Rarely does the translator render Greek words more wordily, such as **swift** <note>original: κοῦφος</note> **2:18**. **For the sake of Absalom** <note>original: ὑπέρ ’Αβεσσαλώμ</note> **20:6**. The words **young boy** or **servants** <note>original: παιδάριον, παῖδες</note> **1:5, 6, 13; 2:17; 15:17, 18, 22; 18:7, 9**; **messengers** <note>original: ἄγγελοι</note> **2:5; 3:12, 14, 26** (but differently in **5:11; 11:22**); **commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds** <note>original: χιλίαρχοι et ἑκατόνταρχοι</note> **18:1**, and the expressions **and may he add these things** <note>original: καὶ τάδε προσθείη</note> **3:9, 35; 19:13**; **and behold** <note>original: καὶ ἰδού</note> **1:6**; **to inquire of the Lord** <note>original: ἐπερώτᾶν ἐν Κυρίῳ</note> **2:1; 5:19, 23**; **and it happened** <note>original: καὶ ἐγένετο</note> **2:23; 3:6** [and following]; **from — until** <note>original: ἀπό — ἕως</note> **6:19; 13:22** are translated in the same manner as in the first book (see pages 8 and 9). 

Memorable are the passages at **16:16** and **1 Kings 10:24** **"Long live!"** or **"Long live, let us take the father!"** <note>original Ge'ez: ሕያው (hayāw) or ሕያው፡ አባ፡ ነንሣ (hayāw abbā nansā)</note> and **20:19** **"Capital city"** <note>original Ge'ez: ደብረ፡ሀገር (dabra hagar), literally 'Mountain of the Land'</note> for the Greek **metropolis** <note>original: μητρόπολις</note>, where, leaving behind the Greek words, expressions peculiar to the Abyssinians <note>term: Abyssinians|A historical name for Ethiopians</note> have been inserted; I do not know whether the passage at **6:19** belongs to the same category, where certain things were substituted without the authority of the Greek.

Finally, those places are to be noted where the Ethiopic text has turned away from the Greek through slight changes of individual words, whether made by the translator or by readers and scribes: **upon them** <note>original Ge'ez: በመልዕልቲቶሙ (ba-mal'eltitomu)</note> **1:25**; **and** <note>original Ge'ez: ወ (wa)</note> instead of **that/because** <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note> **5:6, 19** and **17:10**; **Ark** <note>original Ge'ez: ታቦት (tābot)</note> instead of **of the Lord** <note>original Greek: Κυρίου</note> **6:14**; **for/because** <note>original Ge'ez: እስመ (esma)</note> instead of **but** <note>original Greek: δέ</note> **7:19**; **that he might bring us out** <note>original Ge'ez: ከመ፡ታውጽአነ (kama tāwts'ana)</note> for **to cast you out** <note>original Greek: τοῦ ἐκβαλεῖν σε</note> (or perhaps **that he might bring us out**?) **7:23**; **her beauty** <note>original Ge'ez: ሠናያ (sannāyā)</note> instead of **her and her elegance** <note>original Greek: αὐτὴν καὶ τὴν εὐπρέπειαν αὐτῆς</note> **15:25**; **he might destroy them** <note>original Ge'ez: ያጥፍአዎሙ (yātfe'omu)</note> for **a slaughter occurred** <note>original Greek: ἐγενήθη θραῦσις</note> **17:9**; **and your servant, I did not know** <note>original Ge'ez: ወገብርከሰ፡ኢያእመርኩ (wa-gabrakassa iyā'marku)</note> instead of **and your servant and I did not know** <note>original Greek: ወገብርከ፡ወኢያእመርኩ</note> **18:29**; **his children** <note>original Ge'ez: ደቂቁ (daqiqu)</note> instead of **his sons** <note>original Greek: υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ</note> **19:17**; **or** <note>original Ge'ez: አው (aw)</note> instead of **or** <note>original Greek: ἤ</note> **19:35**; **what** <note>original Ge'ez: ምንት (ment)</note> instead of **who** <note>original Greek: τίς</note> **20:11**; **within** <note>original Ge'ez: በውስተ (ba-westa)</note> instead of **the faithful** <note>original Greek: οἱ πιστοὶ</note> **20:18**; **of the supports** <note>original Greek: τῶν στηριγμάτων</note> **20:19**; **those who** <note>original Ge'ez: አለ (alla)</note> instead of **that** <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note> **22:18**; **I have brought to you** <note>original Ge'ez: እምጽአኩ (emts'aku)</note> instead of **he came** <note>original Ge'ez: መጽአ (mats'a)</note> **23:16**; **your city** <note>original Ge'ez: ሀገርከ (hagarka)</note> instead of **your country** <note>original Ge'ez: ብሔርከ (beherka)</note> **24:13**; **the vessels** and **for wood** <note>original Greek: τὰ σκεύη and εἰς ξύλα</note> **24:22**; **for the Lord of Hosts** <note>original Ge'ez: ለጸባኦት (la-tsabā'ot)</note> instead of **for the king** <note>original Ge'ez: ለንጉሥ (la-negus)</note> **24:23**; the changes are more significant at **6:19, 16:10, 19:6**; the most significant is at **21:16**. Furthermore, the person of the verbs or pronouns is sometimes changed: **1:16 (and she said); 9:10, 10:11, 12, 11:15, 16, 12:27, 13:33, 14:7, 12, 16, 18, 15:8, 16:18, 18:17, 31, 19:19, 38, 41, 20:14, 15, 24:1.**

<margin>24</margin> How then can you turn away the face of a single captain from among my lord’s least servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and horses? 
<margin>25</margin> And now, have we come up to fight against this land without the command of the Lord? The Lord said to us: "Go up against this land and destroy it!"' 
<margin>26</margin> Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, and Shebna, and Joah [Josaphat] said to Rabshakeh: "Speak...

<column-break/>

...in Aramaic <note>original: ሶርያ (Sorya) — likely meaning Syriac or Aramaic, the diplomatic language of the time</note> to your servants, for we hear <note>understand</note> it; but do not speak to us in the Hebrew language <note>original: ዕብራይስጥ (Ebrayset)</note> in the hearing of the people who are on the walls." 
<margin>27</margin> And Rabshakeh said to them: "Did my lord send me to speak these words only to your lord and to you? Did he not also send me to the men who sit on the walls, who will eat their own dung and drink their own urine with you?" 
<margin>28</margin> Then Rabshakeh stood and cried out in a loud voice in the Hebrew language and said: "Hear the word of the great king, the King! 
<margin>29</margin> Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you with his words; he will not be able to deliver you from my hand. 
<margin>30</margin> And do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord, saying: "The Lord will surely deliver us, and this city shall not be given into the hand of the King of Persia [Assyria]." 
<margin>31</margin> Do not listen to Hezekiah!' For thus says the king: 'Make peace with me! Come out to me, and everyone shall eat from his own vine and everyone from his own fig tree <note>original: በለስክሙ (baleskemu)</note>, and everyone shall drink water from his own cistern; 
<margin>32</margin> until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and honey and olive oil; so that you may live and not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah when he misleads you, saying: "The Lord will deliver us."'

</columns>

<summary>This page records the psychological warfare used by the imperial envoy Rabshakeh, who mocks Hezekiah's alliance with Egypt and claims that God Himself ordered the invasion. He addresses the common people in their own language, promising them prosperity if they surrender but threatening them with starvation if they resist.</summary>

### CHAPTER 19
And when King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with <margin>1</margin> sackcloth and entered the House of the Lord. And he sent Eliakim the steward, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz. <margin>2</margin> And he said to him: "This day is a day of distress, and of rebuke, and of punishment; for the <margin>3</margin> pains of labor have come upon the woman who is to give birth, but she has no strength <note>A vivid metaphor describing a crisis where a solution is desperately needed but the power to achieve it is exhausted.</note>. the remnant that is left." <margin>5</margin> So the servants of the king came to Isaiah. <margin>6</margin> And Isaiah said to them, "Say to your lord: Thus says the Lord: 'Do not be afraid because of the words which you have heard, with which the servants of the King of Persia have blasphemed Me. <margin>7</margin> Behold, I will send a spirit upon them, and they shall hear news and return to their own country; and I will kill them in their own country by the sword.'" <margin>8</margin> So Rabshakeh returned and found the king fighting against Libnah; for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish. <margin>9</margin> And when he heard concerning Tirhakah <note>original: ታራ (Tara)</note> King of Ethiopia <note>original: ኢትዮጵያ (Ityopya) — Tirhakah was a pharaoh of the 25th "Nubian" Dynasty of Egypt, often referred to as Kushite or Ethiopian.</note>, "Behold, he has come out to fight against you," he turned and sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying: <margin>10</margin> "Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you, saying, 'Jerusalem shall not be delivered into the hand of the King of Persia.' <margin>11</margin> You yourself have heard all that the kings of Persia have done to all the lands, how they utterly destroyed them. <margin>12</margin> Have the gods of the nations delivered those whom we killed? ## 2 KINGS 19

<columns>

[Lord.] And Hezekiah prayed before the Lord <margin>15</margin> and said: "O Lord, God of Israel, who sits above the Cherubim <note>The Cherubim are high-ranking angelic beings whose wings were depicted over the Ark of the Covenant, representing God's throne on earth.</note>, you alone are the Lord over all the kingdoms of the world, and you created the heavens and the earth. <margin>16</margin> Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me; open your eyes and see; and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he sent to mock the living God. <margin>17</margin> For truly, O Lord, the kings of Persia <note>original: ነገሥተ፡ ፋርስ (negasta Fars) — Throughout this manuscript, the Ethiopian tradition identifies the invaders as Persians rather than Assyrians.</note> have destroyed the nations. <margin>18</margin> And they have cast their gods into the fire, for they were not gods but the work of human hands, made of wood and stone; and so they destroyed them. <margin>19</margin> And now, O Lord our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord."

<margin>20</margin> Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah, saying: "Thus says the Lord, the God of your power, the God of Israel: I have heard your prayer which you prayed to me concerning Sennacherib the king of Persia. <margin>21</margin> And this is the word that the Lord has spoken against him: 'The Virgin Daughter of Zion <note>A poetic personification of the people of Jerusalem, suggesting their protected and sacred status.</note> despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head at you. <margin>22</margin> Whom have you mocked, and against whom have you raised your voice? And against whom have you lifted your eyes? It is against the Holy One of Israel, by the hand 

<column-break/>

of his messengers! <margin>23</margin> You have mocked your Lord and said: "With my many chariots I have ascended the heavens and the heights of the mountains, to the peaks of Lebanon; I have cut down its great cedars and its beautiful cypress trees, and I have reached the very heart of the forest. <margin>24</margin> And I rested; I dug and drank foreign waters, and I dried up every surrounding stream and river with the soles of my feet." <margin>25</margin> I have done it and I have brought it to pass; I have made you the one to remove the Avvites <note>original: አዊላውያን (Awilawyan) — Likely referring to the Avvites, a people conquered by the empire.</note> and the mockers from their fortified cities. <margin>26</margin> And those who dwell in them were weak of hand, they were defeated and put to shame; they were like the grass of the field and the green herb, like the grass on the housetops and the scorched field <note>original: ጼዴማ (Tsedema) — An agricultural term for a field blasted by the east wind before it can grow.</note> before your throne. <margin>27</margin> Your sitting down, your going out, and your coming in I have known, and also your rage which you have raged against me. <margin>28</margin> And because your anger has reached my ears, I will put my hooks in your nose and my bit between your lips, and I will turn you back by the way you came.'

<margin>29</margin> And this shall be a sign for you: This year you shall eat what grows of itself from the harvest, and in the second year what grows from that; but in the third year, sow and reap, plant vineyards and eat their fruit. <margin>30</margin> And the remnant of the House of Judah that has survived shall again take root below and bear fruit above. <margin>31</margin> For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and those who are saved shall come from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord shall perform this."

# 2 KINGS CHAPTER 22

<margin>1</margin> Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath <note>Bozkath was a town located in the lowlands of Judah.</note>.
<margin>2</margin> And he did what was right before the Lord, in His very sight, and walked in all the ways of David his father; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left.
<margin>3</margin> In the eighteenth year of King Josiah’s reign, in the eighth month, the king sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, the son of Meshullam, the scribe of the House of the Lord, saying:
<margin>4</margin> "Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, and let him sum up the gold which has been brought into the House of the Lord, which the keepers of the threshold <note>original: መዓልቀሙ (me'alqemu) — referring to the gatekeepers or guardians of the entrance who collected contributions from the people.</note> have gathered from the people.
<margin>5</margin> And let them deliver it into the hands of those who perform the work on the House of the Lord, to repair the breaches <note>original: ቤያቆ (beyaqo) — referring to the cracks, damages, or structural decay in the temple building.</note> within the House;
<margin>6</margin> to the carpenters, the builders, and the masons, and for buying timber and quarried stone to repair the breaches of the House.
<margin>7</margin> However, there need be no accounting made with them for the gold delivered into their hands, because they deal faithfully."
<margin>8</margin> Then Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, "I have found the Book of the Law in the House of the Lord." And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
<margin>9</margin> Then Shaphan the scribe went to the king and brought back word to the king, saying<insert>ly</insert>, "Your servants have gathered the silver that was found in the House of the Lord and have delivered it into the hands of those who perform the work of the House of the Lord."

<column-break/>

<margin>10</margin> Then Shaphan the scribe told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." And Shaphan read it before the king.
<margin>11</margin> When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes <note>Tearing one's clothes was a traditional Near Eastern expression of deep mourning, distress, or repentance.</note>.
<margin>12</margin> Then the king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Achbor the son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying:
<margin>13</margin> "Go, inquire of the Lord for me, and for all the people of Judah, concerning the words of this book that has been found; for great is the wrath of the Lord that has been kindled against us, because our fathers did not listen to the words of this book, to do according to all that is written as their law."
<margin>14</margin> So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, the keeper of the wardrobe <note>original: ዐቃቤ አልባስ (aqabe albas) — the official in charge of the royal or priestly garments.</note>. ## THE CRITICAL APPARATUS. <note>original Latin: "Apparatum Criticum" — A critical apparatus is a technical resource used by scholars to compare different manuscript versions and identify variations in the text.</note>

---

<note>original Latin: "Pars Posterior, Apparatum Criticum" — The Latter Part, the Critical Apparatus.</note>

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS <note>In the Ethiopian tradition, 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings are grouped together as 1-4 Kings. This section corresponds to 2 Kings 25 in Western Bibles.</note>

<margin>30</margin> ...and [he ate] <note>original Ge'ez: በስ (bas) — likely a fragment of the word for "he ate" (ወይበልዕ/wayibel’e)</note> with him continually. And his allowance <term>allowance: ሲሳዩ (sisayu), referring to royal provisions, a pension, or a regular food allotment</term> from the king was given to him daily, for every single day; he received it from the household of the king <note>original Ge'ez: ቤተ፡ ሎ (beta... lo), likely a transcription error for ቤተ፡ ንጉሥ (beta negus)</note> all the days of his life.

# I. Concerning the *manuscript books*, upon whose authority the Books of Kings were edited by us, as well as the *three versions* contained within them, one may see what has been set forth in the first fascicle of this volume and its latter part, pages 3–6.

# II. Notes on the individual books.

## e) Regarding the Third Book [of Kings]. <note>In the Ethiopian tradition, 1 and 2 Kings are referred to as 3 and 4 Kings, following the 1 and 2 Samuel (1 and 2 Kings) sequence.</note>

### 1) Concerning the integrity of the text edited by us and the character of the version.

As with others, the primary version of this book has also not been preserved in the manuscripts in a completely pure and intact state. a) Not only are those passages *corrupted* which we have corrected in our edition and marked with brackets—namely 1, 41; 2, 24; 3^a, 6, 8, 9; apocryphal additions <note>original Latin: "apocr." — referring to sections found in the Ethiopic and Greek Septuagint that are not in the Hebrew text</note> 6, 21; 7, 35; 8, 36, 44, 48, 53, 63; 10, 8; 16, 28, 9; 21, 22; 22, 25, 42—but also others, especially Chapter 4, verses 9–19, where proper names are wretchedly distorted. The following should be noted: 

3^a, 39 **3** <note>original Ge'ez: ፫</note> instead of **2** <note>original Ge'ez: ፪</note>; 
3^b, 13 **in his kingdom** <note>original Ge'ez: በመንግሥቱ፡</note> instead of **among kings** <note>original Ge'ez: በነገሥት፡</note>; 
6, 5 **within** <note>original Ge'ez: ውስተ፡</note> instead of **he is** <note>original Ge'ez: ውእቱ፡</note>; 
6, 14 **with a cord** <note>original Ge'ez: በመሠንይ፡</note> instead of **in bonds** <note>original Ge'ez: በማእሰርት፡</note>; 
7, 31 **he made** <note>second instance</note> instead of **he made**; 
8, 1 **and thus** <note>original Ge'ez: ወከመዝ፡</note> instead of **and after this** <note>original Ge'ez: ወእምዝ፡</note> and **within** <note>original Ge'ez: ውስተ፡</note> instead of **he is** <note>original Ge'ez: ውእቱ፡</note>; 
8, 53 **you created them** <note>original Ge'ez: ፈጠርከሙ፡</note> instead of **you separated them** <note>original Ge'ez: ፈለጠከሙ፡</note>; 
8, 63 **and he slaughtered** <note>original Ge'ez: ወጠብሐ፡</note> instead of **which he slaughtered** <note>original Ge'ez: ዘጠብሐ፡</note>; 
10, 15 **his surroundings** <note>original Ge'ez: ዐውዱ፡</note> instead of **his tribute** <note>original Ge'ez: ማዕደቱ፡</note>; 
11, 20 see variant readings; 
11, 26 **Serya** <note>original Ge'ez: ሰርያ፡</note> instead of **Serera** <note>original Ge'ez: ሰሬራ፡</note>; 
11, 33 **color** <note>original Ge'ez: ኅብረ፡</note> instead of **union** <note>original Ge'ez: ኅብር፡</note>; 
11, 37 **he raised up** <note>original Ge'ez: አነሥአ፡ (incorrect form)</note> instead of **he raised up** <note>original Ge'ez: አንሥአ፡ (correct form)</note>; 
12, 15 **by the mouth of** <note>original Ge'ez: በአፈ፡</note> instead of **by the hand of** <note>original Ge'ez: በአደ፡</note>; 
12, 18 **to Israel** <note>original Ge'ez: ለእስራኤል፡</note> instead of **to Jeroboam** <note>original Ge'ez: ለአዩረብዓም፡</note>; 
12, 21 **he remained** <note>original Ge'ez: ተረፈ፡</note> instead of **after** <note>original Ge'ez: በተረ፡</note> and **22** <note>original Ge'ez: ፳፪</note> instead of **29** <note>original Ge'ez: ፳፱</note> and **the kingdom of Rehoboam** <note>original Ge'ez: መንግሥተ፡ሮብዓም፡</note> instead of **the kingdom for Rehoboam** <note>original Ge'ez: መንግሥት፡ለሮብዓም፡</note>; 
12, 1 <note>apocryphal</note> **16** <note>original Ge'ez: ፲፮</note> instead of **15** <note>original Ge'ez: ፲፭</note> or **17** <note>original Ge'ez: ፲፯</note>; 
12, 34 <note>apocryphal</note> **to Israel** <note>original Ge'ez: ለእስራኤል፡</note> instead of **to Jeroboam** <note>original Ge'ez: ለኢዮርብዓም፡</note>; 
13, 7 **into my house** <note>second instance</note> instead of **and I will give you a reward** <note>original Ge'ez: ወእሁበከ፡ፍትሐ፡</note>; 
(13, 32 **it was** <note>original Ge'ez: ኮነ፡</note> instead of **it will be** <note>original Ge'ez: ይከውን፡</note>?); 
14, 23 **and they set up with them** <note>original Ge'ez: ወአቀሙ፡ምስሌሆሙ፡</note> instead of **and they set up with him** <note>original Ge'ez: ወአቀሙ፡ምስሌሁ፡</note>; 
15, 4 **let his children stand** <note>original Ge'ez: ይቁሙ፡ደቂቁ፡</note> instead of **let him establish his children** <note>original Ge'ez: ያቅም፡ደቂቆ፡</note>; 
15, 7 **among them to** <note>original Ge'ez: ማእከሎሙ፡ለ</note> instead of **between** <note>original Ge'ez: ማእከለ፡</note>; 
16, 18 **and as he burned** <note>original Ge'ez: ወከመ፡አውዐየ፡</note> instead of **he entered the keep** <note>original Ge'ez: በአ፡በአተ፡</note> (?); 
16, 21. 22 **Gotan** <note>original Ge'ez: ጎታን፡</note> instead of **Gonat** <note>original Ge'ez: ጎናት፡, referring to Tibni</note>; 
17, 12 **to you** <note>original Ge'ez: ለከ፡</note> instead of **to me** <note>original Ge'ez: ሊተ፡</note>; 
17, 19 **and he laid him** <note>original Ge'ez: ወሰከቦ፡</note> instead of **upon his bed** <note>original Ge'ez: ዲበ፡ምስከቦ፡</note>; 
18, 18 and 22, 54 **Balaam** <note>original Ge'ez: በለአም፡</note> instead of **the Baals** <note>original Ge'ez: በዓሊም፡</note>; 
(19, 4 **Termen** <note>original Ge'ez: ተርሜን፡</note> instead of **Retmen** <note>original Ge'ez: ረትሜን፡, the broom tree</note>); 
19, 6 **he rose** <note>first instance</note> instead of **he lifted up his eyes** <note>original Ge'ez: አንሥአ፡አዕይንቲሁ፡</note>; 
19, 19 **there** <note>original Ge'ez: ህየ፡</note> instead of **from there** <note>original Ge'ez: እምህየ፡</note>

b) Only *mutilated* fragments remain of the verses in Chapter 11, 20; 20, 15, 16, 18, 33. Other gaps...

c) **Additions**, several of which are minor, have been mixed in with the genuine words:
**1:2** "to David" and "he became warm"; **1:10** "their"; **1:24** "prophet"; **1:36** "and" before "he makes"; **1:50** "before"; **2:20** "now"; **6:20** "pure"; **7:46** "which is within" (second mention); **8:10** "all"; **8:33** "to your name" (instead of "to you") and "in this"; **9:4** "in righteousness and" and "in all days"; **10:12** "in the land"; **10:26** "their" in the word for "refugees" <note>original Ge'ez: ፈላስያን — usually "strangers" or "sojourners"</note>; **10:27** "and like the trees of Cyprus"; **11:22** "you shall go from my country"; **11:43** "he was buried"; **15:18** "to David" (second mention); **15:22** "all" (first mention); **16:7** "who were"; **17:16** "they did"; **18:40** "to the false prophets"; **19:20** "vessel"; **21:8** "that country"; **21:27** "on account of that word from before the Lord"; **20:14** "they were before you and" and "prophet"; **20:24** "without you"; **20:27** "into their valley"; **20:30** "into the city of Aphek"; **20:38** "bandage"; **20:39** "to the king" (second mention); **20:42** "that prophet"; **22:22** "and he did"; **22:36** "and he cried out and wrote."

Certain other things that seemed barely tolerable we have enclosed in parentheses (), namely Chapter 2:11; 8:65; 10:26; 15:27; 16:26. Furthermore, **transpositions** of individual words, and more rarely of individual sentences, are found; these are minor in 1:2, 19, 25, 28, 32; 2:31; 3ª:16 (apocryphal); 5:1; 6:27; 7:22; 8:65; 16:9; 18:45; 21:5, 15; 20:3; 22:35; while more significant transpositions occur in 11:5 and 20:29.

*The character of the version is roughly the same as that observed in the preceding books of Kings. The translator rendered the Greek words mostly faithfully, and at times even elegantly, and the vast majority of the version he produced is clear and transparent. However, in those sections where this praise cannot be granted, the blame seems to lie less with the ignorance of the Ethiopian translator than with the obscurity of the Greek text: I am speaking especially of the sections describing the buildings constructed by Solomon, the temple vessels, the administration of the kingdom, and so on. The foreign terms provided by the Septuagint could not but be adopted untouched by the Ethiopian, such as 5:11 "machata" <note>likely a dry measure</note>; 6:7, 33; 7:7 etc. "ailam" <note>the porch or vestibule</note>; 6:9, 16; 8:6 etc. "dabir" <note>the inner sanctuary or Holy of Holies</note>; 7:13 and following "mechonoth" <note>the stands or bases</note>; 19:4 "rathmen" <note>broom tree</note>; other things he was unable to express in Ethiopic due to a lack of native words, such as the names of plants.*

It concludes that the Ethiopian translator was generally faithful, but struggled with technical architectural terms and obscure botanical names found in the Greek Septuagint.</summary>
